On a delightful peak of the Himalayas, frequented by gods and asuras,
the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, was seated comfortably in that place.
Bowed down by the lords of the gods and asuras, and worshipped by the siddhas and gandharvas,
the goddess, with her palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
The Goddess said:
By your grace, I have heard the knowledge arising from all the sense-faculties.
What is that Vidyā of the Sākinīs which destroys the destiny of the Daityas?
"In this terrible age, she who has attained perfection is the dispeller of all doubts.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Formerly, O Gaurī, in the most dreadful Karavīraka cremation ground..."
O fair-faced one, I was propitiated by the goddesses during the sacrifice for the sake of worship;
having fashioned you into a beautiful form, I placed you there.
The sixty-four crores of Sākinīs and others, who possess great power,
bestow a share of the sacrifice upon their own kinsmen once the *caru* has been prepared.
O blessed lady, I sport and wander for as long as it takes another day to pass; meanwhile, they are exceedingly intoxicated with passion.
"O Blessed One, please grant me the sacrificial oblation (caru) in its proper sequence and in brief.
I replied, "I have nothing; I am a skull-bearer (kapālī), naked as the sky."
"Always dwelling in the cremation ground, I have no kinsman anywhere. Laughing, they said to him, "Indeed, you have one in Tripurāntaka."
Family traditions are not to be violated, yet we are your servants;
therefore, we shall enjoy this most excellent and supreme body.
"I have already spoken; receive their portions without hesitation.
Whichever portion of the sacrificial pap (caru) you take, upon that shall my head rest."
Having seen that [the world] was utterly deluded, overwhelmed by your face,
and falling into extreme confusion, I remain here at Karavīraka.

Thus having become *uḍḍāmarī*, she forgot her own body;
there, O Great Goddess, she was seized by powerful *sākinīs* through great force.
Then, having taken the nectar that had been consumed,
when he was in a state of motionlessness, the mantra known as *tadvitta* arose from him.
Relying upon the supreme samādhi, the mind is fully established therein;
from the heart arises the Goddess, the bringer of joy to the world.
Having the form of a sleeping serpent, endowed with vibration and bliss,
she is partless in her central portion and possesses a radiance like the fire of time.
She is known as Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī; on the wheel she is Kālāgnibhairavī. She is the foundational support for the life-force, abiding as that supreme digit (kalā).
Pervading all beings, she has attained both unity and multiplicity;
she is the one supreme and inferior power, solely intent upon devouring the universe.

The Full Moon (Pūrṇimā) is to be known as fulfilled; she is remembered as the essence of reality (sattva). She is the peaceful one, both supreme and non-supreme, tranquil, beyond the void, and stainless.
O Goddess, you are Lakṣmī consisting of great splendor, comparable to ten million rays;
you are stainless and partless, yet possessing a manifest, non-material form.
The Great Goddess has five faces, ten arms, and is endowed with fifteen eyes; she is white in color and stands upon a great corpse.
Situated in the midst of the eight measures (mātrās), she is the Siddhi-yoginī worshipped [therein];
gentle yet fierce through the power of recitation, she conforms to the desire of the practitioner.
With her gaping mouth, she licks the world, which has been scorched by her flames;
by the force of her repeated breaths, she causes even the great mountain ranges to tremble.
In some places there is destruction, in some he may be provoked to anger, in some he withdraws all beings;
in some he creates, and in some he protects—he proceeds according to his own independent will.
The goddess has a cow-face, is adorned with ornaments, and is decorated with the lord of serpents;
she holds a noose and a goad, and her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
In his right hand he holds a sword that causes the agitation of the three worlds;
in his left, an extremely fierce khaṭvāṅga, and in his right, an excellent trident.
Others [beheld] a fierce ravine filled with the blood of the three worlds;
likewise, others saw a head, both shaven and with hair, drenched in blood, lying there.
In her left hand, however, she holds a divine flask filled with great jewels;
this one is known as Pratyaṅgirā, born with a body that dwells in the sky.
Pervading the universe through both her singular and manifold forms,
the Goddess, with a delighted mind, spoke everything in a supreme voice.
For the sake of that [purpose], the gods performed the great sacrifice known as the Ḍāmara;
its divisions and sub-divisions number ten million, O daughter of Nanda.
O Goddess, this *Pratyaṅgirā* is the *Siddhilakṣmī* in the *Jayadratha*;
she is the *Jhaṃkārabhairavacaṇḍāśivā* in the *Kulaḍāmara*.
The Goddess said: O Blessed One, O God, Lord of Gods, whose crest is adorned by the moon;
by your grace, O Lord, may I [attain] the meditation that is to be meditated upon according to its true meaning.
"Now I wish to hear about the supreme recitation of the mantra-purification.
Bhairava said:
"O blessed lady, I know the mantra residing in the heart according to its true nature."
I shall speak without doubt when urged by you,
on a level and pure plot of ground smeared with saffron water.
There, one should spread out the Mātṛkā, the supreme mother of all mantras,
whose form is unseen, who is peaceful, and who has emerged from Śiva, the ultimate cause.
But the supreme power, though bodiless, has arisen as having the form of a body;
there, that which is called the *golaka*, whose nature is consciousness and whose form is a star, has arisen.
Having attained the state of *dhvanibindu* by means of the form of sound born from that, there arises,
O Sovereign of the Gods, the production of *nāda* and *rasvara* from the *bindu*.
Then, O lady of excellent hips, the auspicious Mātṛkā was born from the Svaras and Anuṣṭubh;
joined with the Kūṭas, she pervades fifty distinct varieties of letters.
That which is supreme among the supreme and subtle, residing within the vital breath and auspicious—
that is the womb of all mantras, the seventeenth digit, the supreme.
O fair-faced one, the power of will (icchā-śakti) arises from the supreme ether;
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is the sequence of the bindu, which is declared to have action (kriyā) as its purpose.
Then, O beautiful one, Prāṇa is the form of the Sun, Apāna is the Moon;
Samāna is to be known as Varuṇa, and Udāna is Pāvaka (Fire).
Māyā is said to be the binding of all the joints of the limbs;
the leader of the aggregate (piṇḍanāyaka) has arisen in two and fourfold ways.
He is the agent of the creation and dissolution of the world of moving and non-moving beings;
thereafter, O fair-faced one, the *pūraka* [breath-retention] is performed, joined with the weapon-mantra.
Having again extracted the end, one should join it with the beginning of the void;
then one should extract the fifth, the first of the third, and that which ends with *sa* and begins with *ta*.
O Ambikā, [the mantra] is joined with Graṃthīśvara, possesses a multitude of teeth-colored [syllables],
is endowed with all the nine [tattvas], and is adorned by the syllables u-du-ru-ccha-ra-bhū.

O Dear One, the first [syllable] of the last [group] is joined with the cloud (the letter *ma*); then, from the void (*ri*), the first [syllable] is given. At the end, one should give the first and last words joined with the teeth (thirty-two) and life (one).
One should join the face of Śiva, which is conjoined with the *veda* (the letter *va*) and endowed with the *bindu*;
having joined its beginning and end, one should apply the great power of the King of Weapons (*astra*).
O beautiful goddess, the King of Weapons (astrarāja), situated within the nectar of the Vedas and the fire, accompanied by the five dots and the bindu, should be applied in the prescribed sequence.
One should place another *repha* between these two sequences;
O Dear One, when joined with seventeen syllables, they remain as the *Iḍrāvikā*.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra], O beautiful one, for the garland-mantra (mālāmantra):

Then, having joined the *mahāśaṅkha* in the same manner as before,
one should join the *haḍḍamaḍḍa* and thereafter the *abala*.
Just as one who knows the tracks finds the elephant's footprint,
so too, having known the tracks, one likewise finds the footprint of the Teacher.

by her, who is of stainless form, Sadāśiva is eternally manifested.
Śiva is directly the form of sound, devoid of both difference and non-difference; may he, who abides in many places and is endowed with the three states, ever release that eternal sound for you.
This very one is the Lord of the Supreme, whose nature is sound, for he is imperishable;
he is the all-pervading Master, by whom this [universe] is capable of being produced.
This [element] also arises from Īśvara and is endowed with the qualities of sound and touch;
its agent is Śiva, who is peaceful and endowed with all causal qualities.
When that state arises, I am manifested there, adorned with the form of a woman; I am the agent of creation and dissolution, established indeed in the Supreme Will.
By me also was Viṣṇu, endowed with four qualities, emanated,
protecting indeed the entire world within this cycle of existence characterized by refuge.
From its navel arose a lotus-stalk as soft as fine silk;
there Brahmā was born, having his being composed of the five elements.
Then a battle arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu for the sake of the cause of creation;
[each thought], "I shall be the creator," while Brahmā and Viṣṇu likewise [thought the same].
O Pārvatī, being enraged, I severed his head;
O Great Goddess, he too became furious upon seeing Viṣṇu standing above him.
Brahmā, accompanied by great wrath, was red in color and terrifying;
by those very [beings] were men raised up, handsome and endowed with his prowess.
O Dear One, all of them possess impenetrable armor, universal forms, and great strength;
mounted upon swan-chariots, they number ten million times ten million times ten thousand.

indeed, all those created then were true, O you who are worshipped by the hosts of gods.
Now I shall correctly proclaim the *mālā-mantra*:
one should draw the sky (*vyoma*) in the center of the dissolution of the moon, sun, and fire.

This very essence of syllables and the circle of the Yoginīs' hearing do not have authority within a man; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Mother of the Gaṇas.

and likewise the word *namaḥ*, followed by *nityoditānandananditāyai*.

the first Vidyā, joined with the pair at its beginning and end, and endowed with the Māyā at the conclusion.

Having taken the Lord of the World (bhuvanādhipati), which is endowed with the void (śūnya) and the letter ya,
one should place it at the end of that, making it the King of Letters (varṇarāja) of great power.
Having extracted that drop of desire situated on the third seat,
one should join it with the word "namas" and unite it with the great mantra.
The state of the supreme *paramahaṃsa*, likewise the bestower of the path to *nirvāṇa*;
the state that pacifies the onset of calamities, and likewise the state of tranquility.
Likewise, it is the state that crushes all evils, misfortunes, and afflictions;
likewise, it is the state beyond all calamities, and likewise, it is the crossing over the ocean.
O Goddess, crusher of all enemies, come!
[The mantra consists of] two *hasa*s, followed by two *valgata*s, and then "nararudhirāntra."
The word *vasā*, the word *bhakṣaṇi*, the word *mama devi*,
then the word *svaśatru*, and likewise the word *marda marda*.
"Khāhi khāhi," and likewise the word "pada," and "triśūlena pada" as well;
"bhindi bhindi" twice, O auspicious one, and again the word "pada" with the sword.

One should apply the entire mantra first, then the other [mantra] with the words "fulfill my desires," and likewise the supreme [mantra] in two ways.

likewise the word "entire" (*sakala*) and the word "O Mother of Mantras" (*mantramāte*).

should be given, followed by the title "Mahākālī."
I shall also describe another [mantra], the sound *kālanāśini*;

"Prasīda," O Goddess of Gods, followed by the term "Madanāturasamjñakam."
O Supreme Goddess, one should likewise form the letter *Ā* joined with the *bindu*;
having joined the word "Kuru" in two ways, as well as the words "Sura" and "Asura."

one should extract the eight mantras in reverse order.
Then, O Dear One, one should cause the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha, known as Bindu, to be made;

living beings of various forms who are devoid of devotion and hostile toward their gurus [are overcome].

Likewise, the goddess Pratyaṅgirā was pinned down by Jayadratha;

When the intellect (buddhi) is dull, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is weak, and the six organs are inactive, yet it is not distinct from the manifest (vyakti), that is proclaimed as the elephant-life-force (gajājīva).

O Goddess, through the vision of that, one goes beyond the state of being born from many wombs.

otherwise, there would be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of births.
Therefore, having performed the sacrifice with every effort,
one should display it after constructing a four-cornered city adorned with four gates.

beyond that, one should draw an auspicious sixteen-petaled lotus.
Being well-composed, he colored the pure,

she is this Pratyamgirā, O blessed one, pure as the movement of the moon in consciousness.

she is the mother of sound (nāda), the companion of the vital breath (vāyu), and follows the path of both the eternal and the non-eternal.

situated between Fire, Sun, and Moon, she is the creator of the world.

pervading from calamity to the very core of yoga, she is established throughout the universe.

meditation, the arrangement of the mandala, and the six limbs of the retinue.

in a previously mentioned pure place, free from wicked beings.

the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be equal in measure and possess three ridges (*trimekhala*).
One should draw [the design] with chalk for the purpose of fueling the fire;
one should perform the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and cause hymns and sounds to be made.
Beating, sprinkling, and thereafter scraping;
heating, serving, wiping, and finally smearing.
The four crossroads and the gambling hall—these are your ten [sites].
Worship should be performed at the pit (kuṇḍa), and you should indeed prepare a seat (viṣṭara) in the center.
Then Vāgeśī, having bathed after her menses, should go northward toward the summit of Mount Iṣa;
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, one should worship her with offerings of water for the guest (argha), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth.
First, the bringing of the fire; immediately thereafter, its placement;
then the wrapping, the striking, as well as the sprinkling and the raising up.
The immortalization of the mantras, their worship, and the veiling—
these ten [rites] are performed outside the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), while eight are situated within the pit.

The rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), and the formal declaration of intent (vaktra-saṃkalpaṇa) must be performed; this constitutes the purification of the mouth (vaktre-niḥkṛti).
O beloved, after the sequence of the departure and the sequence of birth, as well as the sequence of the emergence from the mouth,
one must perform the purification of the mouth and likewise the purification of the name.
The teacher must perform exactly eighteen sacraments;
beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *nāma*, they should be performed within the heart and not externally.
Then the goddess Vāgeśī, having honored [the deity] according to the ritual rule,
should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire as well as the rite of making [the deity] face [the practitioner].
The offering of a garment, a seat, worship, and the enclosing sticks should be performed;
the Lords of the World are to be worshipped according to the sequence starting from the east.
Having worshipped the fire in the consecrated vessel, one should worship the jar with the Astra-mantra;
the propitiation and worship of the fire must be performed especially.
One should purify the *śruk* and *śruva* ladles with the weapon-mantra while they rest upon the *upayāma*;
thereafter, the twelve consecrations (*saṃskāras*) are performed until the [substance] is well-melted within the vessel.
First, however, there is the heating over the fire (adhiśravaṇa), as well as the secondary heating (upādhiśravaṇa);
then the leaping-up and the immersion, followed by the smearing with collyrium and the inspection.
One should worship the seat of the Goddess and worship within the auspicious maṇḍala;
then one should place the Goddess, whose form is immortal nectar, within the fire.
Then, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with goats, honey, clarified butter, and other offerings;
the three-sectioned mantras (trikhaṇḍās) should be recited one hundred and eight times, followed by libations of food in the tenth part of that number.
The full stream (pūrṇā) should be performed; thereafter, one should cause the formal announcement (vijñapti) to be made:
"O Mistress of the Gods, by your grace, let the initiation be commenced once again."
Emerging from the cavity of the fire of time, that supreme *kalā* rested in the circle of the navel,
trembling within the hollow of the heart.
Divine and supreme, yet possessing the curved form of a serpent,
there is a certain goddess residing within that [power], who brings about the destruction of the bonds (pāśa).
She stands between both the moon and the sun; she is honored by both the moon and the sun.
She is firmly rooted in the moon, the sun, and fire; she is the devourer of the moon, the sun, and fire.
And she who holds a great and fierce hand shall enter into her own essential nature;
then, O auspicious one, she arises as light—she is that supreme digit.
Indeed, by means of the power of the mantras being transferred and through the path of the Fourth (turya),
there is no distinction whatsoever regarding the body of initiation for that disciple within the Three Principles (tritatva) of the Lord.
In the purification of all time-periods, one is not yet liberated from existence;
the performance of the binding of the thread and other rites is prescribed according to the previously mentioned rule.

The placement [of mantras], purification, the petition by the disciples, and immediately thereafter the cutting of the topknot; then the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the union [with the deity], and the ritual bath.
The request [for initiation] is made through worship, along with the entrustment of the disciple to others and the granting of blessings;
this applies to the recipient of consecration (abhiṣeka), the one bound by the pledges (sāmayika), the spiritual son (putraka), or even the practitioner (sādhaka).
O beloved, one should perform the rites with the qualified person in due order, and not otherwise;
I shall now describe the city and the forest, as well as the treasury of rituals, exactly as they exist.
Having risen at dawn, at midday, or at the onset of night,
one should indeed recite this vidyā one hundred and eight times day after day as a practitioner.
Devoted to the recitation of this vidyā, one obtains all desires;
becoming auspicious, one shall possess an inexhaustible lineage of progeny.
Having recited the mantra one hundred times over cow-gallstone mixed with human gallstone, one should apply a tilaka-mark on the forehead; whoever sees it shall be brought under one's control.
Having placed the white Siddhārthakavaca at a temple of the deity at dawn on the fourteenth day, one should cause the worship of the Goddess to be performed.
O Goddess, one should place it in the mouth; thus one shall obtain victory in debate with others.
Having kindled a fire from a Caṇḍāla with wood produced from the Khadira tree, [one should proceed].
Then, on the ground, the practitioner of the vidyā should write [the name] with his foot placed upon it,
while the practitioner is possessed by wrath.
Having prepared a stake of *khadira* wood for a thousand years,
provided with the blood of a goat and covered with flesh, one who is absorbed in meditation shall cause [the target] to be deluded.
When the period of sleep has passed without cause, one should bring [the substance] to the principal temple;
having taken the ashes of the funeral pyre together with a thread of donkey's hair.
Having cast [the mantra] into the army with the mantra recited one hundred and eight times,
one should immediately worship it at the site of accomplishment in the fire of the *ucchiṣṭa* valley.
By not obstructing the ears during the twilight hours, one obtains natural clairaudience; one should drive away any being present in that place and worship the right limb [of the deity].
Having fully understood the auspicious and the inauspicious, O beloved, one attains [the goal] in the third [state];
thereafter, with a concentrated mind, one should go to the cremation ground on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Having released her that night, he— fearless, pitiless, and self-conceited,
smeared with funeral ashes, naked, and eager for devotion— departed.
O beautiful one, the messenger (dūtī) who has come from the left, endowed with the marks of a daughter,
should there prepare the mandala with powdered bone.
Having concentrated on the primordial sacrifice through the consumption of great flesh, blood, and so forth,
one should then invoke the Goddess by means of the application of mudrās, and not otherwise.
Kindled by the wind and other elements with the moon and sun as fuel,
the great and fierce [fire] arising from the *kanda* is fanned by the suns of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
The yogi, established in the state of friction, should rub away the internal impurity;
by means of the upward flow of the path, he should raise up the supreme arising.
When uttered but once, no universal agitation arises;
rather, O Goddess, it becomes the uprooter of hair and causes the fettered ones (paśus) to fall in an instant.
This goddess Pratyaṅgirā, once bound by [this mantra], arises against others;
she destroys thousands of murders of embryos and even the sins of killing Brahmins.
It reduces bondage to ashes, just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree;
it reveals the assemblies of sky-faring goddesses (khecarīs), treasures, and elixirs.
By performing the recitation one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite, one gains access to Pātāla and Rasātala;
likewise, one achieves the disclosure of secrets, the destruction of armies, and the slaying of enemies.
Paralysis, eradication, and even the immobilization of armies—
let these be accomplished through mantra, as well as [the neutralizing] of poison from Khārkhoda, whether stationary or mobile.
O Goddess, other afflictions such as fever and the like,
when employed by others in many ways, perish through this [mantra], and those who are liberated from them are numbered in the thousands.
By the power of Pratyaṅgirā, everything is accomplished by the practitioner;
this supreme secret has not been told by me to anyone.
It should be guarded with great effort, like wealth from thieves;
it must not be given to another's disciple, just as exclusive devotion [is withheld].
If [the recipient] is ill-disposed toward his guru, deceitful, and possessed of lust and greed, the donors go to hell; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, the ritual procedure for Śrī Pratyaṅgirā, in the glorious Tridaśaḍāmara Mahātantra consisting of thirty-four thousand verses; the *Pratyaṅgirā-kalpa* is completed.
Oṃ, homage to the illustrious Caṇḍakāpālinī!
The Goddess said:
O Śambhu, from what I have heard, the Āgamas indeed exist in many ways;
yet the ignorant mantras, fallen into the defects of oral transmission, are utterly destroyed.
O wielder of the trident, explain the *prastāra* (the grid) for the sake of the various causes of the impure, obstructed, broken, and destroyed mind of knowledge.
How and by what means is the Great Goddess Siddhilakṣmī, who has emerged from the five mountains,
established as the seed-syllable?
O Bhairava, I desire to hear that through your grace;
O Śambhu, I am well-pleased, so please dispel my delusion.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, this which you have asked is more secret than the secret;
it has not been declared by me even to Brahmā, nor to Viṣṇu, nor to Indra.
It has not been told by a god, nor by an asura, yakṣa, gandharva, kinnara, or nāga, O blessed lady; how much less so by a human being?
Listen, O Goddess, to this great secret which you have asked about;
I shall fully explain that supreme expansion of the Vidyā.
A *vidyā* that lacks a *prastāra* is impure and corrupted by its speaker;
for the sake of various purposes, one should extract the *mantra-prastāra*.
On a level stretch of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
smeared with cow dung and perfumed with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
Facing the east, the preceptor, having smeared himself with white sandalwood paste,
shall wear white garments and be adorned with white ornaments.
Having tied a white flower to his head and filled his mouth with camphor,
he held a pure, soft, and clean cotton cloth in his right hand.
O lady of excellent complexion, having carefully held the goddess, one should draw [the mandala];
one should cause a cord of twenty-four finger-breadths to be made for the four directions.
One should carefully divide the treasure-store located in the east, west, north,
and south directions into eleven parts across the four quarters.
Indeed, there are one hundred and twenty-one squares;
O Goddess, listen with a one-pointed mind as I describe how to erase [the grid] in their midst.
O Goddess, one should diligently erase one, two, three, four, or five [squares] situated in the corners of the grid, located in the northeast, southeast, south, west, and northwest.
Between the eastern and southern [sides], one should erase three by three squares according to the division of the diagonal-wing from the temple of the prāsra.
O Varārohā, by this path, the remaining [squares] should be protected by Rakṣa, Māruta, and Śūlabhṛt;
one should erase the seventy-two boxes.
O Goddess of excellent complexion, fifty [years] remain;
O one with the beauty of the moon, in the east and south are the lakes, and in the north-east are the leaders, the Moon and Fire.
And one [arrow] alone, held by the wielder of the noose, stands in the direction of the qualities;
while liberation and the worlds abide in the regions of wealth.
O son of Cālā, the chambers situated in the middle are equal in number to the universe (thirty-five),
and they take on the shape of a pond with four gates.
Situated at the midpoint of the rising [horizon] lies the Malaya mountain to the southeast;
it stands to the east of Mount Meru, in the direction of the Lord who holds the noose (Varuṇa).
O lady of excellent complexion, situated between Mount Kailāsa, that gentle realm of Lokāloka stands; O beautiful one, it is the joyous enclosure where the vision of the rising [sun] is established.
O fair-faced one, the number of pleasure-chambers situated in Malaya and other regions is immeasurable;
O Goddess, there is Nandapura of Meru, and likewise Lokāloka.
O Supporter of the Earth, all the square compartments of Kailāśa are established in sequence;
they are known as the five mountains, and one should place the Mātṛkā within their midst.
In the southeast, northeast, and northwest, one should write three syllables each, starting from the east and proceeding to the north, beginning with the first letter of the Mātṛkā.
One should write the letters beginning and ending with that central square of the letter *ha*;
one should write the half of the letter *ha*, the letter *va*, and the remainder of the letter *ha*.
One should write the letter *kṣa* below the letter *śa*, and write the letter *ja* at the beginning of the letter *jha*;
one should write the letter *u* above the letter *ai*, and write this [letter] at the end of the letter *a*.
One should write the letter *ca* below the letter *ṭha*, and the letter *cha* below the letter *jha*;
one should also write the letter *śa* above the letter *ja*, and extract the letter *jha* from the beginning.
One should write the letter *tha* in the middle of the long *e*, and the letter *ṭa* in the middle of the long *o*;
at the end of the long *o*, one should place the letter *tha*, and the letter *dha* situated upon the upper arm.
One should write the letter *ya* in the middle of *śava*, and the letter *va* in the middle of *jas*;
the letter *ma* in the middle of *ṣaḍa*, and the letter *reha* situated in the middle of *daśa*.

One should write the letters beginning with Śa and ending with Ya in the upper part; those beginning with Cha and ending with Bha in the lower part; and the letters beginning with Ṭa and ending with Tha, along with Ṇa and Ḍha, in sequence.
O Daughter of the Mountain, having written the letter *dh* half-way through and the letter *th* at the beginning,
place the letter *l* in the middle of the latter [group] and the letter *h* between the *pa* and *va*.
One should write the letter *bha* situated between *va* and *ma*, with the letter *sa* at the beginning and end;
this arrangement is the great and highly secret "Five Mountains" (*pañcācala*).
In the midst of that, O Great Goddess, daughter of the Immovable One (Acala), she who is renowned as Siddhilakṣmī resides; listen with a one-pointed mind.
The letter situated above the nasal (ṇa), adorned with the vowel *mī*, is called the "Primordial Praṇava"; by its mere recollection, it removes all sins.
Having taken that which stands at Lokāloka and that which stands on the path of the letter *dha*,
one places [the former] below it, situated in the middle of the six, adorned with the letter *dha* as its initial.
On Kailāśa, it is situated in the middle of Hara; at its front, it is located in the middle of the fruit;
it is occupied by the letter *ra* in the position of the head; and at its front, it is situated in the middle of dissolution.
One should draw the letters beginning with *ra*, undivided from the *Meru* and so forth;
having joined them with the eight *Lokāloka*s, they are placed in the middle of *ra* and in front of it.
The eighth syllable should not be separated from the middle;
having extracted the letter at the end of *kha*, it is the seventh on the mountain of sunrise.
The supreme seed-syllable of peace is conjoined with Meru and the others, preceded by the letter *dh* with a dot (*bindu*) above it, and united with Lokāloka and the rest.
One should place the syllable *vaṃ* in the middle of *vam*, and likewise the syllable *raṃ* in the middle of *ram*;
then, joining them in the sequence of *i* and *ṇa*, one should place the word of salutation (*namaskāra*) before that.
Having written the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh [syllables] of this [mantra], along with ignorance (avidyā),
one should arrange them in sequence, joined with the syllable *ḍoḥ* above and *malaya* and so forth.
The syllable *auṃ* in the middle, the syllable *daśa* (*da*) in the middle, joined with *meru* (*ma*) and the first of the sequence (*ā*);
then the eleventh letter of the Vidyā, followed by *namaḥ*, and then again [the same].

One should write the ever-risen state (nityoditā) below and above, adorned with the moon; having extracted the first letter beginning with 'ra', it should be marked with a dot (bindu) below and above.

The *ditā* (the letter *i*) and its *pada* (the letter *u*) are placed before it; it is situated in the middle of *iḍā* (the letter *ī*) and the middle [of the *pada*]. O Goddess, this [mantra] consisting of thirty-two syllables has been extracted with great effort.
One should draw [the letters] situated in the middle of dissolution in Kailāśa, and those for eating in the mountain of sunrise;
one should draw the solitary ones situated in the supreme middle of Kailāśa.

The station of the wheel of the family (kulacakra) is in the eastern half above; the two digits (kalā) are situated in the middle of the speed, joined in the sequence of two and three, beginning with the letter Kha and endowed with the supreme digit (parakalā).
The letter situated after *ra* (ṛ), joined with the upper part of the letter after *ṭha* (ṭha = ḍha);
[the letter] situated in the middle of *va* on Kailāśa (kailāśe = ke), and the sixth [vowel] on the Mountain of Sunrise (udayācala = u).
One should extract the vowels *pa*, *pha*, and *ma* from their respective middle positions, as well as *ta* from its front position, alone;
then *au*, *ṇa*, *ra*, and *i* from their middle positions, joined in sequence.

The letter *cha* above, joined with the digit of the lunar day (*tithi-kalā*), and the letter *e* at the end above, standing alone; the letter *kha* at the beginning, joined with the supreme digit (*parakalā*), and joined with *parā* in the middle of *ga*.
On Kailāśa, it stands in the middle of Hādi, adorned at the beginning by Meru;
it stands above Dhā, situated in the middle of Rā, and is pierced by the middle of Iḍā.
O Goddess, one should join the letter beginning with *ra* situated between the vowels (*auṇa*),
followed by that which is situated between *ra* and *ma*, and ending with the letter *ta*.
Having extracted the first syllable of the Vedas (A), place the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) before it;
then [place] the navel (Ū), the two places (AU), space (M), and the head (Ā), along with the sixth vowel (Ū) conjoined with the supreme digit (Anusvāra).
One should extract the letter *da* mounted upon the letter *pa*, joined with the letter *ma* at its head;
then, before that, one should utter the letter *ca*, followed by *kroṃ namaḥ*.
Having written the first syllable of the Vidyā and the middle of *gava*, one should extract the middle of *thala*;
O Goddess, one should further extract the six [syllables] from the middle, which are entirely distinct.
Having written "nisiham" in reverse order, O Goddess, daughter of the twice-born,
he extracted [the syllables] up to the end of Lokāloka and established them positioned upwards.
Having written the syllable beginning with *ta*, unmixed with that beginning with *ma*,
one should then write the word "Mārgadevi" situated at its tip.
O fair-faced one, having first drawn only the letter *la* situated in the middle,
one should unify it within the *ga* and the *pa* in the center.
On Kailāśa, in the middle of the *phala* syllables, at its end, one situated in the midst of the *go* syllables,
mounted upon the tenth *madhyāsa*, with the word *śama* before it.
In the center of *hara* is the center of *ura*, which is the supreme center alone;
it is mounted upon the first letter and half of *kha*, ending with *da*, accompanied by the bearer of the noose (*pāśabhṛt*).
The letter situated in the middle of *auṇa*, joined with the seat of the buffalo, is the word for misfortune and affliction; it is the first among the fires, and is also [the first] of the vowels.
The letter *dha* joined with the upper *pāśa*, the letter *ra* alone without being split,
the letter *la* conjoined with the supreme *kalā*, and the head (*mastaka*) pierced by the letter *ra*.
It consists solely of the letter *ga* situated in the middle of *go*, joined with the supreme digit (*parakalā*),
with the letter *ṣa* in the middle and the letter *va* in the middle, and it is not pierced by the letter *i*.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should draw the letter ending in the visarga, adorned with Meru in its center, and the word "taraṇi" (the sun) before it.
Having extracted the middle of *raha*, the middle of *uma*, and the end of *vada*,
joined with *tara* and *u* at the beginning.
In the regular and reverse order, adorned with the letter *ra* at the end,
the syllable situated in the middle of the fruit is consecrated by the first *meru*.
Having extracted the first *malaya*, which is purely the upper and lower [parts],
one should utter it doubled from the triad and draw the *hasat* in its proper place.
One should utter the syllable situated in the middle of the fruit, followed by the one situated in the supreme middle before it;
below that, one situated in the middle of the sky-dweller (khaga), doubling each of the two.
Lokāloka stands above, situated on Kailāśa in the middle of the tenth;
having written it as situated in the middle of the *thala*, it is positioned below the middle of the *aka*.
The letter situated at the end of the visarga, adorned with the vowel *i*,
followed by the final letter of the dentals joined with the supreme digit (*parakalā*), and conjoined with the one following *mī*.
O Goddess of the Gods, the *taraja* is written there, with the fruit situated in front of it;
the syllable situated between the *pha* and *bha* is adorned with *malaya* and so forth.
Having uttered *Bhakṣiṇīmada*, [one places] that which is situated in the middle of the six in two locations:
in Kailāsa, situated in the middle of Hara, and positioned below the middle of the fruit.
The letter *ha* alone, with the vowel *o* in its middle and that same [vowel] at its tip;
below that, the letter situated between the tenth and the middle [consonant], endowed with the dot (*bindu*) and the sixth vowel.

Having written the letter situated between the sixth [consonant] and the vowel *ra*, with the letter *ra* above it; and having written the letter beginning with *ga*, located in the second position, adorned by the letter *ma* and so forth.
The syllable situated in the middle of the moon, adorned with the [vowel] of Varuṇa;
having uttered both of these twice, one should then utter the word "triśūla."
On Kailāsa, one should place the Lord (Īśvara) in the state of Kha (the void), marked by the Bindu;
having raised it from below the Visarga, it is adorned at the beginning by Meru.
Having uttered [the mantra] twice for each of the two, one should write "Chindhī" in two places;
[the syllable] situated between *Bhaya* and *Madhya* should be alone, and it arises from *Bhūdhara*.
One should sequentially join the center of *aim* with the center of *kha-gha*, and *ai* above;
[then] *auṇa* is situated below and above the *loka-aloka*, in the middle of that and in front of it.
Having joined it with *ma*, *la*, and so forth, one should write the letter ending in *ṭha* along with its vowel;
having uttered three [syllables] doubled, one should cut [the sequence] and write it doubled again.
One should write the mantra word by word until the end of the visarga;
having written the words in reverse order, one should accomplish the rite by writing them twice over.
In the middle of the *gava* and at its front is the middle of the *thala*, situated in the middle of the six;
these three syllables are pure, while the *kaṇi* is from the reverse order of the vowels.
The middle of *va*, the middle of *kha-gha*, and likewise the middle of *pha*;
at the tip of that [the letter *ma*] situated in the middle of *auṇa*, differentiated by the third vowel (*i*).
Having extracted Mahābhairava, which is situated on the sixth vowel of fire (the letter *ra*),
it is placed alone in the middle of *ga* and endowed with the supreme digit (*kalā*) following the *dodha*.
The middle of the *thala* [group], from *ḍha* to *ḍha*, both pierced by Īśvara;
together with the *tara-ja* [letters] and the Īśvaras, that which follows them is situated in the middle of *tha-dha*.
One should shake, run, and erase the middle of the *vaha* and the middle of the *phala*;
O lady of beautiful hips, if one extracts the vowels alone, they are [the *kevala*s].
The lords should extract the [syllables] marked with *krānta* (the visarga) from within the *auṇ* vowels, joined with *e*;
likewise, those in the middle of *hara*, the middle of *ura*, and the middle of *para*.
The three vowels alone, followed by the half-moon marked with a bindu,
the letter *au* (the middle of *uṇ*), the letter *da* (the middle of *daśa*), and joined with the upper part of the letter *ba* (the front of *dor*).
One should form [the syllable] joined with *ma* and *la*, situated below and endowed with the *visarga*;
on *kailāśa* (the letter *ka*), one should place *ga* in the middle and bestow *agni* (the letter *ra*) below it.
One should write the letters beginning with *tā*, *dyā*, and ending with *cha*, followed by the letter *va* above *dha*;
O lady of excellent hips, these are the letters numbering five, each standing alone.
At its tip is that which stands in the middle of *auṇa*, situated below the middle of *hara*;
at its tip is that which stands in the middle of *para*, pierced by the middle of *iṭ*.
Having written the letter ending in the anusvāra, one should place the letter beginning with *ai* above it;
this is joined with the letter situated in the middle of *pha*, which resides in the midst of the fruit on Kailāśa.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should draw [the syllable] joined with the letter beginning with *i* (i.e.,
*ya*), standing alone in the middle of *bha* and *ḍha*, ending with *sa*, and adorned with the letter beginning with *ḷ* (i.e., *la*).
The food is joined with the power of another (parakalā), and the musical instrument is differentiated by Īśvara;
one should write this first seed-syllable before it once again.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should draw the solitary [syllable] situated in the center;
having written it with the visarga at the end and the upward stroke, it is adorned by the first [syllable].
The letter situated between *va* and *ha*, followed by *dh* with the suffix *ūrdhvaña*; then, conjoined with the third *kalā*, listen further above that, O beloved.
Mounted upon the sixth kalā at the end of the vowel *sā*, adorned by the head of the sky (*vyoman*),
one should perform its threefold utterance when the mountain arises.

Having written *pra*, *sīda*, *mada*, *nā*, *likhya*, *oṇa*, with the middle [letter] and the one situated above [the *o*], having extracted the foremost splendor (*agra-tejas*), and adorned it with *malaya* and so forth.
Having extracted the syllable *khā* ending in *da*, and the two [syllables] situated on the seat of *u*;
having uttered both of them doubled, one places the syllable ending in *ra* preceded by *u*.
Make the tamed [letter] joined with the power of another, resonant, and situated in half of the void;
it resides in Kailāśa in the middle of the tenth, while mercy moves in the middle of *uṇ*.
It encompasses the worlds and the non-worlds, half-darkness, Kailāśa, and the Īśa;
it is the food of the sky, pervaded by the supreme digit (parakalā), and adorned at its summit by the void.
The consonant joined with Lokāloka and others is situated at the crown of the head;
on Kailāśa it stands in the middle of the tongue, and below that is the bearer of oblations (Agni).

Having extracted the final letter (ha) endowed with the nāda, bindu, and kalā, which is distinguished by the Lokāloka [mountain] and other [features], and which resides upon the seat between the letters u and jha.
One should place it at the summit of the sky; this destroys all [evils] from the very beginning.
On Mount Kailāśa, at its peak, is that which is established together with its own color.
Having written the letter ending in 'a' (a) at the top, one should write both [the letters] in three places:
the letter ending in 'la' (la), which is the seat of Hara, and the letter ending in 'sa' (sa) situated in front.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should make both [the practitioner and the deity] holders of the staff while reciting this mantra;
O illustrious lady, this vidyā is renowned as Siddhalakṣmī.
At the end of the syllables, all of them together amount to two hundred and ninety.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic practice has become fruitful.
O Śambhu, O Bhairava, by your grace I have today heard the Great Vidyā;
now I desire to hear the supreme ritual assignment of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).
By the mere placing of which all accomplishments are produced.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O illustrious goddess, to that which you have asked.
I shall tell you, without doubt, what kind of deposit it is;
listen, O Goddess, for this has been declared by the vidyā known as Siddhalakṣmī.
The thirty letters beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *ha*, minus ten, [consist of twenty letters];
one should place the first eleven of those letters on the eastern face.
One should place those numbering nine (Nanda) in front of him, and those numbering twelve (Bhānu) on the faces toward the south; one should place those numbering eleven (Rudra) on the western face.

And for the upward-facing [face], O Goddess of gods, one should place the mantra ending in "namaḥ" upon the face according to the sequence of the number of syllables, starting from twice the number of syllables in the grass-mantra (tṛṇākṣara).
This is declared to be the placement of the face; now listen further regarding that which is before it:
[the placement] on the eyebrows, the navel, the face, and likewise in the left and right nostrils.
One should place each syllable in sequence upon the left and right eyes, the left and right ears, and the linga and its base.
One should apply the twelve syllables from the eyebrows and feet up to the navel;
[the deities] Ṛṣi, Aṅga, Diśā, and Viśva [are assigned] to the heart, the secret place, and the crown in sequence.
From the heart-mantra up to the weapon-mantra, there are syllables according to their respective numbers;
likewise, the suffixes *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* occur at the end.
I have taught the Mantra-yāna; one should apply it at the end of the six limbs.
The syllables "acalābdhiyuga" (442) are for the invocation and the seat of the preta.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should employ [the mantra] in the sequence of the destruction of enemies;
[the deity is] named Kapālarudra, and the khaṭvāṅga consists of the universal syllables.

One should know the trident (śūla) as eightfold; one should place the sword (khaḍga) as seven syllables. The noose (pāśa) is said to have six [syllables], and the goad (aṅkuśa) by the number of the seasons (six).
One should place the number of islands by means of nineteen *varada* [fingers];
likewise, there are one and a half *muṇḍas*, five *camasas*, and fifteen *svarṇas*, as well as fifteen *ghaṇṭās*.
The Astra-weapon is said to consist of syllables; now hear the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands:
one should place eight syllables on the index fingers and eleven on the middle fingers.
The ring finger is called Agni; for a girl, there are twelve syllables [on the fingers], seven syllables on the thumbs, and three on the palms of the hands.
O Dear One, this is declared to be the Kara-nyāsa; one should join it with the word "namaḥ" at the end. One should place the syllables in the womb, the navel, the heart, and the head.
O illustrious one, this nyāsa, free from error, has been described.
Now I shall explain the procedure for the worship of the deity in due order.
By the mere knowledge of which the goals of Dharma, Kāma, and Artha are accomplished—
having performed the ritual bath, O lady of excellent hips, one should wrap oneself in a clean garment.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should fill the argha vessel with water using the weapon-mantra;
thereafter, the gatekeepers are to be worshipped with the water and flowers from the argha vessel.
O lady of excellent hips, O auspicious one, hear from me the mantra for the observance:
one should form the syllable situated below the letter *ṭa* and joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
O beloved, place that which stands in the middle of the *jaya* before it, making it twofold;
join the first part with the supreme digit (*parakalā*) and likewise endow it with the *bindu*.
Oṃ: the letter situated in the middle of *ta*, beyond the middle of *oṇa*, the syllable located in the middle of *ra*, pierced by the middle of *iḍha*.
The phoneme situated between *a* and *ka*, and likewise that which is between the sixth and *ma*;
one should then place the visarga at the end—thus one should extract this phoneme.
O Goddess of the gods, O lady of excellent complexion, one should worship with effort using this mantra the right side of the top of the door-post with the *ga* syllable.
Having extracted the word *kṣetra*, one should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) at its beginning;
having written the word *kṣetrapāla*, one should utter "namas" at the end, O Dear One.
O Goddess of the Gods, with this mantra, one should worship Kṣetrapāla on the left side of the door, using water for the arghya offering mixed with flowers.
Having written the word *pada* for the threshold with the *praṇava* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end,
one should daily worship the threshold and then enter the sacrificial hall.
Having extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ) and so forth, [place] the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) before it,
and the Lakṣmī-bīja (Śrīṃ) before that, ending with "namas" for the Mothers of the Directions (digmātṛ).
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the eight directions with this mantra;
having extracted the Praṇava (Om) at the beginning, the Māyā (Hrīṃ) syllable is placed before it.
Having written "Ādhāra-śakti," then again the word "Padma-āsana," and then the word "Nātha" before it, [one writes] the seat of one's own self.
There, O Goddess, the excellent sage himself sat down above,
having contracted the *ādhāra-śakti*, which possesses a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
At the navel of the palate, the heart, and the throat, one should pierce [the centers] according to the sequence of the stations of the *ājñā*;
with diligent effort, bring about dissolution in the *dvādaśānta*.
O Goddess, one should always contemplate the supreme nectar-essence flowing [downward];
having caused it to flood the body, one then becomes the Goddess herself.
Then, having worshipped the *argha* vessel with the root-mantra, O Sovereign of the Asuras,
the worship of the vessel is performed according to the sequence of the *aṅganyāsa*, ending with the word "namaḥ."
O beloved, make it completely full with substances prescribed for its own class;
and having formed the mudrā consisting of nectar, perform the display of the vessel as well.
Having snapped your fingers three times, effect the expulsion of obstacles;
these are declared to be the worship of the vessel. Listen further than this, O beloved.
Having uttered "Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīpada," one should write "to Ānandabhairava" ending with the syllable "Phaṭ"; then, having written the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should write it before [the name].
Having written the seed-syllable of Śrī (ŚRĪM) three times along with the *visarga*,
one should write the nectar of the goddess Surā, and then write the *dhama* and *māyā*.
O Goddess, one should perform the purification with this mantra;
having written the name of every enemy, one should then add the word "pramathani."
Having written "Astrāya Phaṭ," the purification of the materials is performed by this mantra;
O Goddess, the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must then be performed with great care.
One should fill the breath through the left [nostril] and then perform kumbhaka (retention) in the same manner;
one should exhale through the path of the sun (the right nostril) and slightly contract the rectum.
Join the Śakti with the state of Śiva; place it upon the tip of the tongue.
O Goddess, this internal sacrifice has been described, free from all delusion.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus, complete with filaments and a pericarp;
outside of that, one should carefully draw a sixteen-spoked [wheel].
One should visualize the Preta situated within the pericarp and the Goddess seated upon him,
endowed with ten arms and indeed five faces.
She has thirty-six eyes, resembling pure crystal;
her form is like the jasmine flower and the moon, adorned with necklaces and anklets.
O lady of excellent countenance, the trident, the gesture of granting boons, the bell, the khaṭvāṅga staff, and the noose— these are said to be the weapons held in the left arms.
The goad, the gesture of fearlessness, the shaven head, the sword, and the alms-bowl—
these were held in her right hands for the purpose of slaying the asuras.
One should meditate on that form as established within oneself and install it within the pericarp;
with honors such as the invocation and other rites, one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
One should prepare incense, lamps, perfumes, the water-offering vessel (arghapātra), and so forth;
thereafter, one should perform worship upon oneself by means of the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The previously mentioned Jvālapālas are on the left and right, with those in the center;
Gaṇeśa and Kṣetrapāla are the third, located at the threshold.
The Guru, the Paraguru, and likewise the Parameṣṭhin;
the Pūrvācārya as the fourth, and Ādisiddhi as the fifth.
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, the Goddess always ascends;
one should recite the five gurus, beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should commence the worship of Śakti:
*Kaṃ Ṭaṃ* to Kamalākarṣaṇī, who bears a staff and a lotus-stalk.
Krodhinī, Vajriṇī, Chedinī,
and Kapālinī— these eight Śaktis, joined with Hrīṃ, Śrīṃ, and the Praṇava (Oṃ), end with the word "namaḥ."
One should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Indrā and ending with Īśā, upon the eight petals;
O Pārvatī, listen now to the specific procedure for the sixteen-petaled great lotus.
To Caṇḍā and Pracaṇḍā, as well as Subhadrāmukuṭī,
the one named Lambā, Bhūridhārā, Marutā, and Suvarṇabhā.
Guhanāsā, Jvāladāyī, Vitālā, Guhakā,
as well as Manodhyakṣā, Apracaṇḍā, Khaḍgālā, and Phetkāriṇī.
One should worship the sixteen [deities] according to the previous sequence;
thereafter, O highly fortunate goddess, one should worship Vaṭuka in front.

Having written the word "devi" (O Goddess), then the word "putrapadam" (the state of being a son), and having again written the word "vaṭukanātha" (Lord Vaṭuka), one should utter the words "ehi ehi" (come, come) and "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa" (take, take).
Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, beginning with these and ending with Svāhā, the worship of Baṭuka follows from this point; having written "Kṣetrapālāya," one should again write the words "ehi ehi."
"Accept the offering, accept it, svāhā! Oṃ kṣāṃ, etc., ending with svāhā.
This is indeed the offering for the Kṣetrapāla; now hear the offering for all beings (sarvabhūta).
One should extract the word *devatebhyaḥ* first, followed by *yoginībhyaḥ*; then, having extracted *baliṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa*, one should place *hrīṃ śrīṃ* at the beginning and end with *svāhā*.
This is indeed declared to be the offering for all beings (sarvabhūtabali), free from error;
it should be given in the northeastern direction (īśāna-digbhāga) as the destroyer of all calamities.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Extraction of the King of Mantras" according to the *Śrīsiddhilakṣmīmata*, within the expansion originating from the Five Mountains in the Great Tantra, the *Śrīkālikulasadbhāva*.
Oṃ, homage to the goddess Śrī Pratyaṅgirā!
The Goddess said:
O Supreme Lord, whose crest is adorned with the essence of the flowing stream of nectar;
O Blue-throated One, mounted upon the bull, bearer of the Gaṅgā, Great Lord!
To that goddess Pratyaṅgirā of yours, who destroys the fear of the three worlds and effortlessly neutralizes the spells and malevolent incantations of others.

She brings about peace and nourishment, she is pure, and she devours the malevolent planets and epilepsy; she pacifies spirits and vetālas, and she destroys the effects of sorcery and the khārkhoda poison.
It is common to all, formidable, the destroyer of all calamities,
the bestower of all prosperity, most excellent, and the giver of all good fortune.
When she is correctly realized, her sovereign power proceeds perfectly;
within the belly of the world, there exists no other knowledge more terrible than hers.
O Mahādeva, [I shall describe] her who is indeed known as Viśvanāyikā through [your] grace.
Śrī Bhairava said:
Listen, O Lord of Heroes, for this wonderful secret is now revealed to you who are bowed in devotion.
It destroys the fault of all confusion, annihilates all calamities,
slays all enemies, and crushes wicked poverty.
O Goddess, this incomparable rite, which has never been told before,
[should be performed] in a pleasing, pure, well-concealed place endowed with the proper characteristics.
In a place abundant with the fragrance of fine incense and smeared with sandalwood and agallochum,
the practitioner of the Mātṛkā-mantras should spread them out and perform the worship in the proper sequence.
Then one should extract the Vidyā that destroys the fear of the three worlds,
having first extracted the "Illuminator" (Dīpaka) accompanied by a salutation.
One should likewise offer salutations to the state of all accomplishments and to the state of the Yoginīs;
furthermore, one should again offer salutations to the state of all accomplishments.
Having extracted the word *mātṛbhyaḥ*, then utter the word *namaḥ*;
likewise, [add] the word *nityoditānandapada* and the word *naṃditāyai*.
The word "sakalanāmānam" (the name of all) is proclaimed as that which follows;
having joined the word "cakrapadam" (the wheel-word) to "kule," one should likewise join the word for the "nāyikā" (the mistress).
After [the word] *bhagavatyai*, one should again utter the word *caṇḍa*;
one should then give the word *kāpālinyai* in the same manner as the preceding word was extracted.
One should first extract that which is declared by fifty-six syllables;
then, having extracted three words, the word "ḍambara" follows immediately thereafter.
Furthermore, Sadāśiva should be given together with the Haṃsa and the Aṅkuśa;
having formed it with the Bindu as its stalk, one should fashion the Kuṇḍala joined with the Yoni.
Joined with the *golaka* (the sphere), it again brings about the destruction of all [karmic bonds];
joined with the third foot and adorned with the *bindu*.
One should join the Praṇava (Oṃ), the word "karttana," the syllable Vahni (Ra), and the Bindu (M) together in one place;
then the word of salutation (Namaḥ) should be added, for this is the illuminator of the Great Mantra.
The word "parama" (supreme) should be given, as well as the term "haṃsinī";
the phrase "bestower of the path to nirvāṇa" should be given, which is the most excellent of all excellences.
One should first join the word *viṣamopaplavapada* with the word *praśamani*,
then add *amṛta*, and finally give the word *kala*.
One should again bestow the word joined with *durita*, *ariṣṭa*, and *saṃkleśa*; likewise, one should join the word *pada* with *dalani*, and the word *sarvā* with *pada*.

In the same way, O Goddess, one should again utter the word "Aṃbhodhitaraṇi," followed by "Punaḥsakalaśatrukaṃ," and then the word "Pramathani," after which one should give the word "Padaṃ. Again, O Goddess, one should give the word "Śabdaṃ."
Having joined "āgaccha āgaccha," make it twofold;
having joined the two steps of "valga," one should again give the word "nara."
One should join the words "rudhirātravasā" (blood and fat) and likewise the word "bhakṣiṇī" (eater);
then one should utter the word "mama" (mine), the word "sva" (one's own), and the phrase "śatrunmardda" (crusher of enemies) twice.
Having placed the *khāhi-khākhi* step and likewise the trident step,
one should join them by saying "bhiṃdicchiṃdi dvidhā" (split and cut in two) and then extract [the mantra] again with the sword.
One should apply the word "strike" twice and the word "cut" twice,
continuing in this manner until one reaches the word "mine," after which one should speak that word.
One should say "sakala-saṃjña" and grant the word that fulfills all desires; for accomplishing [the goal], one should give double the word known as "parama-saṃjñita."
Likewise, for the compassionate one, there is another [mantra]: "Bhagavati.
Furthermore, the word "Mahā" should be given, known as the term "Bhairava."
And another word, *rūpadhāriṇi*, followed by the first word of the thirty [goddesses];
then the word *vara* should again be given, and likewise the word *namitā*.
Furthermore, the word "sakala" (all), as well as the words "mantramātāḥ" (mothers of mantra) and "praṇatā" (prostrated),
should then be followed by the word "jana" (people).
O Supreme Goddess, one should employ the word "Vatsale" (O affectionate one);
O Goddess, one should give the word "Mahādevi" (O Great Goddess), and then again give the word "Kāli."
Having joined the word *kālanāśani* with the word *pradīpaka*,
and having added the word *mahānila*, which was bestowed by Brahmā, [the mantra is formed].
Marked by a *golaka* alone, let the *piṇḍa* be divided into three parts;
thereafter, the word "be gracious" (*prasīda*) followed by the word "afflicted by love" (*madanātura*).
Above this, there is a crescent moon marked by a dot on its head;
one should then join the word *kuru* in two parts, followed by the words *sura-asura*.
Having extracted the word *kanyakā*, one should then extract *ḍaṃbara*;
[this becomes] *varuṇānta* (the letter *va*) joined with *ḍaṃbara*, adorned with the fire-seed (*ra*) and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
The giver of all glory and countenance, which brings about great enjoyment,
is Kālānala, the Great Haṃsa, adorned with the half-moon and the Bindu.
By joining the word *bhīma* in three ways and appending the wife of Fire (*svāhā*),
this supreme Vidyā is extracted, which bestows happiness, good fortune, and liberation.
Two hundred and ninety-one syllables have been extracted;
this is the Great Vidyā known by the name Trailokyamohinī.
Lakṣmīśvarī is remembered as the great beloved who bestows all good fortune;
O Goddess of gods, in this stream there is no other equal to her.
It should be known as the subduer of misfortune, the crusher of wicked poverty,
the pacifier of strife and evil dreams, and the destroyer of all calamities.
It pacifies royal calamities and shatters wicked demons;
it is effective in the most terrible forest of thieves and amidst the perils of lions, tigers, and other beasts.
In difficult terrain, in dense forests, in fire, in fear born of spirits or epilepsy,
and in the horrors of sorcery or battle, one should always remember Gaurī.
Remembered but once, this [knowledge] burns away a flood of sins like a heap of straw;
it has been proclaimed by the knowers of Brahman as that which destroys this terrible world.
O Goddess, even a killer of a guru, a killer of a father, a killer of a mother, or likewise a killer of an embryo,
is liberated from sins such as the emergence of [defective] lingas by reciting this but once.
It is traditionally taught that she liberates one from sins, including the great sins (mahāpātaka), the minor sins (upapātaka), and likewise the king of sins (pātakarāja), even if committed but once.
Endowed with fortune, he shall become illustrious like a lordly elephant intoxicated with rut;
O Goddess of Gods, by circumambulating [this] foot even once, one becomes the most excellent among all.

O Goddess of the Suras, by reciting this three times in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, it becomes equivalent to performing ablutions at all sacred fords extending to the seven oceans.
The Goddess shall become one who has bathed at sacred fords; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By means of seven oblations, she becomes auspicious and is initiated into every mandala.
O auspicious one, by ten recitations a son will be born abundantly;
by twenty-seven recitations, he is known within the circle of the Mothers.
This practitioner, a heroic king, just like the leader Bhairava,
shall himself become like Bhairava through fifty recitations.
There is nothing that he does not accomplish, and there is nothing that he does not achieve;
he can always destroy shackles, bolts, and mechanical devices with ease.
O Goddess, by performing this at the three junctions of the day for seven days, there is no doubt that one will certainly be released from bondage, even if bound by Time itself.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should cast a stream of *śakti*;
wherever it falls, O Great Goddess, there shall be the bursting of fetters.
One should likewise paralyze or release the mechanisms of boats and carts;
having recited [the mantra] seven times over sand and scattered it, one shall ward off calamities.

Having recited the mantra seven times over black mustard seeds, the preeminent practitioner, filled with wrath, strikes whichever [being] he wishes— whether it be a ghost, an epilepsy-demon, or consumption.
It quickly destroys each respective [affliction], and thereafter one no longer remembers it;
even quartan fevers and the like are destroyed by reciting it just once for seven repetitions.
They are turned back by this sprinkling; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Likewise, diseases such as epilepsy, convulsions, and various types of boils are likewise [warded off].
O Goddess, in the same way, one may destroy [the obstacle] with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times;
having consecrated excellent water with the mantra twenty-one times, one should [use it] with the hands.
To whomsoever that mantra is given by the practitioner, for one afflicted by poison—
even if bitten by a *kulika*— it shall always effect the total destruction of the poison.
23a) By scattering dust mixed with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and gorocana, one bewilders enemies who have raised their weapons.
O Goddess, whoever applies a tilaka consecrated seven times with these mantras shall be victorious in battle, at the royal court, in gambling, and in dispute.
He shall become beloved by all women and equal to Kāmadeva;
indeed, unthought-of riches shall always accrue to him.
The prosperity of the Giver of Wealth is not equal to that which belongs to the practitioner;
for just as the god Nārāyaṇa always abides as the beloved of Lakṣmī.
In the same way, by the constant remembrance of the King of Accomplishers,
those wicked ones who heap poison and mechanical traps upon the practitioner [are destroyed].
For those of wicked mind who perform these rites, a malevolent spell (*kṛtyā*) arises,
resulting in the destruction of kinsmen, sons, and wealth, as well as the terrible destruction of the body.
There is no doubt that this occurs for those who perform evil toward the supreme practitioner, whether by deed, mind, or speech.
O Bhairavī, beloved of heroes, for those [who oppose], Pratyamgirā shall arise and there will be total destruction; or he against whom this practitioner becomes angry [shall perish].
The destruction of his lineage occurs merely by the goddess’s being remembered;
whatever desire one constantly contemplates, that very thing is desired for the practitioner.
The goddess, assuming all forms, possessing a universal form, and exceedingly fierce, sits upon a lotus and a corpse-throne; she is radiant, bestows boons and fearlessness, and holds a noose.
The goddess assumes various forms, uniquely adorned with diverse weapons;
she possesses many garments, many arms, and many shapes, and is exceedingly fierce.
O Great Goddess, one should meditate on her as having a universal form, with dark, curly hair,
or in whatever form is desired, resembling Mahālakṣmī.
Resembling the cool-rayed moon, she has five faces and three eyes;
she is endowed with ten mighty arms, with various weapons raised in her hands.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who bestows all happiness, clad in garments of deep red;
one should meditate upon the Goddess, who resembles a wish-fulfilling gem and grants the fruits of all desired objects.
One should worship [the deity] in a large vessel or a granary filled with grain and liquor;
for one who is constantly devoted to such worship, there shall be inexhaustible [merit].
When wealth is lost, having worshipped the Supreme Goddess residing within the *bilva* tree,
one’s property will never perish, becoming equal to that of Kubera, the Giver of Wealth.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess at Gajasāla, the bestower of liberation;
elephants shall never perish, and their increase will come to pass.
Having fashioned an image from sandalwood wood and placed it in the temple,
and having worshipped it with supreme devotion, O Lord of Horses, one does not perish.
They always attain growth, like the dwelling of the sun;
one should worship them after having painted them on a picture-board in a cowshed.
O Goddess, those cows that always yield abundant colostrum attain prosperity; likewise, in grain fields and other such places, one should scatter rājikā seeds consecrated seven times with mantras.
O Goddess of the gods, one should cast [the offerings] therein so that no one may enter from there;
through the excellence of the great bed and other such things, they shall always attain prosperity.
One should perform the sprinkling with water consecrated by mantras for the sake of trade;
then those who are always courageous shall always attain valor.
Having instructed the children in the recitation of the Śarṣyapā mantra, they should always wear it around their necks;
when prosperity has arrived, the children shall be long-lived and firm in wisdom.
One who destroys the elder [brother], one who stands upon a vehicle, and one who desires worship shall obtain their wishes;
O Goddess, whatever desire one entertains while mounted upon a vehicle, that shall be fulfilled.
Now, what is the use of much speaking? Whatever I am able to accomplish, that very thing is forcibly accomplished through the application of other texts.
Having recited the mantra twenty-seven times over mustard seeds and milk,
one should scatter them at the site of a crossroads in the evening and morning during times of distress.
Having observed the signs there, one should recite [the mantra] while Bhairavī is present;
the Vidyā and the practitioner remain undisturbed for as long as seven days have passed.
O Supreme Goddess, if she goes to the world of the Nāgas with speed,
she arrives at the treasure-trove without any obstacle.
Wherever one recites this most powerful Vidyā at a place containing treasure,
there the treasure itself comes before the best of practitioners.
Having recited it eight thousand times, O Maheśānī, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus on a mountain peak for all the supreme Mothers of Mantra.
One should offer guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter with a serene mind;
thereafter, Śrī herself will appear face-to-face, bringing forth auspiciousness renowned throughout the world.

pierce, pierce with the goad in your right hand—accomplish all my desires until they are fulfilled!
O Blessed One, you who grant fearlessness with your left hand and supreme compassion and boons with your right hand! Bhagavatī!

O bearer of the form of Mahābhairava, holding a severed head in your left hand; O you who are saluted by the best of the thirty gods, Mother of all mantras, with a bell in your right hand; O you who are affectionate toward those who bow before you, seated upon a corpse and Rudra!

O Goddess Mahākālī, destroyer of Kāla, Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is light! Hūṃ at the base; Hūṃ in the heart; Hūṃ between the eyebrows—[you who are] of the nature of light! Be gracious and make the daughters of the gods and demons afflicted with passion! Subdue the three worlds! Hrīṃ at the base; Śrīṃ in the secret place; Hūṃ in the linga.
Phaṭ at the heart; phaṭ at the throat; phaṭ at the mouth; svā at the center of one's own eyebrows; hā in the Brahmāṇḍa.

This is the *varṇadehanyāsa*. Then, the *bali* offering: *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ kṣmvyūṃ*, accept this *bali* for Kṣetrapāla, who is accompanied by Ambā, the devourer of time, the destroyer of all. *Namaḥ* to the *Śrīpādukās*.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gāṃ Gīṃ Gūṃ Gaiṃ Gauṃ Gaḥ Gmlvryuṃ! O beloved of Gaṇapati, together with [your retinue], accept this offering, accept it! Śrī!
Vmlvryū&! O Vaṭukanātha, together with your beloved, accept this offering, accept it! Śrī!

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Ymlvryīṃ Mmlvryīṃ Sāṃ! To all the Yoginīs, to those who pervade the entire universe, to the self-born beings, to the lords of beings, and to the presiding deities of all cremation grounds, accept this offering (bali)!
Twice! Salutations to the Glorious Sandals (Śrīpādukās)!

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the Gurus. 3. Salutations to the Paramagurus. 3. Salutations to the Parameṣṭhī Gurus. 3. Salutations to the Ādisiddha and all other Gurus. [At the crown of one's own head: Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, salutations to the Mahāpretāsana (the seat of the great corpse). Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Hraiṃ Hrauṃ Hraḥ.

Salutation to the Great Rudra-throne. Having invoked the Goddess with a handful of flowers through the nostrils using the root mantra, and having meditated upon her, one then [recites]: "For the purpose of establishing, settling, and confining: *sthāpana-sanniveśa-sannirodhaka*, *hūṃ*! To the weapon: *phaṭ*!"

In meditation: [I worship] the auspicious Śivā, who shines with her excellent arms holding a skull-topped staff, a goad, a noose, a trident, a boon-granting gesture, a protection gesture, a vessel, a severed head, and a jar;
she rests upon the shoulder of Rudra, resembles the autumnal moon, has five faces, and is beautiful.
I worship the Blessed Lady Śrī Siddhilakṣmī, who is adorned with five and three eyes.
Having offered the seventeenth libation (tarpaṇa), as well as sandalwood paste, vermilion, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
Having performed worship with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [offer] 290 *mālā*s with three handfuls of water (*añjali*). Recite the seventeenth [verse] 17 times according to one's capacity.
Perform the worship of the eight Mothers (*aṣṭamātṛkā*).
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Aṃ Āṃ 16. In this practice, the auspicious [deities] are declared: Brahmāṇī, Aiṃdrī, Akṣa, and Asitāṅgabhairava; obeisance to the venerable sandals (śrīpādukā).
Kaṃ 5: Varuṇā, Ilāyī, Carcikā, Sundinī, Māheśvarī, Āgneyī, and the venerable Īkṣarurubhairava.
And in Caṇḍapura, at Kolāpura, there was the venerable Caṇḍabhairava, the bull [of the lineage], born of the union of Ūhāyī and Yogāyī with Kevatī and Kaumārīyāmā.
3 Ṭaṃ 5: At Aṭṭahāsa is Ṛṣāyī Hara, Siddhāyī Kheṭakī, and Vaiṣṇavī; in the southwest is Ṛkṣa Krodhabhairava, [whose] venerable sandals [are worshipped].
3 taṃ 5 Jayantike, ḷ Śāyī, Bhayayī, Kaṃdhūkī, Vārāhī, Vāruṇī, ḷ Kṣaḥ; salutations to the sandals of Unmattabhairava.
In the south-east (Paṃ), [there is] Elāyikilakilārajakī; in the north-east (Māhendrī) is Vāyavye;
[and] Ikṣa and Kapālabhairava are at the venerable footstool.
3. Yaṃ 4. At Ekāmra: Auhāyī, Kālarātrī, Cchiyyinī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kauverī, Aukṣa, Bhīṣaṇa, Bhairava, and Śrīpādu.
Salutation to the sandals of Śrī Saṃhārabhairava, [accompanied by] the goddess Koṭe, Ahlāyī, Bhīṣaṇī, Koṣaṭī, Mahālakṣmī, and Īśānī, and to Akṣa.
The worship begins from the east and ends in the northeast.
One should perform worship with three handfuls of offerings using the *mālāmantra*.

Again, the *bali* offering: *Khphreṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*, O Great Rudra-eater, destroy, destroy the obstacles! Fulfill, fulfill all my heart's desires! Accept this *bali* offering of wine, meat, and rice, according to my capacity; accept it, accept it! *Hūṃ phaṭ*.
Svāhā!
KHPHREṂ! To the one seated upon the great corpse-seat: destroy my obstacles, destroy them!
Accomplish all my heart’s desires, accomplish them! Accept this offering of wine, flesh, and rice, and this bali-offering according to my capacity; SVĀHĀ!
Ai& 3 a ā 16. In this practice, you who are the narrator, the auspicious one, the beloved of Īśvara, the daughter of Brahmā, and the consort of Indra—Aḥ Kṣa!
O Asitāṅga Bhairava, destroy my obstacles, destroy them! Fulfill all my heart’s desires, fulfill them! Accept this offering of wine, meat, and rice, and this *bali* according to my capacity, Hūṃ!
Phaṭ svāhā!
In this manner, one should offer the bali-oblation to the eight Mothers with the respective mantras of their own fields and seats (kṣetra-pīṭha) as previously stated;
and one should offer the bali-oblation to Kṣetrapāla, Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, and the Yoginīs with the previously mentioned Pādukā mantra.
Aiṃ 3; one should display the five mudrās: the Yoni, the Guhyadrāviṇī, the Kṣobhiṇī, and the Jvālinī.
One should dismiss the goddess with the mudrā of withdrawal into one's own heart.
Thus ends the venerable ritual procedure for the worship of Umā-Jāmaleśvara.
Oṃ, homage to Caṇḍā!
In the Karavīraka cremation ground, crowded with great siddhas,
blazing with the light of bliss from the vast expansion of the Great Multitude (mahāvṛnda).
When the great wheel had been turned in the yoga of the *Tridaśaḍāmara*,
Kulasundarī questioned the Lord who was established in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).
The Goddess said:
In former times, the knowledge that was mine, honored by the three worlds, was correctly indicated in three ways; however, it was not fully proclaimed along with its ritual procedures.
Now, explain that [teaching] in its entirety according to the lineage tradition and the prescribed ritual,
so that it may be understood by those seeking perfect accomplishment for the sake of divine siddhi.
Having thus heard the words of the Goddess, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
filled with intense bliss, spoke to Akula’s lineage.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, the gross, the subtle, and the supreme goddess have been indicated by me;
that which I shall now proclaim belongs to the lineage of the secret of secrets.
Incomprehensible by mind or words, filled with the bliss of absolute liberation (kaivalya),
these seventeen-syllable Vidyās abide in subtle form within yogis.
Subtle in the form of thought and characterized by the activity of the mind, she is mental; when satisfied, she bestows supernatural powers upon practitioners who abide in the gross state.
Furthermore, the triad of mind, speech, and body, when established in its gross form as the primordial nature (prakṛti),
bestows fruit upon yogins.

Therefore, O Dear One, the gross [form] is established with three parts; it is gross with the concluding [parts], extending from the supreme (parā) up to the end of two hundred, increased by ninety syllables.
O Maheśvarī, for those by whom the mantra-body, the letter-body, the word-body,
and the reality-body are known, may perfection be fully attained.
When she becomes one whose body is the reality (tattva), she destroys all obstacles;
when her body is the state (pada), she bestows great siddhi upon the practitioners.
Mahāgaurī, whose body is color, becomes known as being present; Mahāsphārā, whose body is mantra, is present for the accomplishment of worship.
If one does not truly perceive the reality of the syllables of the mantra through the reality of the feet [of the Guru],
then no accomplishment (siddhi) shall arise for them, even after reciting it hundreds of millions of times.
In the Ḍāmara, Kula-jhaṅkāra, and likewise in the Jayadratha, O Goddess,
the number of Vedas pertaining to the Mother of the Kula has been declared by me as being devoid of ritual injunctions.
Those devoid of ritual procedure do not attain success, being bereft of the four bodies;
therefore, with every effort, one should establish the body as a worthy vessel for practice.
Having heard this spoken by Śaṅkara, Bhairavī,
