the beloved of Bhairava, the virtuous goddess, prostrated before Śiva and questioned him.
The Śrī Devī said:
"This speech is most extraordinary; O Lord, out of compassion, tell me its power—how it is endowed with efficacy, free from obstacles, and devoid of attachment."
O Supreme Lord, [I have received] the mantra-body, the letter-body, the third, the word-body, and the fourth, the reality-body (tattvadeha), all clearly manifest.
Having heard the words of Pārvatī, Bhairava, the destroyer of fear,
with a delighted mind, spoke these auspicious words.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O you who are saluted by the lords of heroes, to this wonderful secret which has been declared with effort to someone, having come together from the four seats (pīṭhas).
From Śrīkaṇṭha of divine form, from the Dānava Rāvaṇa,
from Vibhīṣaṇa, and from Dharma who assumes the form of Mahākaṅkāra.
From the Jayadratha-mahātantra, likewise from the Jhaṅkārabhairava,
from the Vibhīṣakāra-tantra, and likewise from the Tridaśaḍāmara.
Herein lies the lineage of the glorious Siddhakula, correctly [transmitted] from the Guhyāśrama through the path beginning with Kāmapīṭha, according to the traditional succession.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra-body, the phoneme-body, and the essential nature of the word-principle (padatattva), along with the procedure that is not devoid of the *anuṣṭhāna*, wherever it may be found within the Kula tradition.
Therefore, I shall first proclaim the highly exalted mantra-vidyā,
which bestows all accomplishments and is honored by all the hosts of siddhas.
On a level stretch of ground, anointed with saffron and agallochum,
strewn with heaps of flowers, and beautified by the splendor of great elephants and flames.
In that auspicious place, filled with the sweet fragrance and aroma of great incense and other perfumes,
replete with great food offerings, and honored with great vessels.
The great assembly of maidens and others, filled with supreme bliss,
resounded with the roar of great laughter and was attended by virtuous beings.
In that place joined with great water-jars, honored with garments and other offerings,
strewn with great oblations, and filled with a great host of satisfied and joyful beings;
In the great yoga, crowded with [practitioners] and filled with showers of the ashes of heroes,
when the great *cakra*-entrance has been attained with devotion;
The supreme preceptor, having been requested and worshipped by the disciples like Bhairavanāyaka himself, [should perform the rite] with the mantra joined with the great *utsava*-chalk.
One who knows the lineage of gurus beginning with Śiva, is endowed with power (śakti),
has practiced the fourfold bodily disciplines, and possesses a form inseparable from that power;
Having sprinkled the great vessel and the pedestal with the weapon-mantras,
the leader of the preceptors, facing either south or north, [proceeds].
The square is considered to be thirty-six finger-breadths;
having placed the Brahma-line there at the back of the house on the right side.
In the Mahāvana, one should rotate [the instrument] four finger-breadths wide while positioned at the mouth of Yama,
and likewise rotate it in a circle measuring four finger-breadths.
By the measure of four finger-breadths, from the measure of four finger-breadths;
and again, by the measure of one finger-breadth, there are five.
Afterwards, one should construct the *dhruva* (fixed point) according to the sixteen-fold measure in due order;
in the first circle, the pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be made, and in the [second] circle, it should have eight petals (*vasu*).
The filaments are on the second [circle], the joints of the petals on the third;
the tips of the petals are on the fourth, while the line of the sky (the center) is on the fifth.
O Goddess, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with the measurement of a syllable-finger (varṇāṅgula);
then, in the center, one should place the seed-syllable of the letter and a cluster of filaments.
At the base of the eastern petal, one should draw an arrow; in the center, a bird;
and at the tip, a cloud, situated upon the letter *maṃ* in the filament of the northeast.
One should place Caṇḍrahāsa in the southeast and Kharapuccha as before;
likewise, having assigned Gajarodha, one should place Añjana at the base of Īśa.
The great seat of Ṭaṅkahasta is surrounded by Rudrakadaṇḍaka;
likewise, O Dear One, there is Aṇḍasphoṭa in Īśāna, as well as Tāraka and Kharaka.
Having likewise placed the syllable *mada* (ma) as the bond, then the letter *ka* at the northeast;
then *padmanābha* (pa), the letter *ra*, and *rāvakuṃbha* (va) in the water.
In a moving house, for the sake of gentle leaves, one should place a garment,
a man, strength, and a corpse— extremely radiant— according to the previously mentioned method, which bestows yoga.
The Saṃvara resides in the gentle hair; he is the man of great splendor.
From the letter *ga* to the letter *ṇa*, there is nectar within the two *gagaṇas*.
Having thus inscribed [the letters], and likewise at the end, having placed two pairs [of vowels] in sequence from the twelve vowels, ending with the harsh *bindu* (anusvāra) as the remainder.
When all things have perished and there is the return to the void, the ocean of sound is complete;
from the eastern limit to the western, nine phonemes are established.
From the southeast to the northwest, O Maheśvarī, they indeed possess upward-pointing colors; from south to north, they have the colors of the planets.
From the southwest to the northeast, ending at the petals, [the letters] beginning with *nā* and *bha* are for the sake of the eternal one;
together with *medha*, all the qualities are in every direction and intermediate direction.
In whatever manner they may be, one should perform them according to the tradition through yoga;
[the letters] from 'a' to the visarga, twenty-four in number, arise from the mandala.
O Dear One, when the Vidyā-mantras arise within the Cakrarāja,
the deities are worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with pairs of garments and sandalwood paste.
From those [syllables] consisting of jewels and gold, which are subject to interruption and arise from the lineage of supreme nectar,
one should extract the Vidyā that bestows all goals without exception.
When worshipped within this [maṇḍala] called the King of Wheels, adorned with fifty vowels,
she swiftly bestows great siddhi.
O Great Goddess, for the practitioner, she is Pratyāṅgirā of great luster,
the Great Caṇḍā who is the Fortune of Siddhi, the Supreme Sovereign known as Śivā.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheel of the Arising of the Vidyā-mantra," in the Karavīra-yoga of the Ḍāmara within the illustrious Mahākula-krama. || 1 ||
Having heard the wheel of the arising of the knowledge-mantras together with its gates,
the Goddess again asks this question concerning the arising of the Kula.
The Goddess said:
Tell me clearly how that which brings forth all the mothers of mantra is extracted at the conclusion of the arising of the Vidyā-mantra. Speak of that, O Doer!
Having heard what was spoken by the Goddess— great and most profoundly secret—
Mahādeva spoke these words according to the prescribed ritual for the purpose of untying [the knot].
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain from within the expansion of the Vidyā:
the six upward-extractions (ūrdhvāra-ṣaṭka) have arrived, which, when devoid of the *kīla*, constitute the divisions.
Having extracted the neutral vowel situated between *o* and *au*, it stands upon the central seat;
at the base of the water-petal is the root of the wind-petal.
Having joined them in descending order from below, marked by *la* and *ḷ* in the middle,
with the head of the Moon (*sa*) and the top of the Sky-traveler (*kha*) placed above— this is the Illuminator (*dīpana*), the arising of the Khecarī.
Blessings upon those who dwell in the cremation grounds, who bear the five mudrās;
[the mantra] beginning with the letter *ga*, consisting of seventeen syllables, endowed with the ninth in the middle.
The Kaulika illumination should be applied, having reached the sky (the crown) through the limbs and the upward breath;
it is joined with the Gāḍimantra and others, adorned from the base to the head.
A lamp situated in the house bestows auspiciousness and spiritual luster;
however, among the three lamps, it is according to the sequence of their respective functions.
One should employ only the first letter as the supreme seed-syllable;
it is joined with the fifth vowel, extending from the tip of the northeast to the tip of the northern petal.
One should take the letter *ṣa*, which has *ta* and *bha* as its arms and stands between *ṣa* and *pha*, with its head positioned between *ṣa* and *pha*;
then, having extracted the letters *o* and *au* from the middle, one should join them with the letter *ja*.
The middle vowels *ṛ* and *ṝ*, joined with the letter ending in *da*, adorned by the letters beginning with *ja*;
joined with the letter *sa* in the middle of *paśu*, beginning with the letter *da*, which is the first of the *dāraṇa*.
Joined at the end with *dāraṇa*, conjoined with that which is born from the tip of *īśa*,
united with the middle of *hara*, and [extending] from the eastern tip downward to the ninth earth.
One should extract [the syllable] joined with the group of four, conjoined with the letter at the end of the second quarter,
having the letter *sa* (Saumya) at its head, pervaded by *Dāraṇa*, and situated below the final letter of the *ṭha*-group.
Again, the Rudra-mantra is joined with the eighth vowel, which causes splitting;
then follow two [syllables] ending in *dvipa*, and finally the tenth [vowel] joined with the short [vowel].
Adorned with the letter *sa* joined by the end of *ha*, the middle of *tha*, and the end of *ha*;
and joined with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, the middle [of *tha*], and the letter *ja*, it resides in the middle of the cloth.
One should write the second [vowel] alone, joined with the letter *ga* at its end;
and the second [vowel] should be modified by the middle of the two *ṛ*s.
One should extract [the letters] beginning with *ja*, divided into twenty-eight;
likewise, twenty-six [letters] should be joined, situated in the middle of *ha* along with the letter ending in *la*.
One should extract the letter 'o', the middle [vowel], the fierce-middle [vowel], that which resides in the middle of the excellent fire-sacrifice (dhūkhaha),
the sixth power of the letter 'ga', and that which ends with the letter 'e'.
Here, the letter *kha* in the middle, joined with the seven fires above it,
and the letter *gha* in the middle, ending with *ga*, is conjoined with that which resides in the middle of *hara*.
Joined with the end of *dāraṇa* (the letter *ṇa*), and endowed with the beginning and end of *cādi* (the letters *ca* and *cha*),
the *rāsana* (the letter *ra*) is joined with the third [vowel *i*], having the western point at its tip.
One should extract the letter situated in the middle of Indra (the vowel *i*), endowed with the letters beginning with *pa* and ending with *dha*,
joined with that which begins with *sa* (the vowel *ā*), and then draw forth the letter situated in the middle of *ka* and *ṭa* (the vowel *u*).

One should place the letter of Īśa (H) upon the seat; then, one should join the letter situated in the middle of the leaf of Yama (Ś), which is conjoined with the fifth vowel [Ū] and the Visarga, at the end of Ga (G), below the letter Kha (K).
The letter *ka* (ke) is situated in water (*ja*), followed by *ga*; joined with the letter *ya*, it resides in the midst of wind (*va*).
At the end of the letter *sa*, there is the letter *sa* joined with wind (*va*); this is the *kesara* (pericarp) situated in destruction (*kṣa*).
One should draw the fourth filament joined with the middle of the vowel *o*;
in the middle of *ṛ* and *ṝ*, it is joined with the end of the consonants and situated in the middle of *ha*.
O Goddess, the first section,
consisting of fifty-six syllables, is proclaimed as being joined with the *ghādhonta* [mantra], known as Brahman, and accompanied by the excellent Mothers (*mātṛkā*).
In the form of knowledge (vidyā), it is called the gross (sthūla), bestowing all commitments (samaya);
it effects the union with the multitude of the Mothers and is the leader of the Mothers.
O Goddess, one should again lift up the lamp established according to the ritual rule;
having divided it threefold in the middle of the *uḍa*, it should be joined with the tips of the gentle petals.
One should cause the bliss of *lāsa* to arise by concealing the fifth letter of the *ga*-group;
it ends with the second [vowel] and concludes with the third *ga*.
Adorned with five triangles in the middle of the chariot and the forest,
the letter situated on the line of the sky is joined with its vowel and the tip of the moon.
The letter *kha* with *ha* in the middle, followed by the letters situated between *pha* and *pa*, joined with the initial [letter] and the northern tip;
likewise, the tip of the Lord (*īśa*) and the northern tip, joined with the lower end.
This second section is proclaimed as being named Viṣṇu;
it consists of nine syllables, beginning with the letter 'ma', for the sake of attaining all perfections through the mantra-syllables.
Having again extracted it according to the rule, O Goddess of the Gods, just as before:
the sixth [syllable] is in Vāyu, and the seventh is the ninth of Yama, O Dear One.

O Maheśvarī, from the southwest, it is joined with five degrees and so forth, reaching the eighth [digit] of the south; it is traversed through the middle of the goat and reaches the tip of the northeast.
Having again extracted it and joined it with the *ābhā* [vowel] along with the *tantrī* [consonant],
one should write the eighth letter of the Rākṣasa, conjoined with the middle of the *ī*.
The ninth [syllable] is the leaf of Yama, adorned with a pair of *ga*s;
having extracted *a* and *ā* as the center, it is marked by fire, seven, and half a *la*.
The letter *ṛ* and *ṝ* are differentiated by the intermediate *la* and so forth; *ḷ* and *ḹ* are situated between them.
It is joined with the lower *jha* and so forth, and stands upon the intermediate seat of *o* and *au*.
The syllable *sa* joined with the letters beginning with *ka* in the middle of the forest (*va*), together with the "water-lotus filament" (*ja*),
and that same [syllable] again situated above and below, located in the midst of *bha* and *sa*.

One should write the triad ending in the thirty-second [letter], beginning with *ṭa*, *ta*, and *la*, followed by *dha*, then the end of the *pa* group, the end of the *va* group, the end of the *na* group, and joined with the *ja* group.

Between *ṛ* and *ṝ*, one should write again that which is joined with the letters beginning with *ḍa*, combined with those beginning with *ya* and *ja*, and conjoined with those beginning with *pa* and ending with *ga*.
In the middle of the *rañtra* (the letter *ra*), at the end of *haṭha* (the letter *tha*), one should write the letter *kha* joined with *la* in the middle;
this is conjoined with the middle of *la* and *ḷ*, forming the right lotus (*dakṣābja*) which is not destroyed.

In the middle of these, one should write the letter *ma* ending with *gha*, joined with *ga* and *tri*; and in the middle of *o* and *au*, one should write the fifth letter (*pa*), conjoined with the letter ending in *gā*.
In the middle of Pha and Ha is the letter at the end of Dha, joined with the middle of I and Ga;
it stands at the western tip of that which has its northern tip [pointing upward], and is pierced by the middle of Ai and Sa.
In the middle of the *ṭa-bha* [group], one should write the letter ending in *ṭa*, the letter ending in *pha*, and the seventh letter *la*, joined with the letter following the lower *jha*;
thus, one should write the triad ending in the thirty-second [letter].
The fourth [syllable] is Mahāntaka, situated on the fourth seat;
it is joined with the letter Ṭha and ends with Pha, established upon the pedestal beginning with Ṣa.
The letters ending with *na* and those ending with *ṭha* and *pha*, joined with the vowels beginning with *ī*;
[the letters] between *ḷ* and *ḹ*, beginning with *la* and *bha*, and those beginning with the vowel *o*.
One should write [the syllable] situated on the seat between *i* and *ga*, and between *ā* and *a*; it is further marked by the [syllable] between *i* and *ga*, and again written between *ā* and *a*.
One should draw the seat of Kānta (the letter *ka*) within the womb of Khānta (the letter *kha*). One should place *o* and *au* in the middle; then, one should extract the second [syllable].
Having extracted the *ha* above and the *ra* above, one should place *a* and *ā* in the middle seat.
Having written those again in two ways, one should write the pair beginning with *gha* and beginning with *kha*.
One should write the upper part [of the mantra] joined with *pha* and the letter beginning with *ḍa*, preceded by *bha* and accompanied by the letter beginning with *ja*,
and conjoined with the letter *ka* situated in the middle of dissolution (*laya*).
The letter *ga* and the others, joined with the vowels beginning with *pa*, are situated in the middle of the spokes;
furthermore, they are joined with those ending in *pa* and *ga*, and stand upon the rim ending in *dha*.
One should write the letter ending in *ī* (i.e., *ī*) joined with the first letter (*ja*), according to the procedure beginning with the northern [direction].
Then, the letter *na*, the letter *ma*, and the letter *la* above it, joined again with the letter *ṣa* above them.
Having properly placed the single-threaded cord marked with the *lāḍha* sign in the center,
one should again duly cover it, provided with the limbs (*aṅga*) at the end.

Furthermore, it is of two kinds: that which is joined with the letters beginning with *ja* in the middle of *śa-ṭa-ma*, and that which is joined with *da* and so forth at the beginning, while the lower part is joined with the letter ending in *ḍa*.
One should again draw the tip of the letter *ī* joined with the half-measure of *lādi*;
then the tip of the letter *ja* joined with *jādi*, its tip being *ī* and situated upon *dhādha*.
Having thus pronounced it twice, with the end of the *khaṭ* struck by the *ja*,
and the tip of the *īśa* mounted upon the lower part of the *pāda*, perform it again in two ways.

Having joined the *gādharā* (the letter *ga*) with the middle of the *dakṣa* (the letter *da*), situated above the middle of the *pūrva* (the letter *pa*), and combined it with the letters beginning with *la* up to *na*, one should draw [the diagram] ending at the northeast (*īśāna*).
One should write this triad, joined with *pāda* and *gānta*, with *u* and *ū* between them, ending with *halānta*, and endowed with *ṭha* and *la*.
One should again write this triad beginning with *ṛ*, *ṝ*, and ending with a middle consonant;
[then] that which ends with *pā* joined with *ga*, and that which goes from *mā* and *tha* to the end of *pa*.
One should join the limbs together in one place, connecting them again from the beginning;
then, one should write the letter Ā on the seat at the tip of the northeast (īśāna) and again in the middle of the nine.
Afterwards, the triad ending with the thirty-second [letter], the middle of the forest [va], and the last of the [vowels] *gha*;
joined with the end of the *la* series, *lādha*, *dādha*, and combined with the *ga* of *gātra*.

Then, having duly recited the mantra ending in *oṃ* for each triad at the heart, the base of the navel, the arms, and again the three joints of the feet; and furthermore, having recited it for the three joints according to the rule.
The first letter [ca], traversed by the final letter [ṅa] and joined with the first letter [ḍa], is followed by the letter below la [va], joined with the first letter [ḍa];
then the letter at the end of Īśa [ha], traversed by the triad [ga], and the first letter [ca] joined with the first letter [ḍa].
The triad ending in the forty-third [letter] is for the water for the feet (*pādya*); beginning with *ja* and joined with the water for the feet and so forth;
joined with the first of the vowels, the middle vowel, and the letter *ga*, it faces west.
It is traversed by the middle of *o*, beautiful (*phānta*), radiant (*bhānta*), and reaching the end of dissolution;
it is joined with the first letter of *ḍa*, the essence of the Tantras (*tāntra*), beginning with *bha*, and endowed with the end of *ga*.
The first syllable is joined with *pha* and *ja*, and the second is joined with *jha*.
The third is joined with *ṭa* and *da*, while *ṛ* and *ṝ* are situated between *ma* and *gha*.

One should write the three ending in *mā*, ending in *khā*, and ending in *maghā*, combined with the letters beginning with *saumya* (s); ending in *ha*, joined with the letters beginning with *lā*; and ending in the thirty-second, combined with the letter *tri*.
The first letter with the second, joined with the last letter of the third;
joined with the last letter of the first, and joined with the last letter of the fourth.
Pha-dhara mounted upon la-dhara, ma-dhara, tha-dhara, and ṛ-dha;
dyā-dya at the end of mā-dya-kaṭa, and followed by para, mounted upon kha-anta.
The letter *la* is conjoined with the middle *ṛ* and *rā*, or else the letters beginning with *lā* are situated between *ṛ* and *ṝ*;
the first [group] is joined with those beginning with *ja*, and the second with those beginning with *cha*, *śa*, and *ṣa*.
One should divide the seed-syllable of the second [deity] into three parts, ending with *pha* and *ha*.
It is mounted upon a seat ending with *pha*, followed by the letter *ma*, and joined with the letter *ja*.
Having joined the letter *ṛ* with the end of the middle forest (*madhyavana*) and the lower *dhā*, which does not go upward;
having made it conjoined with *gā*-ness, it is adorned by the letter beginning with *ḍ*.
The end of *laya* [the letter *la*] with the middle of *i* [the vowel *i*], adorned at its head by the beginning of *ṇa* [the letter *ṇa*];
the lower *kha* [the letter *kha*] joined with the beginning of *ḍa* [the letter *ḍa*], and the lower *ā* [the vowel *ā*] situated in the middle of *i* [the vowel *i*].
Having thus pronounced the pair, place *vaḍ* and so forth between *o* and *au*; then, once again, perform this same procedure joined with the letters ending in *pha* and *ga*.

Having placed the semi-vowels (antastha) alone, [one should place] the letters beginning with *gha* below the letter *kha*, joined by the letters beginning with *śa*; [then] the letters ending with *ha* joined by those beginning with *ga*, conjoined with the letter *au* in the middle.
One should extract the second [syllable] of the second [word], and likewise the third of the third; this is joined with the first letter of the first word and the fourth letter of the second.
Having given the threefold fallen [syllables] accompanied by *mādyā* and so forth,
joined with *igamadhyena*, and joined with *madhyegāntena*.
The collection of phonemes is considered to be two hundred and twenty-five;
it is known as Mantra, named Rudra, and designated as Parā-vidyā.
The third section has been declared from the *Vidyāmantrōdayōttara*;
thus, the Vidyā, divided into its various distinctions, is composed of these three sections combined.
With two hundred and ninety auspicious Rudras,
they are remembered in some places as being arranged in reverse order according to the various divisions of the Siddhas and their attainments (siddhis).
In some places, they are remembered as Mahākāruṇī and Ceti-devī;
Māyā and Lakṣmī are situated in reverse order, followed by Trihaṃsa and Pañcapiṇḍaka.
In some places she is called Ambā, while in others she is called Chhindinī and so forth;
by whatever various distinctions she is endowed, the Eternal One is thus celebrated.
She bestows various fruits upon both the practitioner and the one who conceals [the practice];
this is the Great Vidyā known by the name Trailokyamohanī.
Renowned as Lakṣmīśvarī, she brings an abundance of many enjoyments;
she is Mahālakṣmī, the Great Overcomer, the bestower of all good fortune.
It should be known as the remover of misfortune, the crusher of wicked poverty,
the pacifier of the Kali age and evil dreams, and the destroyer of secondary afflictions.
She who averts royal calamities, who destroys wicked robbers,
the Great Auspicious One (Mahābhadra) who is the counter-pratyaṅgirā, the perfected Lakṣmī of great prosperity.
She is named Caṇḍā, the destroyer of the fierce; she is named Śivā, the bestower of auspiciousness;
she is Guhyeśvarī, named Kamalā, and dwells within the circle of the Mothers.
She is known by the name Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī, and she whose name is Gaurīrakṣaṇā;
she is Mahākālī, Bharaśāntā, and the beloved of Mahābhairava.
The Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who bestows the power of Mahārudra, transcends the dissolution of the Brahmā-array; she possesses a body of knowledge, a body of letters, and a body of words.
O Goddess, the garland within the womb, which is to be extracted from the body of reality (tattva),
is thus extracted within the emergence of the Vidyā-mantra.
By virtue of his own authority, he bestows upon men the desired fruit.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Vidyā," in the Great Karavīra Sacrifice of the Śrī Mahākula-krama.
The Goddess said:
I have heard the extraction of the deities within the emergence of the vidyās and mantras;
now I desire to hear that which pertains to the perfect accomplishment of the four bodies.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the great arising of the body of letters (varṇadeha),
which has come down through the lineage of succession and is unattainable by those of dull fortune.
In this lineage of the Siddhas born of the stream of accomplishment,
it is easily accessible for both men and women who are devoted to the Kula.
In a suitable and delightful place, the practitioner, endowed with the accumulation of the [necessary] requisites,
should draw the maṇḍala there, which brings about the arising of the fruits of all desires.
Either the one called Ekavīra or the Yāmalendra [should be drawn],
using five-colored powder or with great red and other pigments.
Then, having paid homage to the Guru and preceded by the vessel of offering (arghapātra),
one should perform the movement of the breath starting with the exhalation (recaka) within the mandala of the heroes and heroines.
Seated in the lotus posture, the yogi should contemplate her whose form is the mantra,
once the seed-syllable Śrī has been manifested in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
One should visualize the forms of the deities there within that great mandala of the continents;
then, one should visualize Caṇḍā arisen from that, endowed with the yoga of mantra.
One should first visualize the eastern face as it exists with the colors of Rudra;
then its southern [face] with those called the planets, and likewise the northern with twelve.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the sky situated in the east with the colors of Rudra,
and likewise in the middle of the eyebrows, the heart, and the navel, according to the sequence of the wheels.
The first [syllable] is on the mouth, the second in the mind, and the third on the right;
likewise, the pair ending with the fifth is on the left and right eyes.
The two ears are on the left and right, and the two lingas are likewise made of fresh jaggery;
her heart consists of seven syllables, and her head is considered to be the same.

They know the fierce crest-lock (śikhā) by the colors of the directions, the individual soul (puṅgala) by the twelve ends, the collection of eyes by those called the planets, and likewise the life-span (āyuḥ) by the vowels.
One should establish the Goddess using the five-syllable mantra, either on the head or within the mandala;
one should behold her, who is of the nature of grace, as *Hasa-yugma* and *Hasantī*.
One should meditate on Speech (Girā), who bestows the accomplishment born of the four mantras;
one should meditate on her skull-bowl, filled with drink by means of the syllables of Rudra.

One should contemplate the white-colored Khaṭvāṅga, endowed with three [prongs], by means of twelve [syllables]; and the trident (śūla) by means of eight, and the great sword (mahā-khaḍga) by means of seven.
They know that she holds a noose in her hand with six [fingers] and likewise a goad;
with twenty-one [fingers] she grants boons, and with seven she bestows auspicious fearlessness.
One should meditate upon the divine kanda, with four petals corresponding to the [four] letters;
likewise, one should contemplate the jar as being filled with the fifteen letters.

One should meditate upon her, who has the Great Rudras as her food, who is called "Rudra" by the eight [names], who resembles snow, and whose mass of splendor expands both downward and upward, proceeding through the three [stages] in sequence.
The binding of the Mahāmudrā is performed with nineteen syllables;
one should worship with the three seed-syllables of the Moon, Fire, and Sun, using flowers.
The eater should take [the portion] three times with the utterance "svāhā" and the vessel;
he should contemplate the supreme goddess, established in form and having the mantra as her body.
Having expanded from the body of colors those [energies] that reach the end of the states of existence and non-existence,
Kuṇḍalinī, by her very nature, moves through the center of the wheels from the root-center.
The essential nature of the castes has been explained as arising from qualities such as whiteness and so forth,
or as arising from the brahmins and other [classes], or likewise from the letters beginning with 'a'.
Abiding in the eight classes beginning with Viriñca, it exists both eightfold and manifold;
through the division of many groups of eight, it takes the form of color within that which is colorless.
The great sound of Śiva and Śakti is the abode of the Bindu, the Moon, and the Yoni;
it is divided threefold from the letter A onwards, arising as the Vidyā-mantra within the lotus.
And one should meditate upon that white and other forms of the Goddess within the water-born lotus at the left of the heart, which consists of the phonemes and illuminates all phonemes.
Having understood the great expansion with its many divisions— the head, limbs, arms, heart, sides, waist, feet, and so forth— one should arrange everything accordingly.
Likewise, one should contemplate Viriñci and the others as the eightfold group that constitutes the body,
as the non-dual letter Śiva, and indeed as Śakti itself.
Resembling pure crystal, five-faced and ten-armed,
seated upon the throne of Mahārudra, she possesses a beautiful body and a radiant form.
She wears a blue lock of hair and holds the moon; she is adorned with a crest-jewel upon her crown, and her head-ornament is embellished with great necklaces of various gems and other jewels.
White, red, and black, crimson and white, made of acacia wood and blazing;
endowed with various jewels, well-proportioned in its joints, and beautifully adorned with earrings.
Having the reddish appearance of the solar disc, blazing with three and five eyes,
with a slight smile and a lolling tongue, her face is radiant, beautified by prominent fangs.
She wears a garland of lotus petals around her neck, which is adorned by various wicked Daityas and others;
her high breasts are rubbed by the tips of her arms fashioned from many jewels.
She was auspicious, with a slender waist respectfully adorned by the beauty of three folds like waves,
and her hips were decorated with a network of tinkling bells, fine garments, and the luster of a tiger-skin girdle.
In the right hands, he holds an excellent sword, a trident, and so forth, as well as a severed head;
in the left, he holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a *khaṭvāṅga*, an excellent vessel, a noose, and a supreme water-pot.
Her garment is the Vīraghaṇṭā, beautifully adorned by her two broad knees;
her two feet are embellished by the tinkling sounds of small bells and anklets.
She was mounted upon the shoulder of Rudra, who was pure white, three-eyed, two-armed, and single-faced,
and who sat in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
Resembling a blazing fire, consisting of a multitude of gathered flames,
it issued forth from his pores of the skin, making the sky appear like the dawn.
[One should meditate on her] standing in the midst of the eight Mothers, five-faced and endowed with a staff,
surrounded by many Siddhas, and worshipped by the Siddhas and Yoginīs.
Or one should meditate upon Ekavīrā, who holds a bell in her hand and is accompanied by Ghaṭā;
and Caṇḍāmbā at the back of Śiva, holding a curved knife and a shield.

And Śivāmbā has the gestures of giving (*dāna*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), but without the shield (*kheṭaka*); then there is Mahālakṣmīmayīmbā, who displays the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of desired objects.
In this way, the Great Goddess possesses various forms through countless distinctions of state,
or else she is joined with five white-faced [deities], adorned with the lords of serpents.

Having meditated upon [the deity] as being exceedingly gentle or exceedingly fierce according to the nature of its color and body through the yoga of the phonemes (varṇa), one should then become the body of the words (pada).
One should place the first word, consisting of three syllables, upon the regions of the head;
the second, consisting of ten syllables, upon the circle of the forehead.
The third indeed consists of nine syllables, joined with the fierce Nāśāvaṃśa;
the fourth, however, consists of ten syllables and is established in the left eye.
O Goddess, the fifth [syllable] consists of eleven syllables in the right eye;
the sixth is said to consist of four syllables in the third circle of the eye.
The seventh [syllable] is the sixth letter, situated on the left cheek;
O Goddess, the eighth [syllable] is in the three letters on the circle of the right cheek.
The first [section] shall consist of eight quarters and be named Brahmākhaṇḍa;
it is pervaded by the eight Yāmalas and joined with the yoga of dissolution and the rest.
The first should be a single syllable situated on the left ear;
one should place the second, the syllable of liberation (kaivalya), on the right ear.
The third letter, the ocean within the moon (ca), is situated on the lower lip;
the fourth letter, Śiva (śa), is situated on the upper lip.
The fifth [vowel] is white in color and is the witness among the lower teeth;
the eighth becomes single-colored in the circle of the upper row of teeth.
The seventh is the solitary letter situated on the left side of the tongue;
the eighth is the letter of the wing, located throughout the entire circle of the face.
This second section, the Viṣṇukhaṇḍa, is proclaimed to consist of eight verses;
it arises from the eight Siddhas and follows the eight steps of Śakti.
Furthermore, the first [mantra] consisting of seven syllables is prescribed for the middle of the trunk;
the second, consisting of six syllables, should be placed on the left shoulder.
The third [syllable] is established on the left arm with ten phonemes;
the fourth is on the left wrist with thirteen [phonemes].
O Goddess, the fifth [syllable] is with the nine vowels on the fingers of the left hand,
and the sixth is with the letters of the apertures (randhra) on the nails of the left fingers.
One should place the seventh [syllable] with seven phonemes on the right shoulder;
and the eighth with four phonemes one should place on the right arm.
And the ninth [is placed] by the four castes on the right wrist;
the tenth is placed by eleven [fingers] upon the fingers of the right hand.
The eleventh [syllable] should be placed on the nails of the right fingers with the nine [vowels],
and the twelfth with the four letters [of the *caturvarṇa*] upon the region of the abdomen.
Likewise, the thirteenth and those known as the eight are proclaimed for the left breast;
one should place the fourteenth and the four varṇas upon the right breasts.
With fifteen syllables, it resides in the left and right [channels] at the junction;
with sixteen and six syllables, it is established in the middle of the channel.
One should place the seventeenth and nineteenth [syllables] in the abode of Kālānala;
the eighteenth, situated within the womb (yoni), should be placed in the middle with seven syllables.
One should place nineteen [syllables] with four [units] for the Guḍamaṇḍala;
one should place the twentieth [syllable] with ten phonemes on the region of the left buttock.
One should place the [deity] called Ekaviṃśa with eight syllables on the right ankle;
and the twenty-second [deity] with seven syllables should be situated on the left thigh.
One should place twenty-three [syllables] with eight [fingers] on the left arm;
twenty-four [syllables] with eleven [fingers] are situated on the left knee.
One should apply twenty-five syllables to the left ankle,
and thirty-six syllables— eight for each— to the right ankle.
With twenty-seven [syllables] for each of the four [groups], on the toes of the left foot;
and with twenty-eight and seven syllables, on the body and the toes of the feet.
One should place the twenty-ninth syllable, consisting of a single letter, on the right lower lip;
the thirtieth syllable, with the letter Śiva, is situated on the right knee.
Likewise, thirty-one [syllables] are on the right foot with one [syllable],
and thirty-two with three syllables on the toes of the left foot.
Thirty-three [syllables] are established in the spinal column by means of three groups;
and with the syllables of the Guru’s instruction, the thirty-fourth word is formed.
One should install [the deity] in the form of a mudrā from the station of Śakti up to Śiva;
this is declared as the thirty-fourth step, the third section of Rudra.
Then, through meditation on the pure syllables, which bestows the fruit of great accomplishment,
by the union of three into one, there shall be fifty verses.

The pervasion of the principles (tattva-vyāpti) within the body of the Goddess has been perfectly established as an undivided whole. Now, by means of the detailed classification of that pervasion of the principles, I shall describe the body of the principles.
The three bodies, which are the cause for the application of yoga and bestow many accomplishments,
[are found] in the Brahma-section, within the sphere of half the fire of time (kālānala), which is not the reality of the self (ātmatattva).
One should place [the syllable] at the junction of the mouth, which brings about many benefits;
in the second [position], the fragment [is placed] above the half-lotus of the navel-maṇḍala.

The third section of the Rudrakhaṇḍa is the cause for the application of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), which bestows virtuous qualities, and follows the path of the reality-level of Śiva (*śivatatva*).
The meditation on the seat of the form is the cause that grants the perfection of mantra;
it consists of the Rudra, Graha, Arka, and Rudra-dig syllables, with the fifth being the face-syllable formed by the creation-vowels.
Kṛṣṇā, Ākarṣaṇī, Caṇḍā, Śivā, and she known as Praty-aṅgirā—
[these are worshipped] with the seven, six, and ten desires, and with the six limbs [of the mantra] at the vulnerable points of the seizing spirits.
One should visualize [the deity] endowed with the three qualities beginning with omniscience through various sequences:
omniscience, contentment, and primordial awakening.
If Ananta is considered prior to the cities [of the elements], his independence is one whose power is withdrawn;
[one should perform the nyāsa] for the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, eyes, weapon, and the six limbs.
*Namaḥ*, *svāhā*, likewise *vaṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *phaṭ*—these three;
likewise *hasa* doubled [as *hasa-hasa*], preceded by the seat (*pīṭha*) and Sadāśiva.
The third section consists of twenty syllables, while her form consists of one syllable;
thus the mantra-section becomes the seventeen-fold mantra.
O Gaurī, the description of the four bodies has been declared as stainless;
one should mentally apply it within the heart, joined with the introductory and concluding illuminating verses.
One should worship according to the proper rule, and then release the mudrā;
thereafter, one should dissolve one's own seat, pedestal, and form into oneself.
And one should worship oneself with the mantra according to the prescribed rite;
then, with palms joined in the *samāstra* [mudrā], one should perform a prostration with the back [of the hands] using the *nati* mudrā.
Placing the two little fingers foremost, one should arrange the pedestal;
from the little finger to the little finger, by means of a counter-clockwise rotation.
One should assign each form and color according to the oral instruction,
placing the five [fingers] with the little fingers foremost, followed by the six and the seven.
One should remember the mantra for *natya* (prostration) on the left and right palms, the eighth on the left back of the hand,
and the ninth on the right back of the hand.
Placing the two thumbs at the forefront, one should place the faces ending with the little fingers;
placing the two little fingers at the forefront, one should place the five [faces] beginning with the thumb.
Having placed [the syllables] with the backs and surfaces of the weapons, one should contemplate the three unbroken parts;
one should place the food upon the head, throat, heart, navel, and the junctions.
The coloring of the forms, beginning with jaggery and the like, and extending through the three medhas up to Brahmā,
is performed according to the distinctions of the secret parts, the mouth, the ears, the eyes, the nose, and so forth.
One should install the form of the mantra by means of the sequence beginning with the left [channel],
in the eyeball, at the tip of the breath, and on the path of the right and left ears.
One should arrange the five faces according to their respective positions;
having placed the heart-mantra at the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head.
Having performed the *śikhā-bandha* at the crest, [one should place] the armor (*tanutra*) upon the circle of the body;
[one should apply] the three-dot mudrā (*tribindumudrā*) to the eyes, and with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [place] the weapon in all directions.
Thereafter, one should install the three principles (tritatva), beginning with Śiva, according to the sequence of yoga;
then one should perform the installation of the words (pada-nyāsa), and thereafter again the installation consisting of the phonemes (varṇa).
Thereafter, one should contemplate the mantra-body fully perfected by mudrās;
then, established in the form of the Vidyā, one should recollect the entire Vidyā.
One should bind various mudrās by which [the practice] reaches completion;
having thus performed the placement (vinyāsa) upon the fourfold body, the lord of practitioners (sādhakeśvara).
I shall describe how one should perform the sacrifice preceded by the *astra-mantra*:
the vessel, washed with the *astra-mantra*, is filled with wine and other substances while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
It is enveloped by the armor, made nectar-like by the eye-mantra,
protected by the great weapon, and established by the heart-mantra.
Having kindled the crest-lock by means of the application of the secret mudrā,
one should worship the seat in the center with the portions of the form-mantra and the seat-mantra.
Having worshipped with three sections according to the successive application,
one should then worship Gāyatrī, who is honored by the gods, in the center.
O Goddess, I shall now describe to you that [mantra] consisting of twenty-four syllables:
it has the gentle [letter] at the beginning, the middle [letter] situated at the head, and is adorned by the dissolution in the center.
The first seed-syllable leader is joined with *ī* and *ṛ*;
it is preceded by *sa*, has *ma* in the middle, ends with *ga*, and is joined with *mā* and ends with *ṛ*.
The first [syllable] is joined with *jā* (ja), and the middle one is joined with *ṛ* and *ṝ*;
the middle one is further joined with *lā*, and there is again a pair ending in the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The beloved [syllable] *bādha*, joined with *ja* and enriched by *va*, is endowed with the initial vowel;
conjoined with the preceding vowel, it is the fifth element at the tip of the south-western [direction].
The two left feet and again the pair ending with the seed-syllables;
the seventh petal begins with *ja* and is joined with *śā*, *di*, *ma*, and *da*.
Ending with the letter *la*, enriched by the final consonant (*kṣa*), and joined with the vowel *ā* following the letter *ka*;
with *ṛ* and *ṝ* in the middle, ending with a consonant (*ha*), and joined with the letter *na* at the end.
Thereafter, O Ānanda, this [flower] which is threefold should be sprinkled with the Astra-mantra; then one should perform the veiling and other rites.
One should perform the veiling, the protection, and likewise the immortalization,
respectively with the armor mantra, the [specific] mantra, and the eye-mantra.
Then, one should worship Nandin, Mahākāla, as well as Bhṛṅgin,
Vināyaka, Vṛṣaskanda, Śrī, and Caṇḍa at the doors starting from the east.
The new [line] is "vyāghramajāṃ bhadrāṃ karṇāṃsanā balī calām";
the [verse] ending with the gentle one is "vajinī saumyaparyantaṃ dvāradvārayugaṃyugam."

Having worshipped Gaṇeśa together with Ambā and Ambikā, as well as the venerable son [Skanda], one should cause [the offering] to be given with this mantra, beginning and ending with the weapon-mantra (astra).

The two syllables beginning with Sadāśiva are always the name [of the deity] together with Śakti; or else, one should worship according to the oral instruction that which ends with the letter *va* or with the letter *da*.
Then, accompanied by flowers, one should place the two syllables ending in "ta" and ending in "śiva" together in the position of the doorway and the threshold.

Then, O Goddess, one should worship the succession of gurus at the end of the back-halā (the letter *ha*) in the beginning of the wind [the letter *ya*], and with flowers and so forth in the beginning of the earth [the letter *la*], and with the letters beginning with *a* in the beginning of the lamp [the letter *ra*].
One should first worship as one would a guru, and immediately thereafter the Supreme One; thirdly, one should likewise worship the Parameṣṭhin and the former teachers.
One should thoroughly worship the fifth [deity] known as Anādisiddhi;
thereafter, one should protect the person who is the lord of the site (vāstunāyaka) by means of the ritual posture (sthānaka).
One should worship one's own lineage of gurus and deities in the southeast corner;
thereafter, having worshipped them beginninglessly, preceded by the name of one's own guru.
Those beings of various forms who dwell in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space,
as well as those situated in the depths of the netherworld, have been meditated upon within the portions of Śiva.
They always obtain satisfaction among all beings, beginning with Dhruva;
together with a verse, they offer abundant flowers with the *puṣpa* mudrā.
The illuminator (dīpaka) is situated in the gentle (saumya), and the first [syllable] is at the end of the *pala*;
likewise, the sixth, seventh, and first [syllables] of the *gāyatrī* consist of groups of six, three, and three [mātrās].
One should again offer the heart-mantra ending with "tridaśānta" three times with the Gāyatrī;
one should give four [offerings] beginning with "kaṃnyakā," and four at the end of the Gāyatrī.
O gods and asuras, this Gāyatrī is said to consist of twenty-four syllables;
by reciting it three times, one should sprinkle the pericarp and the petals.
One should worship Brahmā and the others, as well as Śakra and the others, in pairs;
likewise, the eight beginning with Amṛtā up to Vīṇā, in due order.
Having recited the *kevala-vāsana* mantra, one should then invoke the form;
thereafter, one should worship it with the mantra according to the division of the four bodies.
In the hall of enjoyment (*bhogāṅgaṇa*), or in fire and so forth, or starting from the city,
one should worship the four gates according to the rule of the solitary hero (*ekavīra*).
Likewise, having invoked according to the rules with mantras the lineage of gurus, the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and the fourfold form, one should then establish the womb (yoni).
One should sequentially display the placement (sannidhāna), the withdrawal (sannirodha), the manifestation (sanmukhīkaraṇa), and the trident (triśūla) by means of the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
Water for the feet, water for sipping, and the three sections of the *arghya* offering should be given in sequence;
likewise, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and the concluding food offering (*pāraṇa*).
One should perform the offering of food (naivedya), the seat (āsana), betel (tāmbūla), and likewise the mirror (darpaṇa),
as well as the pleasing of the head, face, and other limbs, ending with the weapon-mantra (astra).
Then, having displayed the ten mudrās— the *mudrā*, the *mahāmudrā*, the third being the *guhyamudrā*, and the *astramudrā*— one shall become invincible.
O Beloved, [the rosary] may consist of mahākaṃ wood,
crystal, rudrākṣa, or conch shell, according to the divisions starting from fifty [beads] and so forth.
One should offer the six limbs with a tenth part [of the total], saying "Be gracious" (*prasīda*);
then, for the sake of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should proceed toward the southeast, northeast, and north.
Having prayed to the mother of the family at the place of existence (bhavasthāna) regarding one's former dwelling, one should perform the consecration there;
for without consecration, there is no attainment of success.
O beloved, [it may be] circular, or hexagonal, or triangular,
or else four-petalled, or joined with the signs of Aries and Libra.
For one endowed with an even trunk, adorned by a well-proportioned neck,
and possessing arms of equal length extending from the letter *ha* to the end of the alphabet (*kṣa*), he is of standard proportions.
O Dear One, even for a sacrificial ground that has been transgressed, one should perform the ten purificatory rites for the pit (kuṇḍa), such as striking it with heroic ashes and other substances.
One should perform striking, sprinkling, and thereafter rubbing,
as well as extraction and service, using only the weapon-mantra.
O fair-faced one, there is cleansing and dissolution with the armor-mantra;
worship with the heart-mantra at the four paths, and the rosary-bead circle consists of ten [fingers].
The worship should be performed in the sacrificial pit; indeed, perform the ritual in detail in the center.
One should place Vāgīśī, who has bathed after her menses, supine with her head toward the northeast.

One should worship her, who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with offerings such as water for honor and water for the feet; she has two arms and three eyes, and may be worshipped with the Heart-mantra or the Śakti-mantra.
The sipping of water for the fire, its installation in the heart, followed by wrapping and striking, as well as sprinkling and opening; these are the rites.
The eyes should be made immortal and the body veiled;
likewise, the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) [should be performed].
The closing of the mouth should be performed, as well as the opening of the mouth;
likewise the exit, the birth-rite (jātakarman), and the opening of the mouth itself.
Purification of the mouth must be performed, as well as the purification of the name;
however, the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) should be performed with the heart-mantra.
O Dear One, there are ten [rites] outside the sacrificial pit and eight within the pit;
thus, eighteen consecrations must be performed by the Preceptor.
Then, having worshipped the Goddess Vāgeśī, one should dismiss her;
likewise, the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) and the rite of making her face-to-face (saṃmukhīkaraṇa) should be performed.
The offering of liquor, the extensive [offerings], worship, and the enclosing rings;
the weapon of the Lord of the World (Lokeśa) and the complete worship, performed in order starting from the east.
Having gratified the fire by worshipping it with the eight [offerings], one should worship the jar;
the propitiation of the fire and the worship must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Having prepared the *śruka* and *śruva* ladles with the Astra-mantra and placed them upon the *upayāma*,
one should subsequently perform the twelve purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) within the vessel until they are well-melted.
First, there is the heating over the fire (adhiśravaṇa), and likewise the secondary heating (upādhiśravaṇa);
then the splashing with water (utaplavaṇa) and the immersion (saṃplavana), followed by the smearing with unguents (nīrāñjana) and the inspection (nirīkṣaṇa).
One should worship the seat of the Goddess and of the Fire-god within the heart-lotus, performing the satiation of Vahni fivefold and likewise tenfold.
Afterwards, one should install the form of the Goddess, endowed with four bodies;
then the worship should be performed according to the prescribed injunctions as they have been declared.
Thereafter, one should perform a satiation ceremony according to the prescribed rules and as desired,
using goat meat mixed with the three sweets for the sake of pleasing the Goddess.
By means of bilva leaves, fruits, and flowers, misfortune, bondage, and disease are destroyed;
through a hundred lotus-born [offerings], even delusion perishes and sovereignty is attained.
Through red flowers there is gain from trade, and likewise through blue lotuses there is a harvest of grain;
through blue water-lilies (nīlotpala) there shall be nourishment, and through white water-lilies (kumuda) there is the destruction of what is desired.
Through *kunda* flowers one attains peace; through *vakula* flowers, incomparable fame;
through *mallikā* flowers, nourishment (*puṣṭi*); and through *jāti* flowers, the subjugation of Brahmins.
One should bring Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas under control with Campaka flowers; Śūdras with Tagara; and Piśācas with Bandhuka and Pāribhadra flowers.
Through *yakṣā* and *kadamba* flowers, as well as with *arka*, one shall obtain victory;
by offering oblations (*homa*) with *jayantī* flowers, one clearly obtains a treasure-trove.
By means of *palāśa* flowers, the Goddess grants the state of Vāgīśvara;
by means of human flesh, one attains the eight *siddhis*, and even the lowest person shall attain the highest.
Attraction is produced by *rājikā* flowers;
agitation occurs with *karavīra* flowers, and immobilization with *karṇikāra* flowers.
When one offers oblations of guggulu mixed with clarified butter and combined with the "four-fold" (catuḥsama) ingredients,
whatever resides in the mind— all that is accomplished.
By means of an offering of crow feathers, one causes even mountains to be driven away;
by means of round [seeds] and [the flesh of] dogs and other such animals, one brings about muteness.
Having offered oblations with *khadira* wood and *sapala*, one shall kill [the enemy]; there is no doubt in this.
With flowers joined by *dūrvā* grass and sesame seeds, one shall obtain a maiden.
One should increase grain with barley, and one should increase the treasury with grain;
protection arises through the offering of yellow *siddhārtha* seeds.
Through initiation (dīkṣā) and the offering of guggulu resin mixed with *irā* and meat,
as well as with fruit, one attains the fruits [of one's desires], comes under control, and gains an increase in livelihood.
Having thus completed the fire-oblation, one should cause the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be offered according to one's capacity;
having honored the sacrifice with the heart-mantra, one should dismiss the fire with the heart-mantra.
Having worshipped the liquor with three portions, one should unite it with the power within one's own heart,
saying "Forgive me" with the heart-mantra, using the self-seal known as the secret seal.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the sequence beginning with the sons and ending with Gaṇeśa,
thus has the fourfold body been fully elucidated by me to you.
What else does he ask of the Goddess, other than her external and internal [nature]?
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Four Bodies," within the Karavīra Cremation Ground Yoga of the Śrī Kulakrama.
The Goddess said:
O God, I have heard everything concerning the determination of the four bodies; now, speak before me of the initiation that reveals the true divisions of the Kula.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the definitive teaching on the Kula initiation—
the secret transmitted through the Kaula lineage— according to its sequential order.
For one who has been examined and purified, who is devoted to the sequential yoga,
and who has for a long time partaken of the water from the service maṇḍala;
The Guru should bestow grace with a joyful mind upon one whose sacrificial materials have been prepared, yet whose mind is devoid of worldly wealth.
A vessel made of gold and other metals, a red and auspicious cloth for the eyes,
and a water-container made of gold, according to the prescribed ritual for Rudra.
The vessel for clarified butter and the vessel for sesame seeds may be made of silver or copper;
likewise, the tube, the cutter, the knife, and the two containers for incense and lamps.
Sesame seeds and other sacrificial materials, ink, sandalwood and the like,
yellow pigment (rocanā), water-jars, an umbrella, and likewise a moon-shaped ornament;
Dust, the five jewels, and so forth in manifold ways—
these are declared to be the sacrificial materials that awaken one to the path of ritual action.
In the terrible Mahāvīra forest, likewise in the Mahāpitṛvana,
or in the delightful Saṃsthāna, one should construct the temple for the sacrifice.
Having conceived [the site] as being without water, the preceptor, well-composed,
should perform the worship as before, up to the end of the fire-ritual, according to the prescribed rules.
Having offered prayers to the Mother, the Twilight Goddess (Sandhyā), and the noble family of daughters and others,
one should wait with water for the guest-offering (argha) in hand, according to the ritual procedure for the Guru and the Deity.
Sprinkling with water consecrated by the *udyaccha* mantra, one should uplift the mind again and again;
then, by means of the three syllables, one should restrain the two vital breaths (*gāvau*) starting from the left.
One should cause flowers to be placed within the hollowed palms along with the *antaḥkhaṇḍa* mantra;
then, having first uttered the *mātrā*, one should cause [the disciple] to enter the excellent maṇḍala.
At the end of each section, one should place the śakti and offer seven palas of grain;
then, having sprinkled [the area] according to the rule, one should proceed again within the maṇḍala.
Having performed the ritual placement of the mantra-body, one should reveal it with the gaze of the eyes;
O auspicious one, by seven repetitions, one is initiated into all mandalas.
Thus has been fully explained the consecration consisting of the observance;
having attained such conduct, one reaches the state of the power of dreams.
O auspicious one, through the *daśāvarta* [mantra], the state of being a "son" (*putraka*) is established;
this occurs through both service and fire-oblation (*homa*), and there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
And when another day had arrived, having entered within the sacrificial enclosure,
[he performed] the twenty-seven oblations with clarified butter (ājya) that had indeed been sprinkled with the *vipluṣ* drops.
Even by reciting [the mantra] while serving Mahāgaurī with a lotus accompanied by the mantra,
one will undoubtedly attain the state of a practitioner (sādhaka).
Thus, having worshipped the lotus accompanied by mantras, one should serve Ānandabhairava;
then, having sprinkled it with nine jars of water, one should cause the thread and other items to be bestowed.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with devotion in due order,
O Goddess, the great secret lineage of the Mālākulam arises from the Ācārya.
The initiate (samayī), intent on the propitiation of the Guru, should serve the Vidyā;
listen now regarding the spiritual son (putraka), who is the adept (sādhaka) capable in the practice.
The preceptor, motivated by the desire to favor all people, should perform everything— the initiation, the exposition, the consecration, and the various daily and occasional rites.
Thus, O beautiful one, the ritual procedure for the Hotṛ has been proclaimed to you;
I shall further explain another [procedure] which grants success in the Great Melāpa.
When a person possessing a great body and endowed with all auspicious marks has been obtained as one's own object of worship,
one should undertake the sacrifice after receiving his command.
Then, having assumed a heroic form and ascended that body,
one who is composed and single-minded should divide the body into four parts.
One should practice recitation, fire-offerings, and service;
or, if lacking such power, one should take refuge in the power of knowledge.
O lady of excellent hips, the deities cause fear to the practitioner through the application of body, speech, and mind; therefore, one should abandon such dread.
O fortunate one, having undergone initiation in all the mandalas seven times,
he beholds the mandala of the Goddess before him, merged with the sky.
O auspicious one, after ten revolutions, he shall become a son;
O Goddess, one shall behold a son before oneself who bestows great siddhi.
By reciting the mantra twenty-seven times, the practitioner beholds the circle of the Mothers;
he shines before the practitioner—of this there is no doubt.
By reciting it one hundred and eight times, one becomes Bhairava himself;
one beholds the form of Bhairavī, which is the cause of union with Śiva.
Having correctly understood the lineage, the gaze, the speech, the conduct, and the ritual procedure inherited from the family, one shall then attain accomplishment in due order.
Thus, by means of this yoga of union, the initiation of the heroes (vīradīkṣā) has been revealed;
O beautiful one, I shall now further explain the ritual procedure for the Kula initiation.
Having sprinkled water for purification and bound the eye-cloth, one should enter in the proper sequence;
having struck with Kuṇḍalinī, one should place the hand of Śakti.
One should also prepare food for Ānanda in sequence up to one hundred and eight portions;
likewise, one should provide the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the great lamp, which have been handed down through the lineage.
Without the Trika, there can be no perfect accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of aeons;
therefore, having performed the Trika, one should begin the worship of the Guru.
One should worship Gaurī in three ways with one's own body, in eight ways with material offerings, in three ways with speech, and also with the mind.
Thus, whether a mortal man or a woman who is devoted to the one who is compassionate toward his devotees, once initiated in this manner,
shall clearly accomplish every single thing— the entire triad of the hosts of *siddhis*.
O Goddess, the *Dīkṣā-pratyaṅgirā* has been declared in three ways within the Kula;
it has reached the Great Kula as a secret, but only in brief, not in detail.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Three Initiations," in the Karavīra Yoga of the Śrī Kulakrama.
The Goddess said:
O Lord Śaṅkara, please explain how a practitioner may clearly accomplish the assembly of siddhis in its threefold division through proper distribution.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the collection of the threefold attainments (*tridhāsiddhi*),
by which heroes or heroines may accomplish the lineage of the *kula*.

The Vīradīkṣā is not for one who is powerless; having first worshipped according to the rules in a cremation ground, or in the right-hand Śiva tradition, or in a house, or while seated upon a vehicle.
He should always offer lamps and so forth in three ways, and especially on the festival days; he should be truthful in speech, endowed with fortitude, and free from desire and anger.
Whether a hero joined with power and allies,
or one who has allies but lacks resources, or even one who subsists on alms at the onset of night—
First, one should recite the mantra one thousand times for the purpose of purifying the body;
then, the Goddess being pleased, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) exactly as previously described by me.

Then the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day while abstaining from food; if he is unable to maintain the visualization after eating, he should recite it one hundred times at each junction of the day (saṃdhyā).

One should conquer the pair by means of the Gāyatrī, and likewise perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga). Then, at night, one should perform the recitation (japa) according to one's capacity and in the proper sequence.
Thereafter, one should perform the oblation with the ten-fold rite for the sake of attaining perfection in the mantra.
At the conclusion of the homa, a young maiden should be worshipped; then success will certainly be achieved.
Alternatively, the recitation should be performed for double the duration for up to seven days;
in the case of cruel [rites] and so forth, it lasts from the eighth sprinkling until the end of the fire-oblation or the end of the planetary eclipse.
By performing the fire sacrifice (homa) and other rites at the three junctions of the day and at midnight for one, two, or three days,
one who practices them shall obtain the pacification of diseases such as those caused by wind (vāta).
Beginning on either the eighth or the fourteenth day,
by performing the ten-ingredient oblation (daśāṅga-homa) for a period of ten days, great peace will clearly arise.
The mantra practitioner should recite the mantra five hundred times; one should offer three hundred oblations as is appropriate.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, by means of the consecration, one should behold prosperity and indeed attain well-being.
Having recited three hundred times on each occasion until the eighth day,
at the conclusion of the fire oblation, a person attains nourishment of the body through the ritual sprinkling.
Having recited the mantra one thousand times, one should indeed offer five hundred oblations;
by sprinkling [the water], one attains the nourishment of the worlds, including the regions of serpents, horses, and cattle.
By performing this rite at the three junctions of the day, one shall destroy the locks, bolts, and mechanical devices of oneself or another within seven days; of this there is no doubt.
Having taken sand from a cremation ground, one should recite the mantras eight hundred times;
wherever there may be fetters, O Gaurī, their breaking shall occur.
With a staff empowered by Kuśa grass and consecrated three times with mantras,
one may paralyze the masts, carts, and mechanisms of ships, or release them from the wind.

Having recited the mantra seven times over *dūrvā* grass, thread, poison, disturbances, a low-born family, or harmful creatures, one should ward them off by sprinkling great excrement mixed with sand.

Having consecrated a mustard seed seven times, one should strike it upon the heart of the possessed person—whether seized by a spirit or afflicted for days—with the appropriate mudrā; thus, [the affliction] will certainly be cast off.
Fever, including quartan fever and others, are averted by sprinkling water over which the mantra has been recited seven times,
and by the incense of *citrāṅgura* and *rudhūpa*.
It destroys various diseases such as spider-bites, donkey-bites,
and eruptions by sprinkling water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, or by drinking it, or by applying it as an ointment.
Water consecrated twenty-one times will destroy poison, whether stationary or mobile, from the body simply by drinking it.
For the sake of accomplishing the attainment of flowers and food, one should take the ashes of a cremation ground;
by reciting the mantra seven times, one may destroy the enemy and delude him along with his followers.
For one who is constantly devoted to worship, that [merit] becomes inexhaustible when offered into a large vessel, a heap of grain, or jars filled with wine.
Having drawn [the deity] situated within a bilva fruit inside a western treasury on a cloth, one should worship;
wealth equal to that of Kubera shall never perish.
One should worship a string of pearls from a Gajaśāla tree with lotuses and water-lilies;
elephants will never perish, and their increase will come to pass.
Those cows will come to the tree and give much milk.
Having recited the mantra seven times over rājikā (black mustard seeds), one should scatter them in the field of grain and other crops.
There shall be an increase of great crops and the like; insects and such will not enter that place.
White guñjā, serpents, houses, tigers, and cowries [will be found there].
Having recited it seven times, it should be held in the mouth; the breaking of the [protective] seal does not occur.
For children, mustard seeds should be consecrated one hundred times, or an unspecified number of times.
Bound around the neck, these become strengthened by longevity and wisdom;
a *śrīphala* fruit, ripened under the *puṣpārka* [sun], is consecrated with five hundred recitations.
A woman who has not borne a son,
having consecrated herself with its waters and recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, shall give birth to a son when she stands before a jar filled with water.
By that sprinkling, no other [remedy] is required; epilepsy is destroyed. Indeed, a flower garland consecrated one hundred and eight times [is likewise effective].
He upon whose neck this is tied shall become a victor in single combat;
furthermore, he who, having fasted for a day and night, recites it while remaining unassailable, [shall achieve his purpose].
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one is liberated from untimely death;
even if the eighth or fourteenth lunar day falls on a Sunday or a Tuesday.
By reciting half a *lakṣa* starting from this point, one afflicted with leprosy is liberated from leprosy;
[one should visualize] the lotus-like rays revolving within the secret [space], shining upon the face.
Born in the forest, Añjanī beholds a treasure with a thousandfold;
taking earth from a crossroads, she places twenty-five [grains] within half the house.
Having recited [the mantra], one should abridge sleep; even an unfortunate woman becomes submissive.
One should consecrate sesame seeds, rice, and white mustard seeds individually ten times with the mantra.
Having combined these, one should cast them where the enemy cannot set foot;
this mixture of *phalāli* consists of one hundred and twenty-five [ingredients].
When [the ritual] has been performed, one should cast [the substances] wherever the person is ill;
parched grain, unbroken rice, white mustard seeds, and ashes, consecrated one hundred times with the mantra.
Wherever the mantra-practitioner casts [the water], there health prevails;
if one stands in water reaching only to the knees and recites it five hundred times, [the same result follows].
Likewise, by means of oblations to Varuṇa, a great creation will certainly come to pass;
one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times over *arka* and *citraka* flowers.
In whichever village one should cast [the substance], it will burn from side to side within a fortnight;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations and recited the mantra over honey and guggulu resin.
If one should be burned by fire, one should extract [the mantra] from what one has composed;
the practitioner of mantra should then recite it fifty times and likewise perform fifty oblations.
Having recited the mantra five hundred times while using white mustard seeds, the practitioner will undoubtedly bring even the Lord of Śacī under his control within seven days.
If [the powder] is worn on the head, neck, or arm, it destroys the divine [possession];
having offered a hundred oblations of *apāmārga*, one should apply its ash to the person [affected].
It is true that one becomes unfortunate and suffers the destruction of one's joy;
yet, by offering one hundred and five handfuls of *rājikā* seeds, one gains sovereignty over the three worlds.
Within seven days, he by whose name this is performed will be seized by a great eruption;
one should take three hundred pieces of *sidhārtha* and *guggulu*, having combined them together.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, great joy arises, yet that same displeasure may also arise;
one should perform the oblation with eight hundred seeds of gold for seven days.
From that, one quickly becomes intoxicated;
[one should offer] a thousand oblations for three days with round *masūra* lentils mixed with ghee.
An enemy born under [the asterism] Śatabhiṣaj will undoubtedly become deaf;
by offering eight hundred oblations of cow-tusks and alkaline salt, one shall attain blindness.
After seven days, for the night-rite,
one should offer five hundred oblations of cotton seeds, husks, and oil, mixed together, during both day and night.
O Goddess, on the twenty-first day, it may even take away the splendor of Śakra;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Guru, one should recite the mantra a hundred times over the worship-vessel.
Having offered the "three sweets" along with *kāca*, one who has fallen from their vows attains prosperity;
by offering thirty-five oblations of black crow feathers and *aruṣa* grass, one should perform the sacrifice.
The supreme method for the eradication of an enemy is with a banner variegated with ashes;
having mixed ashes with white mustard seeds, one should recite [the mantra] five hundred times.
Having cast [the enemy] into the path of the arrival of his foes, he surely conquers, there is no doubt;
just as one who desires a wick remains victorious over the cloth standing before the lamp.
One should duly worship the women who stand before one’s hundred and five [ancestors],
having fashioned their forms from flour, extending from the feet up to the tips of the thumbs.
Having cut [the thread] five hundred times and offered it, he will marry into his own family;
[this should be done with] vermilion and unbroken rice grains, consecrated one hundred and eight times.
Having performed [the rite], one should place it in the hand of a maiden at the time of the eighth-day offering (aṣṭaka) during the full moon of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
[this consists of] black mustard, soot, and alkali, consecrated ten times with mantras.
Having performed that ritual bath with water, it removes diseases of the spleen and jaundice;
likewise, oil or water consecrated eight times [with this mantra] serves the same purpose.
She who, by her name and through the offering [of water], brings forth pleasant sleep—
one should worship a jar at the location of the head and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
One shall obtain success in matters both beneficial and harmful, as well as in dreams;
or, having recited [the mantra] twenty-five times with wrath, one should employ black mustard seeds and salt.
Due to the binding of the knots at night, one becomes blind in every respect;
having placed a sharp-footed [creature] in the hand, one should mutter [the mantra] over the half-marked corpse.
The accomplishment of the sword (khaḍgasiddhi) arises from a preta and bestows the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
By using half-burnt wood from a funeral pyre, one fashions a pair of sandals (pādukā) possessing a hundred thousand characteristics.
In the same way, success is attained through sandals; from a staff, the power to go among enemies is gained.
Having taken a garment that has been worn [by another] and having performed one hundred thousand recitations of Kṛṣṇa, [one achieves the desired result].
In that very manner, the invisible one sports on the surface of the earth;
awakened by the five-fold fire, he has applied collyrium made from a skull.
When the eyes are marked with half of half of a hundred thousand [recitations], divine vision arises;
having stood upon two most excellent vessels, the wise one should recite half of half of a hundred thousand.
May the spirits, who remove hunger, grant the supreme medicine;
holding twenty-five thousand *vacā* roots in one's hand, one should recite the mantra.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the wise one should consume it; he shall become equal to Vāgīśvara.
A wise person should perform half a hundred thousand recitations, and at its conclusion, on the auspicious day of Śiva (Śivaparvan), [he should perform the rite].
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred times in a cremation ground, one will certainly obtain the perfected rosary;
one should then recite it one hundred thousand times beneath a banyan tree, at the conclusion of which [a mandala] is made with colored powder.
A wise man who, standing in water reaching up to his knees, recites [the mantra] fifty thousand times, will always desire a yakṣiṇī and shall indeed live for a hundred years.
When a hero performs half a hundred thousand oblations with *kadaṃba* flowers, he is born as one named Nāminī, a leader of desire, possessing a lifespan of a thousand years.
Then the vetāla quickly rises from the sacrificial pit and becomes accomplished;
the Kākinī is satisfied by the hero’s homa, as are the hosts of piśācas.
He constantly offers a homa with half of a hundred thousand [oblations], giving one *pala* at each;
taking the hand of a maiden, he performs half a hundred thousand [oblations] in the cremation ground.
Having recited [the mantra], the past, future, and present become fully manifest;
indeed, when one hundred thousand [recitations] have been completed, one stands upon the body of a Vīra.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times more, he goes to the abode of Meru;
at the end of a hundred thousand recitations, he arises in a body within the Vīramaṇḍala.
Having recited it one hundred and eight times, he goes to the abode of Rudra;
at the end of a hundred thousand recitations, however, he reaches Kaliṅga and Vīraka on the summit of Mount Dāru.
Having recited it eight thousand times, one shall attain the world of Īśa.
Thus, O Goddess, has the Geya-mantra been taught, which is middling and supreme.
"Will there be success through the mantras of the three actions, or will the success be uncertain? Listen:
take two *tṛgu* plants and *rocanaka*, consecrated with a hundred recitations of the mantra along with lac."
Having applied a forehead mark (tilaka) made from saffron, agallochum, camphor, and the substance called secana mixed together, whoever looks [at the person] shall bring them under their control.
Whoever makes a tilaka after having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras shall be victorious in battle, in the royal court, in gambling, and in dispute.
