If one is beloved by all women, like the god Kāmadeva himself,

then on the morning of the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], having prepared white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) and a protective amulet (*kavaca*) within a single-vessel belly, one should worship them while mixed with honey.
Having cast it into one's mouth and recited the mantra, one shall achieve victory in debate with others.
Thus, the "Jar-Pillar" (ghaṭastambha) configuration is proclaimed for victory over half-Kāśī;
it is formed by adding one hundred and eighty feathers to the base of a white arrow.
Having placed it upon the crown and the uṣṇīṣa, it wards off the afflictions of others;
[it is empowered] by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times over the ashes, the Lord (Kṣaseśa), and Kālīmātā.
By sprinkling [the victim] with that [substance], one causes enmity toward a hated person;
having recited the mantra one hundred and seven times, [one should place it] dwelling within cow's milk.
One should recite the Siddhārtha mantra one hundred and eight times at the junctions of the day (saṃdhyā) in that place;
however, if on another day a flaw should arise therein, [one must act accordingly].
One should indeed perform the *tapa* rite there during a thunderstorm or a shower of sparks;
at the end of seven days, one should rise up according to the ritual procedure, free from all obstacles.
If it should remain in the hand of the practitioner even after reaching the world of the nāgas,
one should take the ashes from the funeral pyre and combine them with caustic soda (kṣāra).
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, having cast the army [into the fire], it shall go to destruction;
one should then extinguish the fire of a caṇḍāla with fuel-sticks made of khadira wood.
Having cut a figure made of flour into pieces the size of a foot,
one should offer them as oblations for seven days, together with sprouts and ghee.
The entry [into the mandala] occurs through the being, oneself, and wealth;
there should be a thousand [stakes] made of khadira wood, red with goat's blood and provided with leaves.
When seven days have passed, bring the Lord of Śacī;
thus, in the fire of the mango tree, [I shall offer] ashes, pungent substances, bodily impurities, and anger.
By performing oblations at midnight for seven days, the destruction of enemies occurs.
[The materials used are] yellow pigment (rocanā), white dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and black mustard seeds.

When held upon the head after being consecrated one hundred times, it brings auspiciousness in all respects; beginning from Śivarātri, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times at one's ease.
And again, having duly worshipped on Śivarātri,
he then took a human corpse in his hand, or else a beautiful garland in his right hand.
One should go forth like a hero, protecting the virtuous while moving about;
one should continue this going forth until the view has been abandoned seven times.
Placing that lotus in his left hand, ever-arisen in bliss, laughing, singing, dancing,
and leaping, the wise one should proceed to the house of the hero.
Having performed the sacrifice and the *caru* oblation with *korddha* mantras through the application of the maṇḍala,
one of great strength will swiftly behold the Goddess after twenty-one days of recitation.
One should offer them an arghya oblation after piercing the left side of one's own body;
when the arghya has been given, the practitioner will certainly become a manifest sky-walker (khecara).

Then, accompanied by a female messenger (dūtī), the hero (vīra), and the heroine (vīrā), the mantra-practitioner (mantrī) should go to Śrīparvata, which resembles Bhairava himself, and worship Śivā at the mouth of the Śrīmukha cave.
Having recited [the mantra] eight thousand times immediately on the thirteenth day,
and having performed worship on the fourteenth day, one should offer oblations of guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
O God, by constantly offering the sight of lamps three hundred times each night, the practitioner shall become immortal gold; of this there is no doubt.
In other cases, the procedure is likewise, but with three times the quantity of liquor;
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight under the constellation Raudrī, one should gather the materials for worship.
Having gone to the Ātātavana grove, the minister, who is an enemy of heroes, should draw the secret lotus-maṇḍala after having smeared it with fragrant water and cow dung.
Then, having smeared [the seat] with safflower powder or with the ashes of a hero,
one should place it upon the hub of the chariot and fix it facing forward upon the seats.
One should place that lamp in the sky, provided with a wick for desired results,
ignited either with great oil or with fish oil, O beloved.
There, having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite one hundred and eight times,
and having recited the mantra while kneeling with both knees on the ground and placing his joined palms upon his chest;
O Goddess, having informed [the deity] while prostrating with the syllables of Vidiśā,
and then having recited the hundred [times], one should dismiss [the deity] in due order.
Having made the chariot well-protected, one who knows the mantras for subduing the earth should cast it into deep water, a thicket, or an island, facing north.
Having bathed and entered the cave, one shall obtain the fruit at the conclusion of the worship;
for the pacification of calamities, the nourishment of prosperity, and the destruction of passion and other afflictions, a white wick [is used].
For expulsion, she is smoke-colored; for subjugation, she is black and red;
for killing, she is black-colored; and for the purpose of causing disease, she is black-colored.
In incantations for causing enmity, she is five-colored; in paralyzing, yellow;
for the sake of victory, reddish-white; and in attracting, like a ray of light.
Having risen at dawn, at midday, and at the arrival of night,
one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times every single day without fail.
The practitioner endowed with devotion attains all desires;
this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Mahāgaurī, through the repeated sacrifice with bricks.
Thus, all this without exception— the superior, the inferior, and the middling—
is declared to be the treasury of karma when the mantra has been fully accomplished.
O Goddess of the gods, perfect accomplishment (susiddhi) is also achieved through the three wheels;
it is fully perfected, free from obstacles, and endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
Born from sixteen spokes and adorned with seventeen lotuses,
it is endowed with mantras upon its sixteen spokes and brings about the arising of the fruits of all desires.
The great lotus has thirty-two spokes and is adorned with thirty-three lotuses;
it is endowed with eight petals and mantras, and is proclaimed as the Ekavīra.

The third leader of mantras, as proclaimed in the Jāmalatantra, consists of nine lotuses: one with eight petals, one joined with thirty-two petals, and others. It is accompanied by its respective mantra.
Among these three, one should write down a single [mantra] and hold it fast;
upon his body, which is fragrant as birch bark, success shall prevail.
Whether painted on a cloth or carved upon a golden surface,
when the goddess Śrī Sarvatomukhī is worshipped, she becomes present there.

Having written the number of the Vidyās starting from the letter *ka*, endowed each with the splendor of a single syllable, one should worship them according to the secret sequence as they abide in the form of a garland.
By means of the worship mantra (*pūjāmantra*), after six months, one beholds Śrīguhyā herself;
being thus authorized, one attains the glory that is the very nature of the garland.
Having encircled the wheel of phonemes (varṇacakra), O Lord, the goddesses of knowledge (vidyā) are threefold,
fivefold, ninefold, and thirty-two in number according to their sequence.
Through dhāraṇā, there is the destruction of disease, the increase of longevity and prosperity,
the eradication of various obstacles, and the development of intelligence and nourishment.
May the bali offering be complete everywhere; it is the daily rite that destroys obstacles, especially for Vighneśa, Vaṭuka, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Yoginīs.
O you who sleep until midday, accompanied by Nāmanātha, accept this double offering through yoga; grant me success and be gracious!
"Make the armor and weapon free from obstacles, svāhā"—this is the characteristic of the *bali* ending in *svāhā*.
Having thus understood these three, one should offer them according to the words of the Guru.
One should discern that quartet as possessing the seed-syllable, likewise accompanied by the words of the mantra,
descended through the lineage of gurus, and ending with *svāhā*.
One who is initiated and consecrated should extract the wheel of the goddess on Śivarātri,
the new moon day, the great eighth day (mahāṣṭamī), and on the anniversaries of the Yugas.
O Maheśvarī, the purification, the gift, the initiation, and the consecration— along with knowledge of the scriptures at the beginning, middle, and end— are required.
O Goddess, in dispute, victory, a great assembly, or a union,
he who acts otherwise shall not attain success.
Thus has this been fully explained to you, O illustrious one, concerning the sequence of the Guhya-kula,
within the collection of the consecration of the great cremation ground and the worship of the Karavīra.
This most wonderful [mantra] of the fierce Śivā, known as Pratyaṅgirā,
the Goddess of Accomplishment and Fortune, which cannot be obtained even by the gods;
This supreme and divine ritual procedure, transmitted through the scriptures of the Kālī-krama, must be guarded with great effort; one should not give it to just anyone.
To one who is devoted to the guru, who is always immersed in the great scriptures,
and who worships the Ārīśā according to the sequence of the guru’s tradition, [the teacher] shall bestow [this knowledge].
By whomsoever this scripture is written, or in whose hand it remains,
or wherever it is situated— the Supreme Goddess is worshipped there according to the prescribed rites.
O beloved, for as long as he lives, his six-month stay shall indeed be free from obstacles; the sacred site is endowed with deities and devoid of impediments.
He who knows Abhairava becomes like Rudra as a listener;
one who delights in its practice becomes an attainer of all siddhis. || 500 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Application for Accomplishing Siddhi," in the Great Karavīra Yoga of the Śrī Kulakrama.
Thus ends the Five Hundred Verses of Śrī Siddhilakṣmī, as it emerged from the Śrī Kālabheda within the Mahākaravīra Yoga of the Śrī Guhyakulakrama at the Śrī Odyāna Pīṭha.
I bow to the auspicious Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī, who dwells in the Karavīra cremation ground; to Caṇḍā, Pratyaṅgirā, Kālī, and Siddhilakṣmī.
Oṃ, homage to Śivā!
The Goddess said:
By your power, please explain this most secret question, which is profoundly hidden and bestows the ultimate truth— the supreme life-force of the Yoginīs.
Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Sākinī, and Hākinī—
this is the supreme vital breath of these yoginīs, the primary among the primary.
Speak, O God, the secret by which this world is sustained:
the seedless state (*nirbījikaraṇa*), the removal of poison, the self-ignition of fire, the movement through the channels (*nāḍīcāraṇa*), and the shaking of the drops and sounds within the body.
The sequence of the ribs,
the demonstration of the light of the Self, and mastery over death at will— these, O beloved, the sages who know the Vedas declare to be the ten means of realization in the Śaiva tradition.

The internal and external embracing, the movement through the channels (*nāḍī*), and the rites of killing, driving away, causing enmity, and transference—what more need be said? This indeed accomplishes the six supernatural acts (*ṣatkarma*). And this:
How is the Great-Souled One known? How is Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī?
O God, how is worship and adoration performed, and how is one devoted to the Vidyā?
How does the arising of the abode of the mudrās occur? How is the maṇḍala of signs? What is the teaching of the Ācārya? And how does it come to be within the machine of the channels?
How is it that the Great-Souled One is the complexion of the god Varṇarāja? How is his bodily abode the light of the moon and sun, and what is the sequence of the deities?
O Lord, how is the *caruka* offering internal, external, and transmitted?
And how is the third—the *Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī*—threefold as the supreme (*parā*), the intermediate (*aparā*), and the third?
Pratyaṅgirā is the second, while Siddhilakṣmī is the supreme sovereign.
"If you are pleased with me, O God, I am your devotee; speak, O Śaṅkara!"
"O Lord, show me favor; speak to me."
The illustrious Bhairava said:
This is an exceedingly secret internal question, profoundly hidden and bestowing the ultimate truth;
it is a mystery, deep as a cavern, the supreme heart of Khecarī.
Having understood the entire essence of reality, do not strive for that which does not exist,
even through the causes beginning with Brahmā, nor by means of the moon, sun, and fire.
Listen now: that which has not been told to anyone, including the world-protectors and others, shall be spoken to you.
It is not to be told even to the causes such as Brahmā; I shall speak only the absolute certainty, and that which is indeed to be told.
Listen to this great secret, which is endowed with sacrifice and oblation.

Listen to this worship and adoration for the purpose of recitation and oblation; likewise, the practice of *caru*, the assembly of the *samaya*, the threefold sacrifice, and the weapon-mantra of mine bring about the fruit.
I shall describe in brief the most wonderful wheel (*cakra*).

Thus, the wheel descends into the terrible Great Cemetery (*mahāpitṛvana*); the cemetery is the cremation ground, the heart, the totality of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), and the collection of the eighteen channels (*nāḍī*).
He stands.

Where a terrifying, frowning-faced goddess slays the intended victim, that is a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). Or else, there may be a single *liṅga* for the sake of Hara’s consort; whether it be a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) *liṅga*, a *bāṇa-liṅga*, or some other kind of *liṅga*, what other *liṅga* could possibly stand there?
The *liṅga* situated in the middle of the womb, or else located at the *lambikā*;
staying there in that great tree, in your place, in the tree, the staff of breath (*prāṇadaṇḍa*) has its root at the *kaḍoma*.
As far as the *dvādaśānta*, likewise in the forest of the great mountain—there, "mountain" (*giri*) means the peak (*parvata*), and "peak" (*giri*) means greed (*lobha*).
It is peaceful, like a great crossroads; then, having unified the four corners—the Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, and Kuṇḍalinī.
There, it should be four-cornered; or else at a great river—such as the great rivers Gaṅgā or Yamunā.
The place where the iḍā and piṅgalā meet.
In that regard, a river, a great forest,
a night, or a wilderness that is desolate and devoid of people [are suitable].
It extends to the end of the sixteen, is without support, possesses an exceedingly fierce form, is profound, and bestows joy.
Among the great and formidable gods, as if in a village of heroes, [he is] greedy;

the great battle is the death-demoness (mṛtyumaṭakā). The mind of the heroes has been swallowed by her; the meaning is that the "swallowing" of sound and the other sense objects has been performed by them.
Alternatively, wherever the mental [power] becomes strong, that is the place where all things become one; having extracted the Vidyā there, [one should practice].
In each of those places, the high-minded one should proceed with sword in hand.
[This refers to] heroism with sword in hand and personal valor.
O best of heroes, among the Yoginīs and Bhairavas, you are the most excellent.

The eight [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī belong to the Yoginī; O Bhairava, [the eight Bhairavas] beginning with Asitāṅga [belong to them]. Alternatively, there is the man who has conquered anger, and in that very place is Lāmā.
In that excellent and delightful place, one should first perform the worship;
the placement (nyāsa) of the Yoginīs should be done according to rule, with the sixteen others together in one place.
He performs worship there at that former place.
Having performed worship according to the method of the supreme Madhyamaka, through the sequence of the final stage and by means of the sixteen-fold logic,
she— whose nature is the wheel and who is devoted to the realization of the poison— is intent upon awakening.
Residing there, she is the primordial one, who should be worshipped with supreme devotion and with great effort.
It unifies the sixteen-spoked wheel in the manner of a circle.
Brāhmī, Capāktasī, Dhvajinī, Antyajā, Kaṇdukī, Ciñcinī, Chiṣyā, Śoṇakī, and likewise Kṣatriyā.
Mātaṅgī, Carmakārī, Dhīcarī, Mahāmatī,
Śūdrī, Vaiśyā, as well as Īśyā, Dhātakī, and Nartakī.
But these [women], being honored there, are free from the pride of caste. || 16 ||
The Brahmin woman stands at the entrance.
He performs a face-wash.
Wherein the Great Kula Night, which devours the fourteenfold creation of beings, likewise remains as the Wrathful Night.
He creates again. || 1 ||
Puṣkasī is Kapālinī; as Kapālinī, she digests all the channels (nāḍīs), cooks the food, digests the cause, and effects the transformation (saṃskāra).
Likewise, there is the term "puṣkasī. || 2 ||
"She who holds the umbrella" means she holds the umbrella;
the meaning is that she holds the umbrella which is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). || 3 ||
Likewise, she who is the cause of all, the low-born one (antyajā), unites them;
Kubjikā, whose form is the Supreme (parā), licks [everything] as if cutting it all with a sword.
Just as fire burns all grass and wood, so does the lowest caste woman.
Just as from the word *kanda* arise the forms *kandī*, *kandukī*, and *kāndī*.
The Kaṇḍukī, Parapaśyantī, and Madhyamā are the Sovereign Goddess;
she manifests in various forms, appearing individually as distinct essential natures.
Likewise, the state of being a sprout causes the form to mature. || 5 ||
Ciñciṇī stands as the ear-ornament, and likewise she abides in the center of the womb.
He remains with his gaze fixed on something else.
From the center of the womb up to the tip of the uvula,
the Ciñcinī pervades and causes the moon of rasa to flow down.
The washerwoman removes impurity; she burns away whatever impurity there may be— be it merit, sin, or verbal and mental karma—
and likewise causes one to cast off internal impurity and wealth.
It washes away what is impure and externally impure. || 7 ||
Śoṇakī, Khaṭṭakī, Khaṭṭakī—these sever the karma of sound and the rest; they destroy the thirty-six principles, as does Ṣaṭṭakī. 8.
Likewise, the Kṣatriya king, whose nature is that of the vital breath (kṣetriya), sustains the entire body through his power of life-force, and externally, he sustains his subjects. || 9 ||
For the sake of Mātaṅgīkīnī, there is Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī; where she and Nādabindu both regard even a blade of grass as a beast, so too does Mātaṅgī.
The female leather-worker holds the hide; the goddess Māyā holds the hide, or the female leather-worker. || 11 ||
For what reason is she a fisherwoman, and why is she a maiden?
She casts the net of illusion (*māyājāla*) and subsists on fish;
because she does not understand the causes, she calculates [the time], and she sustains a bird in the form of a swan.
Or as a fisherwoman, she maintains whatever karma is auspicious or inauspicious.

The Śūdrī is the bearer of the nectar-portion of the moon; she is the form of the moon, created for the sake of the objects produced by the moon, and likewise, having performed the shaving of the forest for the purpose of creation—this is the meaning of "Śūdrī. || 13 ||
The Vaiśyā is called by the word *veśyā* because her activity (*karma*) abides as the totality of the five causes—Soma, Sūrya, Agni, and the rest.
Thus, the Vaiśyā manifests her activity in the form of the house and the stars. || 14 ||
That which is called Mālinī is the form of the Mother, the flower that arises as the totality of causes.
For the purpose of manifestation (*unmeṣa*), she is likewise the unfolding of the mass of flowers; by means of the root, she is the two ears of the auditory organ, free from destruction.
Thus, she is the "form" (*rūpa*) which is the "flower," and she is the one who produces the flower. || 15 ||
Likewise, the dancer, in the form of the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), moves through the stages of life according to the appropriate half-periods.
There is shaking, leaping, steadiness, and horripilation; there is seeing from afar and hearing from afar; the two ear-lobes are both present and yet devoid of duality.
The meaning is "a female dancer" (nartakī).
Thus, the first family, consisting of sixteen [deities], should be known.
But the arrival [of the sūtra] is for the sake of the subject matter at hand.
When these goddesses are worshipped, they bestow the fruits of all desires;
thus, one who desires specific results should worship them according to their wish.
The Supreme Goddess should be worshipped on the six petals with the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
That which is to be spoken in the east is "bhagna-nāśikā" (broken nose); below that is this "dvirepha" (two *r*s), wherein the letter *i* is seen.
Standing at the side of the moon and sun, there is the sequential vision of the goddesses;
their noses are broken, their voices are broken, and their crests are broken in form.
The heart-lotus is downward-facing, and likewise the lotus and the mouth;
thus the bulb (kanda), the double-repha, the solar orb, and again the repha, the lunar orb, and the moon— these he unites.
For what reason does the sun appear at the very tip of the mouth?
The letter *i* is seen in the form of destruction.
The moon and sun are situated at her sides; likewise, the two eyes on her sides are Soma and Sūrya.
For the purpose of encompassing both the internal and the external, the Goddess does not unite them [into one], but is attained in her own essential nature.
Thus ends [the section on] the broken nose.
One should worship these goddesses, for they bestow the fruits of all desires.
Thus [ends] these [sections].
Having reached those locations there, which are free from depressions and elevations;
Who would worship the eldest in the proper place, observing the supreme seniority of the third [lineage], the supreme seniority of command? Who here would worship that whose sign descends?
At the beginning of that [practice], one should perform worship on ground free from depressions and elevations;
one does not avoid anyone at all, but beholds every person as being composed of the universe.

One should worship there in the argha-vessel at midnight; at that time, during the night, one worships along with the Kula and Kaula [deities]. The place of the itch (kaṇḍu-sthāna) is moistened by the Kulakaula.
Then, at the half-watch of night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one performs the worship.
Having prepared the arghya vessel with auspicious water— water by way of the sound [of the mantra] and the nectar of bliss from the supreme state of Brahman— one should then perform worship.
The Secret of Gaurī.
With Mahāphalguṣa incense and great red pigment,
one should illuminate the bowls and all the continents with great oil throughout the night.
One should cause to be offered fragrant incense for worship, a vessel of great red [substance] as an *argha* offering, a lamp of great oil, and red *karavīra* flowers.
In every respect, during the night, it causes the island of the Brahma-nāḍī to expand.
Having kindled the lamp of the mind at the two openings of the root of the palate—
[the two] which are devoid of duality and non-duality— one should apply the *tilaka* to the heart and dissolve it in equanimity.
Thus are the offerings for the *arghapātra*, whether divine, superior, or inferior.
The offerings are both superior and inferior; these offerings extend from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, up to Sadāśiva.
The five elements— earth, water, fire, air, and space—
and the offerings consisting of superior, middling, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
O best of heroes, one should administer the liquor for drinking, as well as linctuses and powders; it shatters the god of the gods who dwells in the middle station.
There are seventeen kinds of liquors, as well as various types of foods to be licked and sucked; these are the prosperities.
Now, one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
The body does not restrain the mind.
Therein, having extracted from the wheel, that vidyā consists of sixteen [syllables] plus one.
And having raised it upward with the arms extended, one should then lift it up.
One should place the double-tongued [letter] *ū* above *ja*;
likewise, the seed-syllable of fire is *ra*.
But it should not be given above.
That which is joined with destruction is *ī*.
One should conquer the person in one place;
