followed by three *phaṭ* syllables—*phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*—adorned at the end with the word *homa*.

Svāhā || 7 || Section 34 || 225 syllables for this mantra-section || Section 34 || One should indeed join this third section-vidyā together in one place. It consists of exactly two hundred and ninety syllables; it is known as the Mālā-mantra, the eldest [of the three], which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis).
Whatever exists, moving or unmoving, is accomplished through this tantra:
the Samaya, Siddhilakṣmī, Jayadratha, Guhyakālī, Rājalakṣmī, and Śivā-Pratyaṅgirā. There is no auspicious Vidyā equal to this, which performs all rites; this Vidyā is a Mahāvidyā.
The collection of garland-mantras is not recollected; indeed, they are not bestowed [as separate entities], for they are illuminated by their own inherent nature.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Samayāmātṛmālā," in the twenty-four thousand [verse] work according to the system of Śrī Kālasaṃkarṣaṇa.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the supreme recitation (japa),
which is dedicated to the power intent on recitation and meditation, and joined to the path of sound (nāda).

What kind of recitation does he perform? He recites as many times as one thousand from a hundred single-syllable [mantras]. What kind of meditation is it? It is that wherein one does not recall any collection of instruments or any mantra.
That which one should not remember: one should not remember the body; one should not remember shame, suspicion, or fear.

Thus, having become like a piece of wood, one should not conceptualize anything, nor recall anything, even when afflicted by cold or hunger. When that meditation is practiced, one should recall it as soon as it is meditated upon; what else could its nature be?

From the bulb (kanda) to the coiled one (kuṇḍalinī), from the coiled one to the filament (keśara); from the filament to the region of the bulb, situated from the throat to the middle of the eyebrows; from the middle of the eyebrows to the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), and from the twelve to the end of the sixteen. She is curved in form like a serpent and possesses nine colors.
One should rub.
Like a serpent, Kuṇḍalinī is coiled and crooked; she is inaccessible and consists of nine colors. She should strike the nine gates.
With her contraction formed into a bud-like fold, she extends from the *kanda* up to Kuṇḍalinī; from Kuṇḍalinī to the heart;
from the heart to the pit of the throat (*kaṇṭhakūpa*); and from the pit of the throat to the middle of the eyebrows.

From the midpoint of the eyebrows to the *dvādaśānta*; from the *dvādaśānta* to the *ṣoḍaśānta*. Above that, it remains without support. It should be contemplated very gradually, just like the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*).
At the time of rising, one should likewise meditate upon the blazing fire, pure like a clear crystal.
Then, one should contemplate the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) as it emerges from the opening of the palate through the channel of Indra (indragopa), by means of the application of the Brahma-nāḍī.
The indragopa is in the sky, in the space at the end of the twelve; by the word *indragopa*, one perceives the expansion of the five senses—sound and the rest—within that conscious mind.
By the term *indragopaka*, the host of luminaries is seen in the sky.
Emerging from the cavity of the palate, [it reaches] the Pātāla of the palate-guardian; there, within the nine cavities, is the end of the sixteen.
It issues forth from the upper *kanda* as far as the support of *nīla*, or else it issues forth to the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).
By means of the yoga of the flame-form *brahmanāḍī*, one should pierce the solar disc in the center of the well-supported *brahmanāḍī* very gradually,
until the lunar disc is unified with it through the three [channels] at the left and upper apertures.

The left eye is in the left nostril at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*); the right eye and ear are in the right nostril, the portal of Brahmā (*brahmakapāṭa*). From all these, the stone emits flames; then, as if from the hands, there are crests of fire and tongues of flame.
Just as the sun [is obscured] by clouds, and just as the moon [is obscured], one should restrain the mind there. This is the meaning here:

this meditation is indeed external, as before. By focusing on the mantra alone, one shall attain accomplishment (*siddhi*), which brings about the desired fruit. One hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*). With ten million recitations (*koṭi*), the *kanda* [is attained].

I bow to that which is both movement and non-movement for one who has dissolved into the Supreme Reality— having dissected [the body] down to the marrow, until the state of being is attained, and wherever the mind finds rest, there the wheel of Brahma is at the navel and the wheel of Viṣṇu is in the heart; by this, where the mind rests, it effects the destruction of afflictions through a hundred thousand recitations.
When this has been recited one hundred thousand times, by twenty-seven recitations he will become initiated.
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one who seeks fortune clearly attains it;
by reciting it one hundred and eighteen times, there is the destruction of great fear.
Having thus recited it one thousand times, one causes the Daṇḍanāyaka to increase;
then, having recited it a full thousand times, sovereignty is attained instantly.
Alternatively, by reciting ten thousand times, the state of divinity is proclaimed;
and by reciting twenty thousand times, one obtains a vision of me, Rudra.
Likewise, by reciting it three times, one becomes Sadāśiva, the state of Īśvara;
and by reciting it eight times, the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva) arises.
Likewise, by reciting it ten times, one attains equality with me through the goddesses;
O Goddess, as you are, so shall he become equal to me in body.
With body, head, and neck held straight and motionless,
one should gaze at the tip of the nose and not look toward the directions.
Having performed the unsurpassed recitation ten times the number of oblations,
one should perform the *homa* accompanied by the letter *ma*, which is accomplished through the state of purity.

Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at the outset, one should perform the sacrifice— which is free from the destruction of sacrificial animals and performed with a state of intense absorption— while the mind is filled with the bliss of wine.
One who desires accomplishment should first perform the examination of the secret and the non-secret— the five most beautiful jewels— and thereafter carry out the recitation.
In a cremation ground, or at a solitary tree, or else at a crossroads; on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, or in an empty house.
One should perform this recitation and subsequently practice meditation in a cremation ground, a cave, under a tree, or in a peaceful place.
The crossroads are the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* meeting at one point;
the mountain is the space between the eyebrows; the empty house is the *suṣumnā*;
and the heart is the mind.
The rivers are Iḍā and Piṅgalā; these, when recited, perform this [function].
One should meditate upon the supreme goddess, who is formidable, terrifying, six-faced, and three-eyed;
she has thirty-six [forms], four arms, is equipped with weapons, and bestows success.
One meditates on her who has a fierce and terrifying form, possessing six faces and thirty-six arms.
Trilocanā is meditated upon in the midst of the yoginīs.
Mahāyogeśvarī is in the east; Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī is in the south; Karaṅkiṇī is said to be in the north; and likewise, Krodhinī is in the west.
On the left is Vāmeśī, and above is the one called Bhāsā, who is higher than the highest;
one should employ the upper face—thus it is called the six-faced [deity].

A ĀḤ! May the devouring of time, the great fall, the fall of lightning, the fall of thunderbolts, the upward fall, the downward fall, the fall at the end of the eon, and the occurrence of the great dissolution [be averted].
Thus it is established that the seven great portents cause [the world] to fall.
The first [section] consists of five syllables beginning with *pā-ta-ni-pā-ta*. The second is established as being situated in *pā-ta*.
The third *pā-ta* is specified; it is proclaimed to consist of nine syllables.
The thirteenth is known as the state resulting from the fourth sign.
The fifth fall is situated and pervaded by seven locations;
the sixth fall is likewise pervaded, devoid of both the signified and the signifier.
The eastern face is Yogeśī; because of the word "yoga," she is Yogeśī.

Odyāna is the sacred seat (pīṭha). Khphreṃ is the form of withdrawal (saṃhāra). Therein, from the center, arises the five-fold mass (pañcapiṇḍa) of the Lord (nātha), which is the tradition of bestowing withdrawal through the mouth of the true guru.
The second face is Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī, the right face;
the syllable *klīṃ* is the Jālandhara seat. The third face is the northern face; Karaṅkiṇī, Pūrṇapīṭha, and the goddess Kubjikā are produced from the syllable *śrīṃ*.
The fourth and final face is Krodhinī, the Mistress of the Left;
she is the seat of Kāmarūpa, arisen from the syllable HRĪḤ.
The fifth is the seat of Śakti, the goddess Vyomavāmeśvarī, arisen from the syllable AI.
Above that is the seat (pīṭha) called Amā, belonging to Bhāgeśvarī, which is produced from the syllable Hsauṃ; thus the six faces are described in brief.
This six-faced [mantra] is obtained from the mouth of the Guru.

Furthermore: What is the nature of the Blessed Lady Pratyaṅgirā? She is the Goddess Siddhilakṣmī, the thirty-sixth deity, four-armed, and the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). I shall describe her weapons;
listen as I explain them to you exactly as they are: 1. sword, 2. skull-cup, 3. trident, 4. stone, 5. *khaṭvāṅga*.
6. Goad (aṅkuśa), 7. Noose (pāśa), 8. Lute (vīṇā), 9. Axe (paraśu), 10. Double-headed serpent (dviphaṇi), 11. Thunderbolt (vajra), 12. Hammer (mudgara), 13.
Arrow (bāṇa), 14. Bow (cāpa), 15. Wheel (cakra), 16. Lotus (padma), 17. Book (pustaka), 18. Varada (gesture of granting boons).
Thus they have been described for the right side; now hear them for the left, O fair-faced one.
1. mace, 2. dagger, 3. staff, 4. discus, 5. scissors, 6. linga, 7. shaven head.
Ḍamaru 8 || Mace 9 ||
10. Śakti; 11. Kamaṇḍalu; 12. Maṭaka; 13. Kalaśa; 14. Brahmakaṅkāla;
15. Pāśupatāstra; 16. Āgneyāstra; 17. Vāruṇāstra; 18. Abhaya.
O Goddess, it is said that grace from the Great Goddess is obtained on the left-hand path.
And that which is proclaimed in the Left-hand Path (Vāmamārga) possesses thirty-six arms and weapons.
She upholds the thirty-six principles.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well.
Sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; the organs of speech, excretion, procreation, feet, ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; and the mind, intellect, and ego—these constitute the primary principles.
The restraints and observances for the person, passion, time, and knowledge, as well as the purification of knowledge.
Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śiva.
Thus, there are thirty-six principles (tattvas). || 36 ||
And the thirty-six weapons shall now be described.
Thus has reality been fully explained; one should understand it as being without hands. It has many feet and many arms, and its number is not known.
Therefore, this entire form is both with parts and without parts, originating from that which is both with and without parts.

Thus it is said: "The seat is worshipped; the lotus-seat (padmāsana) is worshipped, and upon its back the *preta* is said to be located. Upon its back should be Indramuṇḍa, and behind Indra is Brahmaka."
Upon its back should be Viṣṇumunda, and upon Viṣṇu’s back, Rudraka;
and upon his back, Sadāpūjya, and Sadājya, who is indeed the Muṇḍa.
O Goddess, one should worship these five great pretas upon his back;
[and then] the Great Lotus-heart, in its contraction and expansion.

Behind that, in the central pericarp, is the sixty-fifth, the *preta*, by the word *preta* [is meant] that which exists within it— the sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; this is the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
This certain woman outside is acting like Indra for the sake of being embraced;
O shaven-headed one, the head of Indra is worthy of worship! || 1 ||
In the center, having known the existence of Brahmā as Viśvādya and others, one should worship the Brahmamuṇḍa. || 2 ||
In the center, when the functioning has dissolved and one rests in union with Viṣṇumuṇḍa, that which is to be worshipped is Viṣṇumuṇḍa.
When nothing at all expands through the functioning of the subtle elements—the cause of all—it is Rudramuṇḍa;
thus, Rudramuṇḍa is to be worshipped.
By the practice of always remaining seated, one becomes distinct from other beings; thus, the Lord’s Skull (Īśvaramuṇḍa) is to be worshipped. || 5 ||
The head of Sadāśiva, which is the "Mantra" throbbing with the sound of the half-measure of consciousness (*cid-arddha-mātrā*) and so forth, is to be worshipped;
behind it, the Goddess is to be worshipped. O Goddess, what is that essential nature? It is the outpouring of the flood of supreme bliss of equanimity (*samarasa*).
Then, O Bhagavatī, the support for the stages of absolute tranquility, which is the cessation of one's own essential nature, unfolds.
I worship the venerable sandals of Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī Samayā Khphreṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Siddhilakṣmī Ambā.
Protect me, who have come for refuge; protect me!
By this reasoning, salutations to the essence of the five mudrās.
One should worship with the intention of [pleasing] the bodies of the goddesses. With the mantra *kha pha ra e ma* (khphreṃ), one should perform the worship.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with the mantra "khaphara."
Kha is space; Pha is wind; Ra is fire; E is water; Ma is earth; O is Jālandhara; Pū is Kāmarūpa;
Kā is beyond form (kāmarūpātīta); Ākāśa is the form of Pūrṇagiri; Vāta is the foot Jālandhara; Tejas is Odyāna, the body Piṇḍa, and the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha); Pṛthivī is the skin of the body.

The auspicious water (*śivāmbu*), the bloodless radiance (*apārakta-tejas*), the bone-wind (*asthi-vāta*), and the marrow-space (*majjā-ākāśa*)—thus it vibrates fivefold as the five colors (*pañca-raṅga*). This is the mantra for the determination of the five lumps (*pañca-piṇḍa-nirṇaya*). One should worship in this manner.
For one seeking liberation (*mokṣārthin*), white flowers are prescribed; for one seeking enjoyment (*bhogyārthin*), red is said to be used; for one seeking desire (*kāmārthin*)—
The intention is as follows: yellow color is for [the purpose of] killing, while black is prescribed [for other purposes]. Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhinī, and Saṃkarṣaṇī are worshipped outside on the left side;
now listen to those on the right. The Goddess is of unchanging form (akāmarūpa), and her pervasion of the sun extends from the letter 'A' to the end of the letter 'A'.

The pervasion of Fire extends from the letter *ka* up to the letter *bha*; the pervasion of Soma extends from the letter *ma* up to the letter *sa*. According to this principle, the letter *a* is the power of manifestation (*utpatti-śakti*), while Karaṅkiṇī is the power of form (*rūpa-śakti*) and Saṃkarṣiṇī is the power of extraction (*saṃkarṣaṇa-śakti*).
One should worship according to this principle by way of the left-hand path (vāmamārga).
Khecarī, Lelihānā, and the third, Bhairavī, are worshipped on the right path; Kṛśodarī is to be worshipped in the middle.
The supreme power, the licking one, the transcendent power Bhairavī.
The power of the supreme-and-non-supreme is thus: in the supreme [state], there is the non-supreme-and-supreme, and the supreme.
One should worship on the southern path with the goddess previously mentioned; she is to be worshipped in the center.
First is Trailokyamohanī, who in an instant deludes the three worlds;
she is the second, Jayadrathavatsalā; and the third is the goddess Siddhilakṣmī-Pratyaṅgirā.
In the fourth [chapter], there are two hundred and ninety; likewise in the Siddhisaṃketaka, the Siddhilakṣmī, and the Jayadratha.
One should grasp the name "Pañca," as those who know the past and future declare.
Mahādevī Rājyalakṣmī is the supreme deity of the kingdom; she is not another, but quite distinct—listen now!
I shall describe the worship established through the oral tradition:
Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka are the two vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna), while the Lord (Īśvara) is the Guru. The letter 'A' belongs to the letter 'A';
it is a spark of consciousness from which the fifty phonemes radiate.
And first, O Goddess, they are worshipped as previously described by the Goddess; [the worship] joined with the twelve goddesses. The meditation upon the twelve goddesses will now be explained.
She has five faces, eight arms, and three eyes;
she stands upon a corpse, holds a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and has her hands placed upon a lotus and a severed head.
She holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), while a skull shines in her hand;
the sword is declared to be the eighth [attribute]; and this is the twelfth meditation (dhyāna).
These are the twelve months.
Then there are twelve digits (*kalā*), and then the elements (*dhātu*) equal in number to the Sages (*muni*).
Again, the six-spoked [wheel] is worshipped. One should worship the Supreme Goddess (*parameśvarī*): she is dark, terrifying, fierce, and adorned with a garland of entrails.
She has one face and three eyes, wears a garland of severed heads, and possesses four arms.
She has a shaven head, is radiant, feeds upon lotuses, and holds a noose and a goad.
Alternatively, these six—the sword and the knife—are the supreme meditation;
furthermore, they are worshipped in the center, and thereafter one should worship the Samayas.
She has five faces, ten arms, and is endowed with fifteen eyes;
she is radiant, her food being the *pretas* and Rudras, and she possesses the luster of moonbeams and jasmine flowers.
She holds a skull-topped staff, a sword, a noose, a goad, a trident, and an alms-bowl;
she also holds a jar and a human head, endowed with hands that grant boons and fearlessness.
One should worship Vaiśvānara and Mārtaṇḍa, and in the middle of the lunar disc,
the Goddess who holds various weapons in her hands and bestows desired fruits;
one should also worship Śaṅkhinī and Śivādūtī on the left and right sides.
Having honored all this, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Thus ends the third chapter, the *ṭippaṇaka* on the rules for worship, in the venerable *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇīmata*, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
The Goddess said:
How does the *caruka* and the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) come from mouth to mouth?
How is the mantra, how the external [ritual], and how is the location established?
O Lord of Gods, O Supreme Lord, tell me how that state [is attained].
And this [is as follows]:
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this secret that is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
it has never before been declared as the supreme life-force of the Yoginīs.
The best, the lowest, and the middling, as well as onion and garlic,
*gañjana*, *viśvakṣāra*, *harāmbu*, and *rudra*.
The sheaf of grain, clarified butter, the womb-flower, the fish, the Prākāśika-caru, and Hālāhala, the best of gods—these sixteen are proclaimed. (16)
Thirteen principal [oblations] and a caru oblation.
Mind, ear, eye, tongue, nose, intellect, ego, and the state of mind-transcending.
Compassion, suspicion, fear, shame, disgust, lineage, and character. || 16 ||
And furthermore:
The bath is performed with the *janma*, *kanda*, and *nābhi*; the heart is the tortoise;
the subtle is the middle; the half-moon is the end of the *nirodhinādā*; and the blue lotus is the support.
Thus, there are thirteen principal locations; they are worshipped from the new moon day until the first lunar day (pratipad) has arrived.
One should worship in direct order from the first day (pratipadā) up to the fifteenth day;
[and in reverse order] from the new moon (amāvāsyā) until the end of the first day.

Having worshipped one *caruka* on the full moon day, one should worship them in reverse order until the new moon; thus, for both the dark and light fortnights, one should take up one [offering] each day.
Likewise, listen to [the description of] the dark fortnight and the full moon of the bright fortnight.
Henceforth I shall explain the ritual procedure; listen now.
Whatever [image] is fashioned from a boat-pole and melted with mercury—
One should kill the mind there, yet one should not consume "great meat" (māhāmāṃsa).
"Taraṇḍa," "taraṇḍa," refers to the staff, the left-hand path, or the nature of the wind.
The letter *ta* is the pole of the boat on the southern path, having the nature of fire (*vahni*).
The pole in the form of the letter *ra* is in the middle, having the form of the *anaskalā*.
That place, being covered, should kill the mind.
One should not eat human flesh.
And furthermore: || 1 ||
The ear, the skin, the eyes, and the tongue—these two pairs are devoid of duality;
one should not consume even a tiny fragment [of it], let alone eat beef.
It does not hear sound, it does not see form, the tongue does not taste; the heart does not grasp. Free from duality and devoid of the two, it abandons all this.
The yogi eats and consumes the essence of *sāmaṃrambhikā* day after day; he becomes free from old age and death. [This is] the *gomāsa* [chapter], the second.
The support of the *kanda*, the radiance (*ullāsa*), and the form of sound (*nāda*) are located at the *ghaṇṭikā*;
that digit (*kalā*) should consume the nectar (*amṛta*), and not the flesh of birds.
From the bulbous foundation (kandādhāra) up to the uvula (lambikā), that is the digit of nectar (kalāmṛta).
One should avoid thirst that is characterized by a parched throat and a craving for water. || 3 ||
One who has heard the teachings of the Moon, the Lord of Indus, which are as sweet as molasses and warm as honey, and who possesses a treasury of youth and immortality, shall not eat onions.
"Palasya aṇḍum" means onion; it is hot and causes the growth of the uvula.
One should slowly cause the fire to ascend from the seat of the kanda to the dvādaśānta in the form of the moon and vital air;
or else, one becomes ageless and immortal. || 4 ||

The letter *la* is the *lambikā*, and the letter *ma* is food; by means of that, one should take the garlic (*laśuna*) which is intoxicated by the juice of drink. Then, the fire of the crescent moon (*śaśikalā*) dissolves the *lambikā* at the letter *ma*.
The ankle does not succeed; nor do the yogas. 5.
The flame-olfactory [sensation] at the tip of the tongue is the consumed circle of fire;
it is called "roaring" by way of the path of the fire-root-teeth.
Whence should one bring the *gṛñjana*? That which is the *viśvacaru*, situated within the fire of Vātraghna;
the meaning is that one should take the excrement from where there is the swallowing of the Moon and the Sun.

The *viśvāgni-caru* [offering]; the swallowing of the moon and the sun. For what purpose? On the path of the left (*vāmamārga*), one should not awaken the Kuṇḍalinī by means of the touch of air through inhalation (*pūraka*).
Thus, when the swallowing of the moon and sun has been performed, one should bring forth the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*) into the excrement there. || 7 ||
Having joined the tube and the instrument, the [substance] melted by fire and moon,
and the warm fluid of the uvula, from where would one obtain the water of Śiva?
The Kuṇḍalinī is caused to flow; there, in that quadrangular assembly of the apparatus of the channels (nāḍī-yantra), one listens. || 8 ||
One should ward off blood, the sun, the moon, Venus, and the planet Mars;
by that, one eats not of flesh, and one should gather the flowers of light.
The sun is the male seed (rakta), the moon is the female sphere (golaka), and the wind is the vital breath;
the Puruṣa is Śiva and the woman is Śakti—thus the triad of Śiva and Śakti experiences bliss.
The source, the flower, is obtained as its own essential nature. || 9 ||
Having applied the vāḍava-karaṇa, the three impurities are burned away;
the nectar [is held] in the pit of the throat, but one should not swallow the phlegm.
His intention is as follows: "The goddess is the digit of the moon situated above; she is perfectly tranquil, full, immortal, and consists of the essence of bliss."
There are three fears because of the specific conjunction with fire, since there is both heat and the liquefaction of the moon.
Because it has abandoned both brilliance and clothing,
that form of the descent of the Sun arises from that Lord who has entered the state of rest in the twelvefold [cycle].
One should rub away the cause that has fallen from all states of existence;
one should not rub away the sacrificial pit, the food, nor the female and male organs.
Thus it is said.
The staff, which is the very life-force, is established at thirty-six finger-breadths;
the yogi devoted to practice therein should not draw it out.

The movement [of breath] consists of thirty-six finger-breadths; the life-staff (prāṇadaṇḍa) corresponds to the thirty-six principles (tattvas). Therein, the yogi devoted to practice attains a certain degree of that true nature (svarūpa). || 12 ||
The moon and the sun are the two eyes; when they are merged at the center of the eyebrows, the yogi who delights in practice there does not perceive external light—this is the meaning. || 13 ||
The sky is the vessel, and that which abides there is without support;
the yogi intent on practice dwells therein, and not in the *hālāhala* sacrificial oblation.
The yogi should practice the meditation on the *hālāhala* oblation, the sky, the ether, and likewise the blue space at the limit of twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśānta*). || 14 ||
The gods and the asuras dwell within the left and right channels;
that [channel] wherein the liquor is drunk is indeed the liquor, and no other should be known as such.
On the left are the gods; on the right are the asuras. He brings about the unification of these two.
The essential nature of bliss is obtained through the grace of the Guru;
the central channel has dissolved, and the body is filled with Bhairava.
One may drink that [liquor] produced from molasses or from sugarcane, but not that which is produced from grapes or from jujube. || 15 ||
One should join the middle *vālava* with its own nature;
by drinking the juice of that liquor, one does not experience the thirst born of small desires. 16.

"In this way, O Dear One, the Lord has declared that when the Wheel has thus arrived for the purpose of relishing [the reality] through the methods of yoga, the Yoginīs attain it and achieve perfection."
First, one should perform the external [practice], and afterwards, one should practice internally;
practicing by means of the application of the five, [one should contemplate] the triangle rooted in Śakti.
The slender-waisted woman is constantly nourished by it and finds satisfaction therein.
Whether it be one's mother, wife, daughter,
or even a courtesan, at the appropriate time, one should avoid treating them with contempt.
They desire success through concealment; otherwise, there will be a fall.
Thus ends the fourth commentary, titled "The Tradition of the Caruka," within the *Śrīkālasaṃkarṣaṇīmata* consisting of twenty-four thousand verses. 4.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak again of that which was previously declared:
Gayā is the first channel (nāḍī); Gayā is the Suṣumṇā and the Kuṇḍalinī.
The *kalevara* mantra shall be the essence.
Its twelve roots, as well as the six limbs beginning with the heart, are likewise twelve. (6)
He is said to be in the paternal vessel situated above.
In the vessel for the six ancestors (*ṣaṭpitṛpātra*) on the path of the gods (*devayāna*), there are six; by means of the six [vessels] on the path of the gods, eighteen are proclaimed. Thus, 18.
That which has gone through the six cavities of the palate is said to belong to the six suns;
that which is between the two [cavities] of the head and the excrement is pervaded by one.
The Kuṇḍalinī carries the wind for three nights, and the Śukravāhā [carries it] for three nights; whatever action is performed during that time, it is accomplished through the Suṣumnā channel.
The *iḍā*, the *piṅgalā*, and the third, the *suṣumnā*—
the yogin who is devoted to their practice shall not undergo birth again.
I shall now proclaim another [mandala]; listen to it now.
One should daily smear [the ground] with cow dung; cow dung is the thread of truth and is of equal flavor.
The *sūtra* is the mind; the practice of austerity and recitation is performed. One should prepare five-colored powders and the powder of the five jewels from rice.
One should then grind the rice powder together with the powder of the *yoni*.
A hexagon should be drawn there; the hexagon is the heart, wherein one's own true nature is obtained.
In the center, the *yoni* is given; outside that *yoni* is the solar disc, and outside of that is a square.
Or that which is full.

On the left and right, two second lines are for the two vital breaths, prāṇa and apāna; below, two and two [lines] are given. Then, with the overflowing of Śiva and Śakti, the wise one should fashion the form of Māyā as a square. He should construct a gateway (toraṇa) provided with banners and arches, along with a boat-shaped staff (taraṇḍadaṇḍa).
The banner extends to the limit of twelve finger-breadths.
And furthermore:
The swing, the movement of the machine, the fivefold Kuṇḍalinī, and the fivefold banner in the unblemished state—this is the illustration.
The flag is the five causes; Kuṇḍalinī is fivefold, [attained] through inhalation and descent.
The true nature is attained. Within the hexagon are the twelve Ādityas belonging to the Goddess. || 12 ||
In the center of Śivādūtī and the others is Kṛśodarī, the vital power (prāṇaśakti). In the middle of that square, one should worship [the goddess] on the left and the right. Of the Goddess.
One should worship Śaṅkhinī and Śivādūtī as a pair in the upper [direction]; Kṛśā and Pūrṇā in the lower; and one should always worship Vyomavyāpinī in the center and Samayā in the middle.
Siddhilakṣmī, in the form of the letter *An*, is to be worshipped outside of that on the right.
Likewise, there is the worship and adoration of the Guru; salutation to the Guru. The letter *A* was explained previously.
On the left path is Gaṇeśa, and on the right is Caruka; [there are] the threads of Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka, and Prāṇa and Apāna. "O Goddess, one should worship these," thus said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Altar and the Mandala," in the commentary on the Śrī Kālasaṃkarṣaṇīmata.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the fire-ritual according to the rule:
a hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made with a measurement of thirty-two finger-breadths.
Kuṇḍabrahmabila has thirty-two heroic deities;
furthermore, the group beginning with the letter 'ka' and ending with 'kṣa' consists of three parts, starting from Aries.
Having formed [the mudrās] of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, and of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara: with one finger [is] Viṣṇu, with two [is] Rudra, and the third [is] Brahmā;
thus I shall explain to you correctly the manner of making the *meṣalā*.
O lady of excellent hips, a wise man should perform the fire sacrifice with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and a thousand bilva fruits for the sake of attaining enjoyments.
One should perform a homa with three red karavīra flowers combined with goat’s blood; this destroys great fear.
When great danger has arisen and there is a massive conflict with enemies,
one should offer flowers from the Brahma-tree and guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter.
A fire sacrifice should be performed with three oblations to destroy great fear:
ghee, food smeared with ghee, and milk-rice mixed with curd.
Sesame seeds and clarified butter are prescribed, as are mustard seeds; each one is followed by sugar.
Milk-rice mixed with sesame and clarified butter is mentioned, along with bilva and jāti fruits; guggulu is recorded as the tenth.
Barley, ghee, sesame seeds, and rice, as prescribed.
They perform their daily rites, which accomplish their desired fruits.
"One who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge; one who seeks objects of enjoyment obtains an abundance of enjoyments;
and one who seeks desires obtains their fulfillment—thus spoke the Supreme Lord. (6)
Thus, I shall now further explain another method of killing; listen.
At night, one should perform a *homa* in a cremation ground or at a crossroads.
Under a solitary tree on a riverbank, or at the edge of a forest,
[one should perform the rite] with powdered *rājikā* mixed with honey.
O Goddess, one should worship with eight small sticks of fuel together with great oil; indeed, one should arrange them in the shape of a wheel.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one may slay even the gods;
now I shall declare the second [method], and one should commence the fire-rite.
Having prepared a doll from twenty-seven hundred thousand units of alkali, the wise one should cause it to be offered limb by limb every day;
having first applied the mudrā, he may destroy even the gods themselves.
For this reason, O Goddess, the determination of the rite of fire has been declared.
Thus it is said.

Now, the characteristics of the signs: smoke-colored, blue in hue, tawny, accompanied by sparks, and intensely blazing—these are the vehicles for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
The goddess Raudrī is the one who effects withdrawal; she possesses ten qualities of Vaiśvānara.
Now, the characteristic signs are described.
This [flame] will declare: when fumigated, it indicates fear of death;
when blue in color, fear of enemies; when tawny, increase of life-span and all desires;
when emitting sparks, health; when emitting flames, the giver of liberation; when possessing great luster, the attainment of a son.
By the words *havya* and *kavya*, he emits the syllable *su*.
It bestows longevity, health, sovereignty, and the attainment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation;
and by the sounds "caṭa caṭa" used for offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya), knowledge and spiritual attainments are granted.
In the [phase of] withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), it becomes fierce, of terrifying form, and fearsome; it is eyeless and moves about licking [everything].
It [removes] all diseases, ailments, fevers, dysentery, wounds from weapons, and [the suffering of] entering fire.
It becomes golden-colored; thus it grants the accomplishment of all desired aims. Thus, the tenfold merit will be described. || 10 ||
By joining the thumb and the index finger, one obtains the fruit that bestows liberation;
by joining the thumb and the middle finger, the act of enchantment is always performed.
By joining the thumb and the ring finger, one performs the supreme rite of subjugation;
by joining the thumb and the little finger, it becomes the highest rite of eradication.
Through the application of the five fingers, every desire is accomplished;
I shall now describe these characteristics, which must be explained with great effort.
I shall proclaim another [teaching], O Kaulika of exquisite intellect:
the supreme life-force of the Yoginīs, which has never been revealed even with effort.
In the Jyeṣṭhā constellation, one who desires worship shall obtain a vehicle;
whatever vehicle the deity contemplates upon the pedestal, that indeed shall be attained.
Having placed the venerable feet upon the swift vehicle Vātamajaryā, which belongs to the southern direction of the eldest limb, to its south—
In the *Aṇḍalva* [text], the word *śulva* refers to a copper vessel; and for the killing of iron, one should worship the iron as the third [element].
Whatever action obstructs wealth or desire should be honored [as an obstacle] within the context of karma.
Having established the preliminary framework with these three, one should place the liquid upon it and perform the worship with the fivefold offerings.
Having given the mudrā as previously described,

one should worship the vessel of offering (arghapātra) there in the southern direction; then, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at night, one should cause [the deity] to ride upon the back of whichever vehicle he travels.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious, moving or stationary, he beholds;
[he sees] a woman performing her task, clad in red garments and adorned with garlands and ornaments; his consciousness is intoxicated with wine, and he holds a sword and a shield in his hands.
Laughing, singing, and leaping, he should go to the house of the best of heroes;
there, with a mind fixed on remembrance, the wise man should enter the center of the altar.
As many as are the deities of the seven classes, so many gods shall arrive;
one should offer them the arghya water by piercing the left side of one's own body.
And when Khecarī is directly bestowed, that practitioner shall become [a master].

Having fashioned a mandala adorned with red garments, red unguents, and garlands of red flowers, [one should depict] the Heroic Splendor (Vīrabhūti) with a sword in his right hand and holding a severed head in his left; intoxicated by wine and reeling, he wanders about at night.
Khecarī resides in the mouth; one becomes her lord.
Thus ends the establishment of the person (puruṣa).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Fire-Rite Sacrifice," in the commentary on the *Śrī Kālasaṃkarṣaṇīmata*.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
I shall now fully explain the *tilaka*, as well as the methods for its preparation, along with the procedures for collyrium, pills, and so forth, including subjugation and attraction.
O Goddess, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by one who shatters the netherworld (pātāla).
Listen to him.

The beloved eye of the preceptor, the *rādhra* plant, realgar derived from the *pippala* tree, and *manaḥśilā*, combined with the saliva of a horse— by means of this forehead mark (*tilaka*), the world is brought under control.
In the royal court, at gambling, and in battle, one shall be victorious;
beloved by all women, one shall become equal to Kāmadeva.
Indeed, his goals will always be inconceivable and unimpeded. Furthermore, I shall now describe another supreme protective pill.
The wise should cause all these substances— rocanā, saffron, camphor, and sandalwood— to be prepared.
We shall provide an explanation right here: *gorocanā* is well known; *kuṅkuma* is also well known;
by the word "moon" (*candra*), camphor is meant; *malaya* is *śrīkhaṇḍa*, that is, sandalwood from the Malaya mountains.
I shall now describe the fragrant substances and the essence of meat: musk (*mṛganābhi*) and *kaṃbūrikā*;
*kuṇḍagolaka*, which is produced from the union of Śiva and Śakti;
and the *svayaṃbhu* flower, which is the blood from the vulva of a woman during her first menstrual period.
This entire assembly, possessing the consciousness of the bliss of wine, is joined with the form of a hero;
it includes the moon and betel leaf adorned with collyrium for the eyes,
and on the left, the Śakti together with him, reeling with radiant splendor.
With flowers, one should extract the knowledge and cause it to be written upon a very beautiful sheet of gold or silver leaf in the form of golden figures.
Alternatively, one should have [the name] engraved upon a piece of *mālatī* wood, or a peacock feather,
or the tail-feathers of a peacock, using fragrant wood.
First, having drawn a hexagon, a yoni is placed in its center;
outside of that, a sixteen-petaled lotus is given, and the *māyā* (the syllable Hrīm) is likewise applied.
Furthermore, there are thirty-two petals, and on the outside is a square;
upon its back is a trident, provided with the *māyā-aṅkuśa*.
Now hear this supreme and most excellent wheel and its seed-syllable:
in the center of the womb, within the six-spoked [wheel], the central section is bestowed.
Furthermore, the wise one bestows the sixteen digits (kalās);
from the letter 'A' to the final 'A', there are sixteen digits.
In the center of that, however, the Mātṛkā-khaṇḍa is bestowed;
it consists of the letters from *ka* to *ha*, as far as the back of Mount Mandara.
O Queen of the Gods, the section on praise (stuti-khaṇḍa) is located right there on the ivory leaf;
one should fill it with three thousand ten verses, as prescribed for the King.
O Daitya, that Mātṛkā-cakra was first established by Brahmā for the very purpose of creation,
and it is now upheld by Viṣṇu for the sake of slaying the Daityas.
It was formerly worn by Śiva during the subduing of the Asura Tripura;
it was also worn by the guardians of the world for the sake of sovereignty and power.
In a royal court, at a gambling match, in a dispute, or in danger from an enemy;
when a severe fever has arisen, or likewise in a forest or a desolate place.
When great fear has arisen, one shall destroy it; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, I shall explain another auspicious *indrajāla*:
having taken the head of a dog, one should cause it to appear black in color.
One should cause the seeds of *viḍālapada* to be placed upon the back of the head;
having taken the fruit from that [head], one should carefully sow its seeds.
The forms of a dog are indeed real; of this there is no doubt.
Then he will assume the form of a cat and the form of a lizard.
The body may take the form of a tiger, a lion, or an elephant, and it cannot be otherwise;
furthermore, I shall now describe another supreme method for the immobilization of fire.

Gorocanā, the root of *bhṛṅgarāja*, mixed with dates, clarified butter, and saffron— this fivefold divine remedy, possessing incomparable luster when combined with mercury, remains in the mouth and brings about paralysis.
The meaning of this is as follows:
Gorocanā, the root of Bhṛṅgarāja,
and dates mixed with *piṇḍakhajūra*.
The flower of clarified butter, the venerable *kṛśara*,
the remnant of the oblation, the *muṇḍatika* elixir, and mercury— all these,
when placed within a bedstead, produce the incense known as *gagaṇadhūpana*.
One should not discharge urine or feces that have remained in the teeth, nor should one cast them into the mouth or the stomach.
This is the meaning: in what manner does the fire-stambhana (the paralyzing of fire) paralyze the five divine elements?
I shall further proclaim another [rite] for the purpose of subjugation, O fair-faced one: snake-head,
*tagara*, *jana*, *koṣṭha*, *nārīmada*, and the wings of a bee—
when these are properly combined on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, they bring [the person] under control.

From the sky, the moon; the head of a serpent, the nakha-vīta, a piece of tagara, collyrium from the forest, the interior of the *koṣṭha* which is the nature of Brahman, the wing of a bee, the nose, the ear, and the pure tongue are to be taken. Likewise, the wine of women and the semen—thus, by Rudra, with both spheres (*golaka*).
On the first day, he distributes [the portions] according to the rule.
It is processed with woolen cloth and the like;

all medicinal herbs are placed outside of it. On the morning of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the time of sunrise, it is subjected to *puṭapāka* and burned with hidden smoke (*antadhūma*).

The ash should be applied to the back of a young girl; it should be given with half a stone and used to make a sectarian mark (tilaka) together with a ball of clay. Whoever sees the sky [with this] shall bring forth the moon.
Alternatively, one should not perform this practice with the thought that food, drink, man, and woman are for mutual enjoyment; rather,
one should know that it is accompanied by sacrifice and oblation through eight thousand [recitations]— this is the truth, there is no doubt.
I shall further proclaim another supreme incense and collyrium:
garlic, āmalaka, uśīra, saffron, and nāgakeśara.
One should prepare equal parts of *āmrapātra*, *balā*, and *moṭā*,
along with *āmrapatra* and *nāgavuvvudī*.
And with *valā*, *moṭā*, and *rakta*—this incense, the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), brings the king under one's control.
And having gathered *valāmoṭā* as well as the crests of red peacocks, [he should proceed].

On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Nabhas, one should offer a lamp and proceed with the rite. Using a wick made from a dead cotton cloth, one should conceal its wick within a hollowed-out gourd.
Likewise, at night, one should take soot from a lamp of *mahātaila* oil; by this means, one becomes invisible.
They always worship various forms, remaining in vain in their state of *khecaratva* (sovereignty of the sky).
Having traveled a hundred or even a thousand *yojanas*,
if the ritual action is performed by one who has displayed the *mudrā*, [the goal is attained].
The mudrās have been explained previously.
I shall now describe another form that is exceedingly supreme:
on an auspicious lunar mansion, a favorable day, and a beautiful, pleasing month.
Having seized the head of a vulture, one should perform the entire formidable ritual bath;
during the midst of that entire bath, one should meditate upon the head.
And for one month.
There, in the center, one should cast the skull; one month should not be omitted.
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed, one should perform the recitation (japa) eight thousand times.
O Lord, after the Brahmins have been honored with guggulu and the preceptor, the maiden should then honor them;
according to her capacity, she shall give gifts and receive their blessings.
One should cast the skull into the middle of the Varuṇa [element] as far as the range of the quarters;
once the skull has been removed from the Varuṇa, one should place an anthill or sand there.
Having firmly cast the seed-syllable into the word "bhūmi," one should place the golden drop.
One should cast the kanakaphala, the dhuttura fruit, the kṛṣṇaphala, and then the guñjā fruit.
Either red guñjā or adārikā, the seed of the mango tree, or whatever [seed] the practitioner prefers, or what the Guru may recommend;
having cast it into Varuṇa, one should plant a most beautiful tree.
As long as the practitioner holds the fruit,
the goddess— assuming various forms such as a lion, a tiger, or a beast— clearly reveals her face, her mouth, and her form by placing the fruit within her mouth.
Those born from eggs, those born from sweat, those born from a womb, and likewise those born by sprouting.
And just as a stone produced from a sprout is called "manasi."
"Wherever your mind is directed, whether toward movement through the sky or movement upon the earth, there you shall attain success; thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva."
I shall now proclaim another [mantra] by which one may slay this world;
it is obtained through the grace of the Guru, provided that the slender-waisted goddess is directly perceived.
Taking the fruit of the *vanaspati* (lord of the forest) with the four-faced [mantra] and the *sahasra* [mantra]—
the word *vanaspati* being pronounced as *aṭotkaḥ*— and those [fruits] produced in the land of Kashmir,
one should worship the fierce four-faced [deity] during the dark fortnight in an empty house.
And I shall proclaim another mantra by which this world is deluded:
it consists of the word *kuṇḍalākṣam* joined with *yonim*, or else with *dīpakena*.
And that which is to be given is of two kinds, yet [is considered] as one.
Thus, *ha-u* and *haḥ*.

The great mantra of the three goals (trivarga), which resides in the mouths of the Yoginīs, is found together in a single mantra: *haiṃ hūṃ hūḥ*—these are the three syllables. O fair-faced one, by this [mantra], the vessel for the offering (arghapātra) belongs to Viṣṇurasa-ketu.

The Viṣṇu-fluid, the Śiva-water, the heart-cleansing, and the liquefied vehicle— that which flows upon its back and, having gone toward the directions, then utters the sound *hūṃ*. One should draw forth the twelve digits from the bulb (*kanda*) up to the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).
The *ḍākinīs* should bring the vessel for the water offering (*arghapātra*), which is the sun divided by twelve.
The throbbing wealth is said to be the sound of fire;
joined with the bindu at the end of the throat, it extends as far as the sixteenth step.
From the letter *ma* to the letter *sa*, one should extract the sixteen digits of the moon.
The devotion to the Moon belongs to the Ḍākinī; from the west, it is drawn upward.
As long as the universe remains bound together, they employ it for even a single moment.
One should perform neither recitation nor austerity; the sacrificial oblation (caru) is seen with the mouth.
Thus is the mantra of the ḍākinī; now hear the ritual application.
The roots of the *kāka-jaṅghā* plant, the belly of a vulture,
blood from its eye, its bile, and its skin as well.
In this manner, the collyrium should be prepared for the sake of subjugating all people;
even with a single application, it may destroy even the gods.
O you who always delight in worship without the performance of the primary sacrifice,
you shall be cast into the terrible Raurava hell until the dissolution of the earth.
To that extent they suffer there, and afterwards they are born as [low beings];
one should not form an attachment to cattle, like a lamp-bearer with his oil-vessel.
For that many years, O King of Mantras, he shall fall into the terrible Raurava hell and its lower regions,
and in every land he shall wander, speaking ill of ten thousand people.
Having performed the worship of the wheel extensively with offerings of fragrances and the like,
he [attains] the earth and other sacred sites, as well as the entire cosmic egg with all its moving and unmoving beings.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—all are fully satisfied at its conclusion; such is the fruit of that primordial sacrifice.
Down to Kālāgnirudra or up to Śiva above that,
as well as the seven continents and oceans and the fourteen worlds.
And for one who is a Śiva-yogin, that is the fruit of the first sacrifice;
the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, as well as the killing of a cow or even an embryo, are destroyed.
The preceptor, mother, father, brother, and kinsmen are indeed everything;
all sins are destroyed by resorting to the primordial sacrifice.
For him, there shall be the fruits of enjoyment and liberation, as well as good fortune and abundance of wealth;
the three-eyed Lord Hara shall eternally reside in his world, Rudraloka.
Sixty thousand million cows and a maiden are given;
or else, the fruit of that belongs to those who perform the first sacrifice, [the Aśvamedha].
Having formed a heap of sand reaching up to the limit of Śiva,
even if one were to extract each grain individually seven times ten million times over;
They enjoy as many worlds as there are earths and suns;
yet for him, that [merit] reaches exhaustion, whereas the merit of the primordial sacrifice is inexhaustible.
Those who revile the guru, whoever they may be; those who defile the mantras, whoever they may be;
those who defile the sacred seats (pīṭha), whoever they may be; and those who defile the yoginīs.
And whoever reviles heroes, or those who defile Śiva and Śakti,
are cooked in a terrible hell for as long as the earth endures.
For as long as the period of Raurava lasts until the state of Sadāśiva,
there shall be poverty in this world and the destruction of other lineages and families.
Marrow, fat, marrow-fat, testicles, flesh, and blood—one should offer these;
she would destroy the Yoginī known as Manyā along with all her attendants.
To those who are devoted to the Guru, the Devas, and the sacred fire, and who are intent upon mantra and meditation, it should be given there in their midst; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.

Thus ends the commentary titled "The Determination of the Rituals of the Mouth" within the section on the *mātṛkā* of the *mālāmantra* of Pratyaṅgirā, in the venerable *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇīmata* consisting of twenty-four thousand verses.
Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Mahādevī.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the secret that grants all desires:
one is the supreme single-syllable [mantra], and likewise another is the garland-mantra (mālāmantra).
The third is Parāparā, known as Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī;
she is the triple knowledge (vidyātritaya). Listen, for I shall now extract her from this.
There, having raised the *mātrikā* from the sacrificial grass— the *mātrikā* which is the source of all speech—
with its arms uplifted and joined with the head of radiant energy below;

This Vidyā, known as the Mistress of the Seventy Million (Saptakoṭīśvarī), consists of the syllables beginning with Niṣkilikā; it is joined with the letter *nāśa*, marked by a crescent moon upon the head of the excellent person (*supuruṣa*).
O Goddess, one should thereafter place the Mālā-mantra upon the form;
in this Tantra, however, Samaya, Siddhilakṣmī, and Jayadratha [are the deities].
In the *Jhaṃkārabhairava* and the *Caṇḍapratijñā-ḍāmara*,
it is said that the eight deities, beginning with Brahmā, are situated each upon their own meditative seat.
The *māyā* [syllable] consists of four parts, beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*,
just as it was previously indicated in the venerable *Jayadratha-tantra*.
O Goddess, when worshipped as two hundred and ninety letters without distinction, she bestows all accomplishments.
I shall now fully explain the third [syllable], which is the supreme designator of Śivā;
it is known as Kuṇḍalā, joined with fire (R) and adorned with the nasal drop (M).
This is the third supreme [form] established in form;
it is designated as the third Vidyā, auspicious and the performer of all rites.
And this [power] is not joined with the lamp; it is not illuminated at all in its own nature.
The supreme power, intent on the near-meditation (*upadhyāna*), is employed in the path of sound (*nāda*).
From one hundred thousand recitations, success shall arise, bestowing whatever fruits are desired.
One should meditate upon the supreme Ghorā, the terrifying one, who is red and black and fearsome in appearance.
Mounted upon a corpse, emaciated in body, naked, with a distorted face, she was bound by a crown of skulls; she was tawny in color, and her hair rose upward like flames.
The goddess has eighteen arms, is formidable, possesses five faces, and has a slender waist;
she assumes various forms and is adorned with various weapons in her hands.
Mounted upon a red lotus throne, accompanied by a pair of messengers,
Khinkhinī and Śivādūtī are situated on the left and right [sides].
Śivādūtī is the supreme knowledge (parā-vidyā); now learn of Khiṅkinī.
Khiṅkinī, preceded by Māyā and beginning with the Praṇava, ends with "namaḥ."
In the center, the slender-waisted goddess, the bestower of all accomplishments, is meditated upon;
she is endowed with sixteen arms and has a corpse hanging from her ears.
In the left [hands], there is a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a staff, and likewise a bell;
also a noose, a lotus, a shield, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness.
In the right [hands], he holds a sword, a trident, a goad, and a thunderbolt;
as well as a spear, a severed head, a mace, a mallet, and a boon-granting hand.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread—this is your form in its entirety; now hear, O Pārvatī, of your partless form.
That goddess, however, is in the form of sound (nāda), tawny (piṅgalā), following the resonance (dhvāna);
resembling a charcoal fire that has gone out, she is peaceful and established at the crown of the head.
Subtle, in the form of a lamp-flame, stainless and consisting of the nature of will,
she dwells in the center of the Suṣumṇā and the Ḍākinī, having emerged from the splendor of Śiva.
Mounted upon the machine of sound, following after the mouth of Śiva, she is supreme;
O fair-faced one, she has been explained by millions of nameless names.
Having understood the sacrifice to be of such a nature, one should thereafter perform the external worship.
For the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), one meditates on her as red, with the brilliant luster of white vermilion.
Dove-colored for deafness, reddish-white for deluding;
green for causing enmity, O Goddess, and resembling a crow for eradication.
The Goddess, who performs various deeds and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is here;
I shall now describe her mudrā, which strikes fear into all beings.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should remember the Ghorā; one should contemplate her form-mantra, having placed her at the tip of the mouth with the hands joined hollow below.

Having performed that [rite] here with the little finger, and having repeatedly moved the tongue around both lips and the mouth with the index finger, one becomes a Mistress of Mudrās with a distorted face.
The supreme mudrā of these heroes is Mahīvīrā, which bestows accomplishment;
and if one recites [the mantra] correctly and in sequence while enraged at the end of a cave, [success is attained].
For the rites of inciting enmity, killing, pacification, attraction, and likewise for nourishment,
one should perform the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) through the yoga of the five faces.
O Goddess of the Gods, as soon as it is placed, great accomplishment arises upon the earth; however, regarding the garland-mantra, it has been indicated but not revealed.
The great mantras beginning with Bhairava, those consisting of Śiva, Āgama, and Gāruḍa;
the pill, collyrium, incense, and the illusions of Indrajāla and Śambara.
Whether established in coarse or subtle supernatural powers (ṛddhi), one shall go to the city of Śiva after eating;
this is that supreme secret, this is that supreme state.
This is that supreme abode; this is that most wonderful [teaching].
This great knowledge, together with its secret, must be guarded with diligent effort.
He who bestows [a gift] in one way, but it is received in another way—
both of them go to hell for as long as the moon and stars endure.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, it should be given to one's own disciple only after careful examination—
not to an atheist, a rogue, a fool, one who is negligent, one who is corrupted, or one who is lazy.
To one who reviles the guru, the scriptures, and the conduct of the virtuous; to one who delights in quarreling, to a slanderer, a kisser, a base person, a destroyer of the samaya, and a hypocrite.
In the presence of those devoid of courtesy, those who have abandoned virtuous qualities,
the arrogant, or animals, the name of the Goddess must not be uttered, nor should [the offering] be given.
Thus, in the glorious Kuladāmara, the triad of Siddhalakṣmī-mantras is completed in brief.
Oṃ.
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā that accomplishes all aims;
having extracted it from Pattigiri, it is indeed [taught] hereafter, O Great King.
Then, having placed the *mahāśaṅkha* and likewise the *di-uṣāna*,
the *hadumuṇḍa* should then be joined, followed by the word *acālini*.
Having given the *jñāna-mahekarī*, one attains the supreme state;
likewise, having joined the *vivī* and *avi*, one destroys the knot and likewise attains that state.
The supreme is this very place, the abode of yogis;
likewise, the mind and its actions find their footing there, and again, they attain the mountain.
Likewise, having abandoned the *n* and *v*, the nine-syllable [mantra] is illuminated by two;
this seventy-eight-syllable Vidyā resides in the mouths of the Goddesses of Speech.
Having heard that bodiless, supreme speech from the Lotus-born One,
it was then obtained by Nārada— vibrant and granting all desires.
Through the assemblies of perfected ones (siddhas), she was brought down to the earth from Nārada;
Vakrā remains established in the lineage of the crooked succession (vakrakrama).
Thus ends the Prākṛta Siddhalakṣmī Vidyā in the Śrī Mahākullālaka.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī. The illustrious Īśvara said:
e& khphre&! Homage to you, O Great Illusion, who transcends the body and is stainless;
homage to you, O Pratyaṅgirā, Mother of the World, Sovereign Fortune!
The great Gaurī, whose body is color, proceeds according to the will of the practitioner;
the great expansion, whose body is the word, has arisen as the supreme accomplishment.
O Goddess, she who abides within one's own body is known as the *grahā* (seizer) of practitioners;
having pierced through Mahākuṇḍalinī, she pierces the thousand-petalled lotus.
Situated between the iḍā and piṅgalā, she has become the wind, moving through the sky;
she moves within the suṣumnā, which has the form of a lotus fiber.
She who is beyond sound, whose form is not established by sound, who transcends sound, and who is stainless;
she who is to be worshipped in her gross and subtle forms, possessing an inconceivable and unthinkable body.
O Supreme One, beyond the high and the low; O Peaceful One, merged in Brahman, the supreme Śiva;
whose form and conduct are inconceivable, and who bestows the fruit of inconceivable goals.
The Mother of the Universe dwells alone in Karavīra;
she is the eternal bestower of great expansion and the performer of the great assembly.
The Goddess resides in the center of the Bindu, as Kuṭilārdhā and Candrikā;
she is the Goddess whose abode is the Dvādaśānta, dwelling in the sixteen supports.
The channel of consciousness, which permeates cause and effect, resides in the middle;
it is established in nine ways within the great wheel at the root of power.
The supreme goddess is bodiless, yet she exists within the body in the form of the vital breath;
her nature is like the flow of nectar, and her supreme form is the syllable Om.
The Goddess, resembling a flash of lightning, is devoid of existence and non-existence;
she dwells eternally upon the lotus at the end of space, the Supreme Mistress whose form is peace.
Consisting of the three qualities— sattva, rajas,
and tamas— you alone, O Goddess, are the giver of life to all beings.
You alone create the universe, abiding in manifold ways through your divine play;
you are the supreme goddess Mālinī, who is bound to the station of the cremation ground.
O you who pierce the heart and the navel, the beautiful one who pervades all the wheels (*cakras*) and the *vicakras*,
you who are divinely pervasive through the obstruction of the door of the *bindu*— homage be to you!
Resembling ten million suns, more stainless than ten million moons,
more enchanting than ten million Kamadevas, and possessing a form equal to ten million cosmic eggs.
O Great Illusion named Sakala, granter of boons, worshipped by the gods, who art spaceless, appearanceless, stainless, and unrestrained!
O beautiful one, the letter *kha* and the letter *pha* are situated in the fire (*vahnistha*) between two *e*s;
O Śivā, within the groups of letters ending in *m*, they consist of five syllable-clusters (*piṇḍa*).
Coiled like a serpent, O Supreme One, you are the power of resonance (nāda-śakti);
the Goddess resides within the center of the bindu, established in Jālandhara.
She who resides on the seat of the fourth state beyond the musical instruments, established in the Pūrṇa-pīṭha;
she who dwells in desire yet transcends all parts (kalās), known as Kāmā, born from the womb of the Bhaga.
Flowing through the central channel between the forehead and the *brahmagranthi*,
she moves within Śiva, who is all-pervading, subtle, and the great festival of eternal bliss.
O Mistress of Mantras, Knower of Mantras, you who dwell within the corners of consciousness;
eternal one, resting in the five seats, Mistress of Meru, the Excellent One.
She is Khecarī and Bhūcarī, the flow of the three powers;
she is born from the fire at the end of time, the one who brings an end to even the Destroyer of Time.
The twelve mandalas of Kālī are connected to the sequence of Kālikā;
she is the goddess who incinerates the three worlds, and she is the thirteenth form.
In the Great Krama known as the Inexplicable, there are emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal;
its radiance is the venerable Guhyakālī, the Mistress of Nirvāṇa and the Queen of Night.
Jhaṃkāriṇī, Bhairavī, Svarṇakoṭeśvarī,
Śivā, Rājarājeśvarī, Caṇḍā, Aghoreśī, and Niśeśvarī.
Sundarī, Tripurā, Ugratārā, Pūrṇeśvarī,
Jayā, Krameśī, Kubjikā, and Ambikā reside in the center of the Krama-maṇḍala.
Ugracaṇḍikā is known as Kujā through the distinction between the elder and the younger;
Brāhmī, Raudrī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī are those with long noses.
One should worship Vajriṇī, Carcikā, and Lakṣmī as the divine Mothers;
and [the lords] known as Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa, and Unmatta.
Kapālī, the one named Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra as the eighth likewise bestow the fortune of perfection upon devotees and practitioners.
Pratyaṅgirā is proclaimed by Bhairava as Siddhilakṣmī;
she bestows the perfection of prosperity upon devoted practitioners.
O Goddess Pratyaṅgirā, who shatters all the rites of those who harbor hatred toward the practitioner and performs contrary actions, homage be to you!
She who devours everything, including time and the like, as well as the grahas, bhūtas, and ḍākinīs;
the Goddess who protects the practitioner, Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī—homage to her!
The Goddess bestows auspiciousness and protects the world with ease;
I bow here to Pratyaṅgirā, who grants the fulfillment of all that is meditated upon.
I bow to the Goddess Pratyagīrā, the sovereign of kingdoms who bestows the attainment of sovereignty, who is compassionate toward her devotees, and who grants unthought-of perfections.
I pay homage to Pratyaṅgirā, who crushes all enemies, destroys misfortunes and afflictions, is the very fortune of accomplishment, and bestows victory.
I pay homage to the auspicious Pratyaṅgirā, the fierce Kāpālinī, who carries one across the ocean of calamities and bestows supreme nirvāṇa.
I bow down to Pratyaṅgirā, Mahālakṣmī, and Caṇḍakālī, who bestow sovereignty and wealth, and who destroy the afflictions caused by the planets.
I pay homage to Pratyaṅgirā, who crushes wicked enemies, destroys evil planets, bestows the fortune of accomplishment, and grants victory.
I bow to Pratyaṅgirā, who pacifies the evil dreams of the Kali age, destroys great portents, is the very embodiment of the fortune of success, and bestows victory.
I pay homage to Pratyaṅgirā, the nurse who grants inconceivable aims and bestows the fruit of desired objects, for the sake of accomplishing inconceivable purposes.
I pay homage to Pratyaṅgirā, who averts calamities to the kingdom, destroys great misfortunes, is the very embodiment of the fortune of success, and bestows victory.
I bow to Pratyaṅgirā, the mother of kings, the royal fortune who bestows the fruits desired by kings, the goddess of success and prosperity, and the giver of victory.
The great vidyā, the goddess Siddhilakṣmī, who bestows the great siddhis—
whether one recites this hymn named Pratyaṅgirā or causes it to be recited;
By reciting this, one may paralyze or destroy the enemy forces in an instant;
by reciting it, one shall attain success in all inconceivable matters.
It pacifies great faults, destroys great diseases,
[removes] the fear of lions, tigers, and malevolent planets, and destroys all enemies.
O Goddess, this great hymn, which bestows peace, destroys the afflictions of the planets and the dangers of water and fire; those practitioners who shall recite it at the time of worship—
For them, the accomplishment that grants satisfaction to the Goddess is not far off;
however, that which does not exist cannot be accomplished by a Kaulika practitioner of the Kula.
Whatever desire one contemplates, that very thing is accomplished and not otherwise;
this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Great Goddess, for it is indeed equal to the Kaulika [teaching].
Rising at midnight when the lamps are lit in the night, this hymn should be recited; it grants the accomplishment of all that is desired.
Even without the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*), success is achieved through this hymn alone,
provided one recites it before a mandala, an image, or at the front of a mandala.
This great hymn has been proclaimed as the bestower of the accomplishment of inconceivable aims;
it should never be given to those who are devoted to other deities.
It should be given to one endowed with devotion and intent upon the family initiation;
otherwise, they go to Putanā—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the chapter on the Great Hymn to the Goddess Pratyaṅgirā in the glorious Tridaśaḍāmara.
In the year 738, Śrī Kālīdāsa compiled this for the pleasure of the venerable Bhavānīśaṅkara.
This was compiled by Kālīdāsa for the pleasure of Umā and Īśa.
Oṃ, homage to Śivā.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Indeed, Maheśa dwells forever in the Karavīra cremation ground for the benefit of humble beings— a place trodden by the departed—
there he commands the primordial Śrī, who is as white as snow, possesses five faces and ten arms, and is the very embodiment of success and prosperity.
Aiṃ Khphreṃ! Victory, victory, O Mother of the World! You whose lotus-feet are fanned by the fragrant clusters of *mandāra* garlands from the crowns of the gods headed by Harihara and Hiraṇyagarbha;
you who possess the pure moonlight of the Mandākinī flowing from the conch-like hands of the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu and others.

Victory, victory to you, O Mahākālī, destroyer of Time, illuminator of the assembly of the *samaya* circle, Siddhagaṇa-yoginī! When you— who possess a bodily luster as beautiful as a mass of jasmine petals— are being worshipped by a multitude of Vīras, Vidyādharīs, and throngs of sages, what need is there for mere men?
O Karālā, who bestows the fortune of accomplishment upon those who perform rituals; O Virūpākṣā, who dwells within the vision of the Three-eyed One;

O Nandarasadāyikā, Sovereign of the three worlds! You stand amidst a mass of shimmering, priceless jewels and pearls, adorned with earrings of serpents that produce a tinkling *jhaṇajhaṇā* sound like the creepers of a tree.

[She was] adorned with a garland of human skulls smeared with fresh blood, intoxicated by the drinking of fierce gore, and [seated upon] a corpse; her cheeks were made rosy by the mass of her intense radiance which reddened the entire circle of the quarters, and she wore the sun and moon as earrings; her body was slender between a pair of lofty, yellow, firm, jar-like breasts, and she was decorated with a string of human heads dripping with fresh blood.

She who dwells in the cremation ground of the ever-new hero, which resounds with the terrifying sound of the *kalottāla* beat of the *vetālas*' hand-claps, the rhythmic *tāṇḍava* dance of the *tālavas*, and the startled cries of the circle of *naṭa-ḍākinīs* as they traverse it; she who flashes with wonder at the wailing screams of the *piśācas* at the time of universal dissolution.

When the Rudra-skandha and other [centers] have ascended, within the temple of the lotus in the middle of the six supports, the serpent-like power of the Kula-kuṇḍalinī— slumbering yet rising through contraction and expansion—
becomes a lamp of radiant light; she is the blissful, fragrant breeze in the space of the senses.

In the pavilion of precious gems, perfumed by the fragrance of the unguents of moonstone, saffron, agallochum, and musk, and honored by the circle of the Mātṛkās, all the practitioners— whose minds are intent on proceeding to the ocean of nectar from the stream of the lunar orb and whose laughter has arisen— perceive her.

On the mountain of the reddish dawn, which is thick with breezes fragrant and beautiful with various scents— where the moon-fragment ornaments the thighs, where water-lilies and karavīra flowers are gathered, where noble hands hold golden ketakī and fresh mālikā garlands, and where madayantikā and mādhavī vines abound— one should meditate upon his form.
O you with startled, three-eyed gaze, O moving one! Oṃ, victory, victory, O Mother of the World! Victory! Khphreṃ! Victory, victory!

O Mistress of the nine-syllable mantra and the garland of one hundred and ninety syllables! O Kālikā, O Tyāyinī, O Kāpālinī! You who hold a skull-bowl filled with human blood, fat, and flesh, and a sword and trident!

O Goddess of gods, Great Goddess, whose hands are adorned with the *khaṭvāṅga*, bell, skull, noose, goad, boon-granting gesture, and gesture of fearlessness; who sits in the bound hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*); O Sovereign of Siddhas, whose lotus-feet are meditated upon by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and the lords of serpents; O Goddess whose majesty is the manifestation of Śambhu!
O Unnameable One, O You named Umā, O You eternally Full, O You whose name is the shining Star,
O You whose form is the sky throbbing within the womb of the letter A— in that Great Void, O Vyomavāmeśvarī,
Kubjikā, Kṣecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, Śāmbarī, the Power!

O Great Dancer, who transcends the qualities of the wheel, action, will, knowledge, and form; O Eternal One, source of immortal and perpetual enjoyment; O You whose playful grace is the dance at the time of the nine-fold awakening; O You who wear the river of matted locks as Your ornament; O You who possess the full range of poetic arts and a profound intellect regarding the composition of the three qualities.

O Goddess of manifold kinship, beautiful poetry, bestower of perfection, prosperity, intellect, knowledge, honor, and eloquence; O sixteen-syllabled mantra, you who are adorned by the six marks, whose surrounding forest regions are filled with bees drawn by the fragrance of flowers, and who cause the serpent-king to dance— O enemy of the host of adversaries!
